general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which of the following is the earliest ultrastructural change typically seen in reversible hypoxic cell injury?
o: Coagulative necrosis of the whole cell
Cellular and mitochondrial swelling due to failure of ATP-dependent ion pumps
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Hypoxia rapidly depletes ATP, impairing the Na+/K+-ATPase pump, causing influx of sodium and water leading to cellular and organellar (mitochondrial, ER) swelling, the earliest reversible change.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which type of necrosis is characteristic of myocardial infarction, in which the tissue architecture is preserved for several days despite cell death?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Coagulative necrosis, typical of ischemic infarcts in solid organs like the heart and kidney, preserves the basic outline of the tissue architecture despite denaturation of proteins and enzymes.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which type of necrosis is characteristic of the central nervous system following an ischemic stroke?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Brain infarcts undergo liquefactive necrosis due to the high lipid content and autolytic enzyme release, resulting in a cystic, softened area rather than a preserved architecture.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which type of necrosis is characteristically seen in tuberculosis granulomas, appearing grossly as a cheese-like, friable material?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Caseous necrosis, classically seen in tuberculosis, combines features of coagulative and liquefactive necrosis, appearing as a soft, cheese-like, granular material microscopically composed of amorphous debris.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which type of necrosis occurs in acute pancreatitis when lipase acts on peripancreatic fat?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: In acute pancreatitis, released lipases hydrolyze triglycerides in fat cells, and the released fatty acids combine with calcium to form chalky white deposits (saponification), characteristic of fat necrosis.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which type of necrosis is typically seen in the walls of blood vessels in malignant hypertension and some immune-mediated vasculitides?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Fibrinoid necrosis is characterized by deposition of fibrin-like proteinaceous material in vessel walls, seen in malignant hypertension and immune complex-mediated vasculitis.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which reversible morphological change is characterized by intracellular accumulation of triglycerides, commonly seen in hepatocytes with alcohol excess?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Fatty change (steatosis) refers to abnormal intracellular accumulation of triglycerides, commonly seen in the liver with alcohol abuse, obesity, and diabetes, and is typically reversible.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which cellular adaptation refers to a decrease in the size and functional capacity of cells, often due to reduced workload or disuse?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Atrophy is the reduction in cell size and function, occurring in response to disuse, denervation, reduced blood supply, inadequate nutrition, or loss of hormonal stimulation.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which cellular adaptation describes the reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another, such as squamous metaplasia in the bronchial epithelium of smokers?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Metaplasia is a reversible change in which one adult cell type is replaced by another, better able to withstand the altered environment, exemplified by squamous metaplasia in chronically irritated bronchial epithelium.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which cellular adaptation is defined as an increase in the number of cells in an organ or tissue, often in response to hormonal stimulation or compensatory demand?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Hyperplasia refers to increased cell number, occurring physiologically (e.g., breast during pregnancy) or pathologically (e.g., endometrial hyperplasia from excess estrogen).

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which term describes disordered, premalignant cellular growth characterized by variation in cell size and shape, increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and loss of normal maturation, without invasion through the basement membrane?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Dysplasia describes disordered cellular growth with cytological atypia and architectural disorganization, considered a preneoplastic change, distinct from invasive neoplasia because the basement membrane remains intact.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which intracellular organelle is primarily responsible for detoxification of free radicals via catalase, and whose proliferation is stimulated by certain lipid-lowering drugs?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Peroxisomes contain catalase and other oxidative enzymes involved in detoxifying hydrogen peroxide and free radicals; their proliferation can be induced by fibrate drugs, particularly in rodent models.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which mechanism of free radical-induced cell injury involves the peroxidation of unsaturated fatty acids in cell membranes?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Free radicals attack double bonds in unsaturated fatty acids of membrane lipids, triggering an autocatalytic chain reaction (lipid peroxidation) that damages membrane integrity.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which enzyme system serves as an important intracellular antioxidant defense, converting superoxide radicals into hydrogen peroxide?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide anion (O2-) into hydrogen peroxide and oxygen, an important step in cellular antioxidant defense, with catalase and glutathione peroxidase subsequently detoxifying hydrogen peroxide.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which morphological nuclear change in necrosis refers to fragmentation of the nucleus into small, scattered basophilic particles?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Karyorrhexis refers to fragmentation of a pyknotic nucleus into multiple small basophilic fragments, one of the sequential nuclear changes seen in necrosis, following pyknosis and preceding karyolysis.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which type of cell death is characterized by cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, and formation of membrane-bound apoptotic bodies, without eliciting an inflammatory response?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Apoptosis is a regulated, energy-dependent form of cell death characterized by cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, and formation of apoptotic bodies that are phagocytosed without triggering inflammation, unlike necrosis.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which family of cysteine proteases plays the central executioner role in the apoptotic pathway?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Caspases are a family of cysteine-aspartate proteases that mediate the initiation and execution phases of apoptosis, cleaving key cellular substrates leading to the characteristic morphological changes.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which apoptotic pathway is triggered by withdrawal of growth factors or DNA damage, and is regulated by the balance of pro- and anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins at the mitochondrial membrane?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: The intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis is triggered by internal cellular stress such as DNA damage or growth factor withdrawal, and is regulated by BCL-2 family proteins controlling mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and cytochrome c release.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which apoptotic pathway involves binding of ligands such as FAS ligand or TNF to their respective cell-surface death receptors?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: The extrinsic pathway is initiated by binding of death ligands (e.g., FasL, TNF) to death receptors on the cell surface, leading to formation of a death-inducing signaling complex and activation of initiator caspases.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which pigment, a golden-brown, granular intracellular material derived from lipid peroxidation of membranes, accumulates in aging or atrophic cells and is often called 'wear and tear' pigment?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Lipofuscin is an insoluble, brownish-yellow pigment composed of lipid-protein complexes derived from free radical-mediated peroxidation of membrane lipids, accumulating with aging and considered a marker of past free radical injury.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which pigment represents an iron-storage complex that accumulates within macrophages after breakdown of hemoglobin, particularly evident in conditions of local or systemic iron overload?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Hemosiderin is a hemoglobin-derived, golden-brown, granular pigment representing aggregates of ferritin, accumulating in macrophages during states of local hemorrhage or systemic iron overload (hemosiderosis).

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which term describes pathological calcification occurring in dead or dying tissue, in the setting of normal serum calcium levels?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Dystrophic calcification occurs locally in areas of necrosis or degenerating tissue despite normal serum calcium levels, commonly seen in atherosclerotic plaques, damaged heart valves, and caseous necrosis of tuberculosis.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which term describes pathological calcification occurring in otherwise normal tissues, as a consequence of hypercalcemia from disorders such as hyperparathyroidism?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues secondary to hypercalcemia (e.g., from hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D toxicity, or renal failure), depositing calcium salts in tissues such as kidney, lung, and gastric mucosa.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which abnormal protein accumulation, composed of extracellular fibrillar deposits with a characteristic beta-pleated sheet configuration, can be identified by apple-green birefringence under polarized light after Congo red staining?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Amyloid is an extracellular, fibrillar protein deposit with a beta-pleated sheet secondary structure; Congo red staining shows characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarized light, a key diagnostic feature.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which type of cellular swelling, also called hydropic change, is an early, reversible manifestation of cell injury characterized by accumulation of water within the cytoplasm?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Hydropic (vacuolar) degeneration refers to intracellular accumulation of water due to failure of ion and volume regulation, often the earliest reversible morphological sign of cell injury.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which term is used for a localized area of coagulative necrosis resulting from ischemia in a solid organ, such as the kidney or spleen?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: An infarct is a localized area of ischemic (coagulative) necrosis caused by occlusion of either the arterial supply or the venous drainage of a particular tissue.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which type of infarct is typically seen in organs with a dual blood supply or extensive collateral circulation, such as the lung or liver?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Hemorrhagic (red) infarcts occur in organs with dual blood supply or loose, collateral circulation (e.g., lung, intestine) or venous occlusion, where blood re-enters the necrotic area, and in loosely organized tissues.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which type of infarct is typically seen in solid organs with end-arterial circulation, such as the spleen, kidney, and heart?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Anemic (white) infarcts occur in solid organs with end-arterial (single) blood supply, such as the heart, kidney, and spleen, where arterial occlusion prevents blood from re-entering the infarcted zone.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which term describes necrosis complicated by superimposed bacterial infection and putrefaction, typically affecting the lower limb or bowel?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Wet gangrene occurs when coagulative necrosis is complicated by bacterial infection and liquefactive changes, producing a foul-smelling, edematous, and rapidly spreading lesion, in contrast to the mummified appearance of dry gangrene.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which cellular structure, when it accumulates undigested material within a lysosome-derived vacuole, forms a residual body seen in conditions such as lipofuscinosis?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Residual bodies represent undigested cellular debris remaining within secondary lysosomes/autophagolysosomes after incomplete digestion, and their accumulation is linked to lipofuscin formation in aging or diseased cells.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which term describes an increase in the size of individual cells, resulting in an increase in the size of the affected organ, often as a compensatory response to increased workload?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Hypertrophy refers to an increase in cell size (not number), leading to increased organ size, classically seen in cardiac myocytes responding to chronic pressure overload (e.g., hypertension).

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which mechanism best explains reperfusion injury following restoration of blood flow to previously ischemic tissue?
o: Sudden depletion of ATP with no further injury
Complete cessation of all cellular metabolism
Immediate and total recovery of function without further injury
Generation of reactive oxygen species by returning neutrophils and other sources, causing additional oxidative damage
Loss of all inflammatory mediators upon reperfusion
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Reperfusion injury results from generation of reactive oxygen species by infiltrating neutrophils, activation of complement, and calcium influx during reperfusion, causing additional injury beyond that produced by ischemia alone.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which of the following best describes the role of intracellular calcium accumulation in the pathogenesis of irreversible cell injury?
o: Sustained elevation of cytosolic calcium activates phospholipases, proteases, and endonucleases that damage cellular components
Calcium influx has no role in irreversible injury
Calcium accumulation always protects the cell from injury
Only extracellular calcium depletion, not intracellular accumulation, is relevant to injury
Calcium is exclusively involved in blood clotting, unrelated to cell injury
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Sustained increases in cytosolic calcium, resulting from damaged membranes and impaired calcium extrusion/sequestration, activate a variety of enzymes (ATPases, phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases) that cause further cellular damage, contributing to irreversibility of injury.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which point in cell injury is generally considered the 'point of no return', beyond which the cell cannot recover even if the original insult is removed?
o: Any degree of ATP depletion, however mild
Point of irreversibility, marked by severe mitochondrial dysfunction (e.g., high-amplitude swelling, mitochondrial permeability transition) and extensive membrane damage
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: The transition from reversible to irreversible injury is marked by severe mitochondrial dysfunction, including high-amplitude swelling and the mitochondrial permeability transition, along with extensive plasma and lysosomal membrane damage.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which of the following histological features is a hallmark of coagulative necrosis on light microscopy?
o: Preservation of the basic cellular outline with loss of nuclear detail (ghost cells) due to protein denaturation
Complete loss of tissue architecture with liquefaction
Marked fatty infiltration of the tissue
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: In coagulative necrosis, denaturation of structural and enzymatic proteins predominates over enzymatic digestion, preserving the basic tissue architecture (as 'ghost outlines') for some days despite loss of nuclear detail.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which term describes a form of physiological hyperplasia occurring in the endometrium and breast tissue in response to normal hormonal cycling?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Hormonal hyperplasia is a physiological process seen in tissues such as the endometrium (under estrogen influence) and breast (during pregnancy/lactation), representing normal proliferative responses to hormonal stimulation.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which of the following mechanisms is primarily responsible for cell injury caused by carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) toxicity, a classic model of chemical injury?
o: Osmotic lysis due to excess extracellular water
Direct inhibition of DNA replication only
Conversion to a free radical (CCl3•) by cytochrome P450, causing lipid peroxidation of the endoplasmic reticulum and other membranes
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: CCl4 is converted by hepatic cytochrome P450 to the highly reactive free radical CCl3•, which initiates autocatalytic lipid peroxidation of the endoplasmic reticulum and other membranes, leading to fatty change and cell injury.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which of the following best distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis in terms of the surrounding tissue's inflammatory response?
o: Both apoptosis and necrosis always provoke a brisk inflammatory response
Necrosis never provokes inflammation, only apoptosis does
Apoptosis typically does not provoke inflammation, since cell contents are not released into the extracellular space; necrosis typically provokes inflammation due to leakage of cellular contents
Neither process is ever associated with inflammation
Inflammation occurs only if the necrotic tissue is infected, but never with sterile necrosis
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Because apoptotic cells maintain membrane integrity and are rapidly phagocytosed as intact apoptotic bodies, they do not typically trigger inflammation, whereas necrosis involves membrane rupture and release of cellular contents that provoke an inflammatory response.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which vitamin/cofactor deficiency classically impairs collagen synthesis by preventing hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues, contributing to poor wound healing and a bleeding tendency?
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Vitamin C is an essential cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase enzymes required for stable collagen triple-helix formation; its deficiency (scurvy) impairs wound healing and increases vascular fragility.

general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.s: Which best describes the concept of 'accumulation' in the context of intracellular substances, as distinguished from adaptation?
o: Accumulation refers only to extracellular deposits, never intracellular
Accumulation never occurs in normal physiological states

Accumulation refers to abnormal buildup of substances such as lipids, proteins, glycogen, or pigments within cells, which may be harmless or may impair cellular function depending on the amount and substance
general-and-systemic-pathology/cell-inju.e: Intracellular accumulations represent buildup of substances (endogenous or exogenous) that a cell cannot immediately metabolize or eliminate; the clinical significance ranges from incidental to functionally significant, depending on the substance and degree.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which vascular event occurs first in acute inflammation, immediately following injury?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Acute inflammation begins with a transient vasoconstriction lasting seconds, followed by vasodilation of arterioles, increasing blood flow to the area (causing redness and heat).

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which mechanism primarily accounts for the formation of exudate (protein-rich fluid) in acute inflammation?
o: Increased vascular permeability allowing plasma proteins to leak into the interstitium
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Increased vascular permeability, mediated by endothelial cell contraction and other mechanisms, allows protein-rich fluid (exudate) to leak from vessels into the interstitial space, a hallmark of acute inflammation.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which cell type is the dominant leukocyte in the first 24 hours of acute inflammation?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Neutrophils are the first responders in acute inflammation, typically predominating in the first 6-24 hours, later replaced by monocytes/macrophages.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which adhesion molecule pair mediates the initial 'rolling' of leukocytes along the endothelium during the leukocyte extravasation cascade?
o: Selectins (P-selectin, E-selectin) on endothelium with sialylated Lewis X on leukocytes
Integrins on leukocytes with ICAM-1 on endothelium
Cadherins on both leukocytes and endothelium
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Selectins expressed on activated endothelium (P-selectin, E-selectin) bind sialylated Lewis X-modified glycoproteins on leukocytes, mediating the initial rolling step of the leukocyte adhesion cascade.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which step in the leukocyte adhesion cascade follows rolling and is mediated by firm binding of leukocyte integrins to endothelial ICAM-1/VCAM-1?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Following rolling, chemokine-induced activation of leukocyte integrins increases their affinity for endothelial ICAM-1 and VCAM-1, resulting in firm adhesion (arrest) of the leukocyte to the endothelium.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which term describes the directed migration of leukocytes toward a chemical gradient at the site of injury?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Chemotaxis is the process by which leukocytes migrate along a concentration gradient of chemoattractants (e.g., bacterial products, complement C5a, leukotriene B4, chemokines) toward the site of injury.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which of the following is a well-known chemotactic factor derived from the complement system?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: C5a is a potent chemotactic factor for neutrophils generated during complement activation, also possessing anaphylatoxin activity that increases vascular permeability.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which process involves coating of a microorganism with molecules (opsonins) such as IgG or C3b to enhance phagocytosis?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Opsonization refers to the coating of particles (e.g., bacteria) with opsonins like IgG antibody or complement C3b, which are recognized by specific receptors on phagocytes, greatly enhancing phagocytic efficiency.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which of the following mediators is primarily responsible for the pain (dolor) experienced in acute inflammation?
o: Prostaglandins (particularly PGE2) sensitizing nerve endings to painful stimuli
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Prostaglandins, particularly PGE2, sensitize nociceptive nerve endings to painful stimuli and act synergistically with bradykinin, contributing significantly to inflammatory pain.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which class of drugs reduces inflammation and pain by inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes, thereby blocking prostaglandin synthesis?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase enzymes (COX-1 and/or COX-2), blocking the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins, thereby reducing inflammation, pain, and fever.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which lipid mediator class, derived from arachidonic acid via the lipoxygenase pathway, is a potent chemotactic agent for neutrophils?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Leukotriene B4, produced via the 5-lipoxygenase pathway, is a potent chemoattractant and activator of neutrophils, promoting their adhesion and aggregation at sites of inflammation.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which cytokine is a major mediator of fever during infection or inflammation, acting on the hypothalamus to raise the thermoregulatory set point?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: IL-1 and TNF act as endogenous pyrogens, stimulating hypothalamic production of prostaglandin E2, which resets the thermoregulatory set point higher, producing fever.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which type of inflammatory exudate is characterized by high protein content, numerous neutrophils, and is often associated with pyogenic bacterial infection?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Purulent (suppurative) exudate, or pus, contains large numbers of neutrophils, necrotic cell debris, and edema fluid, characteristically produced in response to pyogenic bacteria such as Staphylococcus.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which term describes a localized collection of pus surrounded by inflamed tissue?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: An abscess is a localized collection of pus within a cavity formed by tissue necrosis, typically surrounded by a wall of inflammatory cells and fibrous tissue in chronic cases.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which type of chronic inflammation is characterized by the formation of organized collections of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), often with multinucleated giant cells, in response to persistent but poorly degradable antigens such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Granulomatous inflammation is a specialized pattern of chronic inflammation featuring aggregates of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells), often with Langhans-type giant cells, classically seen in tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, and fungal infections.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which type of giant cell, characterized by nuclei arranged peripherally in a horseshoe pattern, is classically associated with tuberculous granulomas?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Langhans giant cells, formed by fusion of epithelioid macrophages with nuclei arranged peripherally in a horseshoe or circular pattern, are characteristically seen in tuberculous and other granulomas.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which phase of wound healing is characterized by formation of granulation tissue, composed of proliferating fibroblasts and new capillaries (angiogenesis)?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: The proliferative phase of wound healing, occurring after the initial inflammatory phase, is characterized by fibroblast proliferation, collagen deposition, and angiogenesis, forming granulation tissue.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which growth factor is a major stimulus for angiogenesis (formation of new blood vessels) during wound healing?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: VEGF is a key mediator of angiogenesis, stimulating endothelial cell proliferation and migration to form new capillaries essential for granulation tissue formation during wound healing.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which type of wound healing occurs when a clean, surgically incised wound is closed primarily with sutures, resulting in minimal scar formation?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Healing by primary intention occurs in clean, approximated wound edges (e.g., surgical incisions), involving minimal tissue loss, a small amount of granulation tissue, and a fine scar.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which type of wound healing occurs in wounds with significant tissue loss, gaping edges, or infection, requiring a larger amount of granulation tissue and wound contraction?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Healing by secondary intention occurs when wound edges are not approximated (large defects, infected wounds, or significant tissue loss), requiring more extensive granulation tissue formation, wound contraction (via myofibroblasts), and a larger scar.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which cell type, a specialized contractile fibroblast expressing smooth muscle actin, is primarily responsible for wound contraction during secondary intention healing?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Myofibroblasts, which express smooth muscle actin and have contractile properties, are responsible for wound contraction, reducing the size of the wound defect during healing by secondary intention.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which factor is essential for cross-linking of collagen fibrils, contributing to the tensile strength gained during wound maturation?
o: Lysyl oxidase-mediated collagen cross-linking (requiring copper as a cofactor)
Zinc alone, with no enzymatic role
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Lysyl oxidase, a copper-dependent enzyme, catalyzes cross-linking between collagen fibrils, which progressively increases the tensile strength of a healing wound over weeks to months.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which complication of wound healing refers to excessive collagen deposition that remains within the boundaries of the original wound?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: A hypertrophic scar results from excessive collagen deposition confined to the boundaries of the original wound, in contrast to a keloid, which extends beyond the original wound margins.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which complication of wound healing refers to excessive scar tissue that extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound and tends to recur after excision?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: A keloid is an exuberant scar that extends beyond the original wound margins, results from excessive collagen (particularly type III initially, then type I) synthesis, and has a higher recurrence rate after excision, more common in individuals with darker skin pigmentation.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which local factor most significantly impairs wound healing by reducing oxygen delivery to the healing tissue?
o: Poor local blood supply/ischemia (e.g., in peripheral vascular disease)
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Adequate blood supply is essential for delivering oxygen and nutrients required for collagen synthesis and cellular proliferation; ischemia (e.g., from peripheral vascular disease) significantly impairs wound healing.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which systemic condition is well known to impair wound healing through multiple mechanisms including microvascular disease, impaired neutrophil function, and reduced collagen synthesis?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Diabetes mellitus impairs wound healing through microvascular disease reducing tissue perfusion, impaired neutrophil chemotaxis and function, and reduced collagen synthesis and cross-linking.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which of the following inflammatory mediators is stored preformed in mast cell granules and is responsible for the immediate increase in vascular permeability seen in acute inflammation?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Histamine, stored preformed in mast cell (and basophil/platelet) granules, is released rapidly upon degranulation and causes immediate vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, the earliest chemical mediator response.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which plasma protein cascade, when activated, generates products such as C3a, C5a (anaphylatoxins) and the membrane attack complex, playing roles in both vascular changes and direct microbial lysis?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: The complement system, activated via classical, alternative, or lectin pathways, generates anaphylatoxins (C3a, C5a) that increase vascular permeability and recruit leukocytes, and forms the membrane attack complex (C5b-9) that can directly lyse target cells.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which plasma-derived mediator, generated by the kinin system, causes pain, vasodilation, and increased vascular permeability, similar to histamine?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Bradykinin, generated via activation of the kinin system (Hageman factor/Factor XII pathway), causes vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and pain, similar in effect to histamine but with a slightly delayed onset.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which term describes the process by which tissue that cannot regenerate is replaced by fibrous (scar) tissue after injury?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Repair refers to the replacement of damaged tissue by fibrous connective tissue (scar formation), occurring when the tissue's regenerative capacity is exceeded or the tissue is composed of cells with limited/no regenerative capacity (e.g., cardiac myocytes, neurons).

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which of the following cell types is classified as labile, meaning it continuously divides and regenerates throughout life, such as epithelial cells of the skin and gut?
o: Labile cells (e.g., epidermis, gut epithelium, bone marrow)
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Labile cells, including epidermal keratinocytes, gastrointestinal epithelium, and hematopoietic bone marrow cells, continuously proliferate throughout life to replace cells lost through normal turnover or injury, allowing complete regeneration if the supporting stroma is intact.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which of the following cell types is classified as permanent, meaning it has essentially no capacity to regenerate after injury and is replaced by scar tissue instead?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Permanent cells such as cardiac myocytes and mature neurons have left the cell cycle and cannot regenerate after injury, so damaged tissue in these organs is repaired by fibrous scar formation rather than functional regeneration.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which of the following cell types is classified as stable (quiescent), normally in the G0 phase but capable of re-entering the cell cycle and proliferating in response to injury, such as hepatocytes?
o: Stable (quiescent) cells (e.g., hepatocytes, renal tubular cells)
Only stem cells, not differentiated cells
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Stable cells, such as hepatocytes and renal tubular epithelial cells, are normally quiescent (G0) but retain the capacity to re-enter the cell cycle and proliferate in response to injury or loss of tissue mass, exemplified by liver regeneration.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which chemical mediator, generated from arachidonic acid via the cyclooxygenase pathway, is a potent vasodilator and inhibitor of platelet aggregation, produced mainly by vascular endothelium?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Prostacyclin (PGI2), synthesized predominantly by vascular endothelial cells, is a potent vasodilator and inhibitor of platelet aggregation, functioning in balance with platelet-derived thromboxane A2 (a vasoconstrictor and platelet aggregator) to regulate vascular tone and hemostasis.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which term is used for the histological pattern in which pus accumulates beneath an epithelial or mucosal surface, distending and lifting it, such as in the appendix or gallbladder?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Empyema refers to accumulation of pus within a pre-existing anatomical cavity or hollow viscus (e.g., pleural cavity, gallbladder), as distinguished from an abscess, which is a localized collection of pus within a newly formed cavity in solid tissue.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which cytokine, produced by activated macrophages and other cells, is a major mediator that both promotes acute inflammation and, when chronically elevated, contributes to cachexia in chronic disease?
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: TNF-alpha, produced mainly by activated macrophages, mediates local inflammatory effects (endothelial activation, fever, acute-phase response) and, with chronic elevation, contributes to systemic muscle and fat wasting (cachexia) seen in chronic disease and malignancy.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which of the following best describes the acute-phase response seen during systemic inflammation, mediated substantially by IL-6 acting on the liver?
o: Decreased hepatic synthesis of all plasma proteins
Complete cessation of hepatic protein synthesis
Selective increase only in albumin synthesis
Increased hepatic synthesis of proteins such as C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, and serum amyloid A, along with fever and leukocytosis
No changes in liver protein synthesis during inflammation
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: The acute-phase response, driven substantially by IL-6 (along with IL-1 and TNF), induces hepatic synthesis of acute-phase reactants such as C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, and serum amyloid A, along with fever and neutrophilic leukocytosis, as a systemic response to inflammation.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which of the following best describes the role of C-reactive protein (CRP) as a clinical marker?
o: It is a nonspecific acute-phase reactant that rises in response to inflammation from various causes, including infection, tissue injury, and some malignancies
It is a specific marker for viral infections only
It is only elevated in autoimmune disease, never in infection
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: CRP is a nonspecific acute-phase protein whose serum levels rise in response to a wide variety of inflammatory stimuli, useful as a general marker of inflammation but not diagnostic of any single specific condition.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which of the following best explains why chronic inflammation, rather than resolving, can persist for weeks to years in certain conditions?
o: Chronic inflammation always resolves within days regardless of the underlying cause
Persistent infection, prolonged exposure to a toxic or foreign agent, or an autoimmune reaction against self-antigens sustains the inflammatory process
Chronic inflammation is caused exclusively by physical trauma
Only neutrophils are involved in chronic inflammation, allowing rapid resolution
Chronic inflammation cannot occur without a preceding acute phase
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Chronic inflammation persists when the causative stimulus is not eliminated, such as ongoing infection, continued exposure to an exogenous or endogenous toxic agent, or an autoimmune response perpetuating tissue damage and repair simultaneously.

general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.s: Which of the following best describes the role of platelet-activating factor (PAF) in inflammation?
o: It has no role in inflammation
It is produced exclusively by hepatocytes
It functions solely as an anticoagulant
It causes vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, platelet aggregation, and leukocyte activation, acting at very low concentrations
general-and-systemic-pathology/inflammat.e: Platelet-activating factor is a potent phospholipid mediator, active at extremely low concentrations, causing vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, platelet aggregation, and leukocyte activation and adhesion during inflammation.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which term describes a benign neoplasm arising from glandular epithelium?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: An adenoma is a benign tumor of glandular epithelial origin; malignant counterparts arising from glandular epithelium are termed adenocarcinomas.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which term describes a malignant neoplasm arising from mesenchymal (connective) tissue such as bone, muscle, or fat?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Sarcomas are malignant tumors of mesenchymal origin (e.g., osteosarcoma from bone, liposarcoma from fat, leiomyosarcoma from smooth muscle), in contrast to carcinomas, which arise from epithelial tissue.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which term describes a malignant neoplasm arising from epithelial tissue?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Carcinoma refers to malignant tumors of epithelial origin, further subclassified as adenocarcinoma (glandular) or squamous cell carcinoma (squamous epithelium), among others.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best describes the term 'anaplasia' in the context of tumor pathology?
o: Complete loss of differentiation, with cells bearing little resemblance to their tissue of origin, a hallmark of high-grade malignancy
A term applied only to benign tumors
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Anaplasia refers to a lack of differentiation, characterized by pleomorphism, abnormal nuclear morphology, high mitotic activity, and loss of normal tissue architecture, features associated with aggressive, high-grade malignant tumors.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which term describes the spread of tumor cells to a distant site, forming a secondary tumor discontinuous with the primary tumor?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Metastasis refers to the spread of tumor cells from the primary site to distant tissues, forming secondary tumor deposits, and is a defining feature of malignancy (benign tumors do not metastasize).

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which route of metastatic spread is most common for carcinomas (epithelial malignancies)?
o: Direct seeding of body cavities exclusively
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Carcinomas most commonly metastasize initially via lymphatic channels to regional lymph nodes, although hematogenous spread also occurs, particularly in later stages.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which route of metastatic spread is most characteristic of sarcomas (mesenchymal malignancies)?
o: Only local invasion, never distant spread
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Sarcomas characteristically metastasize via the hematogenous route, commonly to the lungs, in contrast to carcinomas which favor lymphatic spread initially.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which term describes a preinvasive stage of malignant epithelial neoplasia in which abnormal cells are confined within the epithelium without breaching the basement membrane?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Carcinoma in situ represents a preinvasive stage in which malignant-appearing cells occupy the full thickness of the epithelium but have not yet invaded through the basement membrane, and is considered curable by local excision if detected.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which class of genes, when activated by mutation, amplification, or translocation, drives uncontrolled cell proliferation and contributes to carcinogenesis (e.g., RAS, MYC, HER2/neu)?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Proto-oncogenes are normal genes that regulate cell growth; when activated by mutation, amplification, or chromosomal translocation, they become oncogenes that drive uncontrolled cellular proliferation, as with RAS mutations or HER2/neu amplification.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which tumor suppressor gene, often called the 'guardian of the genome,' is mutated in the majority of human cancers and is central to the Li-Fraumeni syndrome?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: TP53 encodes the p53 protein, which regulates cell cycle arrest, DNA repair, and apoptosis in response to DNA damage; its loss of function is one of the most common genetic events in human cancer and underlies Li-Fraumeni syndrome when inherited in mutant form.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which tumor suppressor gene, when mutated in the germline, predisposes to retinoblastoma and osteosarcoma, and exemplifies Knudson's 'two-hit' hypothesis?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: RB1 was the first tumor suppressor gene identified, and hereditary retinoblastoma (with a germline first hit and somatic second hit) provided the basis for Knudson's two-hit hypothesis of tumor suppressor gene inactivation.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which tumor suppressor gene mutation, associated with familial adenomatous polyposis, leads to numerous colonic adenomatous polyps with a high risk of progression to colorectal carcinoma?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Germline mutations in the APC gene cause familial adenomatous polyposis, characterized by hundreds to thousands of colonic adenomatous polyps, virtually all patients developing colorectal cancer if untreated.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which pair of genes, when mutated in the germline, are most strongly associated with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer syndrome?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes involved in DNA double-strand break repair; germline mutations markedly increase lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best describes the concept of tumor grade?
o: The anatomical extent of tumor spread
The size of the primary tumor only
A measure of the degree of differentiation of tumor cells, reflecting how closely they resemble their tissue of origin
The presence or absence of distant metastasis
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Tumor grade reflects the degree of cellular differentiation and mitotic activity, ranging from well-differentiated (low grade) to poorly differentiated/anaplastic (high grade), correlating with aggressiveness.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best describes the concept of tumor stage?
o: The mitotic count per high-power field
The anatomical extent of tumor spread, typically assessed using the TNM system (tumor size, nodal involvement, metastasis)
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Tumor stage describes the anatomical extent of disease spread, most commonly using the TNM classification (T = primary tumor size/extent, N = regional lymph node involvement, M = distant metastasis), and is generally a stronger prognostic indicator than grade.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which tumor marker is most classically associated with hepatocellular carcinoma and certain germ cell tumors?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Alpha-fetoprotein is a well-established tumor marker elevated in hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk sac (endodermal sinus) tumors, useful for diagnosis, monitoring, and detecting recurrence.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which tumor marker is most classically associated with epithelial ovarian carcinoma?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: CA-125 is a widely used tumor marker for epithelial ovarian cancer, useful for monitoring treatment response and detecting recurrence, though it lacks sufficient specificity for population screening.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which tumor marker is most closely associated with prostate carcinoma and used for both screening and monitoring?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: PSA, a serine protease produced by prostatic epithelium, is elevated in prostate cancer (also in benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostatitis), used clinically for screening (with limitations) and monitoring treatment response.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best describes the Warburg effect observed in many cancer cells?
o: Increased dependence on oxidative phosphorylation even in the presence of oxygen
Exclusive reliance on fatty acid oxidation
A preference for aerobic glycolysis (increased glucose uptake and lactate production) even in the presence of adequate oxygen
Absence of any altered metabolism in cancer cells
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: The Warburg effect describes the tendency of cancer cells to favor aerobic glycolysis, converting glucose to lactate even when oxygen is available, providing metabolic intermediates for rapid biosynthesis and forming the basis for FDG-PET imaging of tumors.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best describes the process of angiogenesis in tumor growth and its clinical significance?
o: Tumors never require new blood vessel formation
Tumors beyond a small size require formation of new blood vessels (often via VEGF) to receive adequate oxygen and nutrients for continued growth, making anti-angiogenic therapy a treatment strategy
Angiogenesis inhibits rather than promotes tumor growth
Tumor angiogenesis is identical in mechanism to normal wound healing angiogenesis with no therapeutic relevance
Tumors obtain all nutrients by diffusion regardless of size
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Once a tumor exceeds roughly 1-2 mm in diameter, diffusion alone is inadequate, so tumors induce angiogenesis (often via VEGF secretion) to establish a blood supply supporting continued growth, providing the rationale for anti-angiogenic drugs like bevacizumab.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best explains the concept of tumor cell heterogeneity and its clinical implication for treatment resistance?
o: All cells within a tumor are genetically identical, ensuring uniform treatment response
Heterogeneity applies only to benign tumors
Heterogeneity has no bearing on treatment outcomes
Tumors often consist of genetically diverse subclones, some of which may be resistant to a given therapy, allowing selection of resistant clones during treatment
Tumor heterogeneity decreases as tumors progress
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Tumor progression generates genetically diverse subclones within a single tumor; treatment can select for resistant subclones, contributing to relapse and treatment failure, an important concept in modern oncology.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following viruses is most strongly associated with the development of cervical carcinoma?
o: Human papillomavirus (HPV), particularly high-risk types 16 and 18
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: High-risk HPV types, particularly 16 and 18, are causally linked to the vast majority of cervical carcinomas, with viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 inactivating p53 and RB tumor suppressor proteins respectively.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which virus is most strongly associated with the development of hepatocellular carcinoma, particularly in regions of high endemic prevalence?
o: Hepatitis B virus (and hepatitis C virus)
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Chronic hepatitis B and hepatitis C viral infections are major risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma, acting through chronic inflammation, cirrhosis, and, in the case of HBV, direct genomic integration.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: EBV is associated with several malignancies including Burkitt lymphoma (via MYC translocation cooperation), nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and certain lymphomas in immunosuppressed patients.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which chemical/environmental carcinogen is most strongly linked to the development of bronchogenic (lung) carcinoma?
o: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and other carcinogens in tobacco smoke
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Tobacco smoke contains numerous carcinogens, including polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and nitrosamines, and is the leading cause of lung cancer, with a well-established dose-response relationship.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which occupational carcinogen exposure is classically associated with malignant mesothelioma of the pleura?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Asbestos fiber exposure, particularly in occupational settings (e.g., shipbuilding, insulation work), is strongly associated with malignant mesothelioma, as well as increased risk of bronchogenic carcinoma, with a long latency period.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which fungal-derived toxin, found as a contaminant in improperly stored grains and nuts, is a known risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, especially synergistic with hepatitis B infection?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Aflatoxin B1, produced by Aspergillus flavus and related fungi contaminating stored grains and nuts, is a potent hepatocarcinogen that causes characteristic TP53 mutations and acts synergistically with chronic hepatitis B infection to increase hepatocellular carcinoma risk.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best describes the term 'field cancerization,' relevant to head and neck and other epithelial cancers?
o: Widespread exposure of an epithelial surface to a carcinogen (e.g., tobacco) leading to multiple independent, genetically altered clones with potential for multiple primary tumors across the exposed field
A single isolated mutation causing cancer at one specific point
A term referring only to metastatic spread
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Field cancerization describes the phenomenon whereby an entire epithelial surface exposed to a carcinogen (e.g., the aerodigestive tract mucosa in smokers) accumulates multiple independent genetic alterations, predisposing to multiple, separate primary tumors and local recurrences distinct from true metastasis.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best distinguishes benign from malignant neoplasms in terms of growth pattern?
o: Malignant tumors are always encapsulated, benign tumors are not
Both benign and malignant tumors always invade surrounding tissue equally
Growth pattern does not differ between benign and malignant tumors
Benign tumors typically grow by expansion with a pushing border and are usually encapsulated, while malignant tumors typically infiltrate and invade surrounding tissue
Benign tumors always metastasize, unlike malignant tumors
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Benign tumors generally grow slowly by expansion, remaining well-circumscribed or encapsulated, whereas malignant tumors characteristically invade and infiltrate surrounding tissues, a key distinguishing feature on both gross and microscopic examination.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best describes a teratoma?
o: A tumor composed of cells/tissues derived from more than one (often all three) germ layers, arising from totipotent cells, typically in the gonads
A tumor composed of cells derived from a single germ layer only
A tumor exclusively of epithelial origin
A tumor found only in the liver
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Teratomas arise from totipotent germ cells and characteristically contain tissue derived from more than one germ layer (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm), such as hair, teeth, and neural tissue, most commonly found in the ovary or testis.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following describes a Krukenberg tumor?
o: A primary ovarian tumor of germ cell origin
A primary tumor of the stomach with no metastatic potential
A primary tumor of the pancreas
A metastatic tumor to the ovary, classically from a gastric (signet-ring cell) primary carcinoma
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Krukenberg tumors are metastatic deposits to the ovary, classically originating from a gastric adenocarcinoma with signet-ring cell morphology, though other primary sites (e.g., colon, breast) can also give rise to this pattern.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best describes paraneoplastic syndromes?
o: Symptom complexes directly caused by local tumor mass effect or invasion
Symptoms only seen with benign tumors
Symptom complexes occurring at sites distant from the tumor or its metastases, caused by substances secreted by tumor cells (e.g., ectopic hormones) or immune cross-reactivity
A term describing tumor recurrence after treatment
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Paraneoplastic syndromes are clinical manifestations occurring at sites distant from a tumor or its metastases, mediated by substances the tumor secretes (e.g., ectopic ACTH, PTHrP) or by immune-mediated cross-reactivity, and can sometimes be the presenting feature of an occult malignancy.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which paraneoplastic syndrome, characterized by hypercalcemia, is most commonly associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung, mediated by secretion of a PTH-related peptide?
o: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung classically causes humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy through secretion of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP), which mimics PTH action, raising serum calcium.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which paraneoplastic syndrome is classically associated with small cell carcinoma of the lung, resulting from ectopic secretion of antidiuretic hormone?
o: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Small cell lung carcinoma is classically associated with ectopic ADH secretion causing SIADH (hyponatremia), as well as ectopic ACTH secretion causing Cushing syndrome, and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best describes the process of dysplasia-to-carcinoma progression exemplified by the adenoma-carcinoma sequence in colorectal cancer?
o: A single genetic mutation is sufficient for full malignant transformation with no intermediate steps
Malignant transformation occurs randomly with no identifiable stepwise progression
Multistep accumulation of genetic alterations (e.g., APC, KRAS, TP53 mutations) drives progression from normal epithelium through adenoma to invasive carcinoma
Dysplasia always regresses spontaneously without progression to cancer
Carcinoma can only arise de novo, never from a preexisting adenoma
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: The adenoma-carcinoma sequence in colorectal cancer exemplifies the multistep model of carcinogenesis, in which sequential genetic alterations (APC loss, KRAS activation, TP53 loss, among others) drive progression from normal mucosa through increasingly dysplastic adenomas to invasive carcinoma.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best describes the difference between a papilloma and a polyp?
o: A papilloma is a benign epithelial tumor forming finger-like projections on a surface, while a polyp is a general term for any mass projecting from a mucosal surface, which may be neoplastic or non-neoplastic
A polyp is always malignant, a papilloma is always benign
Both terms are entirely synonymous with no distinction
A papilloma can only occur in the colon
A polyp is always a benign tumor of connective tissue
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: A papilloma is specifically a benign epithelial neoplasm producing finger-like or wart-like projections, whereas a polyp is a broader clinical/morphological term for any projection above a mucosal surface, which may be neoplastic (benign or malignant) or non-neoplastic (e.g., hyperplastic, inflammatory).

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following genetic alterations is classically associated with chronic myeloid leukemia, resulting in a constitutively active tyrosine kinase fusion protein?
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: The t(9;22) translocation creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene (Philadelphia chromosome), encoding a constitutively active tyrosine kinase that drives chronic myeloid leukemia, and is targeted therapeutically by tyrosine kinase inhibitors like imatinib.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best describes the concept of tumor 'dormancy'?
o: A term describing tumors that never grow at all
A state in which disseminated tumor cells remain viable but non-proliferative for a prolonged period before potentially resuming growth, sometimes explaining late recurrences
A state occurring only in benign tumors
A term describing rapid, uncontrolled tumor growth
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Tumor dormancy refers to a period during which micrometastatic or residual tumor cells persist in a quiescent, non-proliferative state, potentially for years, before resuming active growth, providing one explanation for cancer recurrence long after apparent cure.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best describes the concept of tumor initiation and promotion in chemical carcinogenesis models?
o: Initiation alone, without promotion, is always sufficient to produce a clinically evident tumor

Initiation causes an irreversible DNA mutation in a cell, while promotion (by an agent that need not be mutagenic itself) stimulates proliferation of the initiated cell, together being required for tumor development
Promotion alone, without prior initiation, is sufficient to cause cancer in normal tissue
Initiation and promotion are synonymous terms
Neither initiation nor promotion is relevant to human carcinogenesis
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: In the classic two-stage model of chemical carcinogenesis, an initiating agent causes a permanent, irreversible genetic alteration in a target cell, while a promoting agent (which need not itself be a mutagen) stimulates the clonal expansion of the initiated cell, both being necessary for tumor development.

general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.s: Which of the following best describes microsatellite instability as a mechanism of carcinogenesis, relevant to hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (Lynch syndrome)?
o: A defect exclusively in double-strand break repair
A defect in mismatch repair genes leading to accumulation of errors in short repetitive DNA sequences throughout the genome
general-and-systemic-pathology/neoplasia.e: Microsatellite instability results from defects in DNA mismatch repair genes (e.g., MLH1, MSH2), causing accumulation of errors, particularly within short repetitive DNA sequences (microsatellites), a mechanism underlying Lynch syndrome and a subset of sporadic colorectal cancers.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which type of anemia is characterized by microcytic, hypochromic red cells and is most commonly caused by chronic blood loss leading to depleted iron stores?
o: Hemolytic anemia due to G6PD deficiency
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Iron deficiency anemia is the most common cause of microcytic, hypochromic anemia worldwide, frequently resulting from chronic blood loss (e.g., gastrointestinal, menstrual) exceeding dietary iron intake.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which laboratory finding is most useful in distinguishing iron deficiency anemia from anemia of chronic disease, both of which can present with microcytosis?
o: Serum ferritin is typically low in iron deficiency but normal or elevated in anemia of chronic disease
Serum ferritin is elevated in both conditions equally
Total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) is decreased in iron deficiency
Reticulocyte count is always elevated in both conditions
Mean corpuscular volume is elevated in both conditions
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Serum ferritin, an acute-phase reactant reflecting iron stores, is characteristically low in true iron deficiency but normal or elevated in anemia of chronic disease (where iron is sequestered rather than depleted), helping distinguish the two.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which type of anemia results from impaired DNA synthesis due to vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, characterized by macrocytic red cells and hypersegmented neutrophils?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Megaloblastic anemia results from impaired DNA synthesis (typically from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency), producing macrocytic red cells and characteristic hypersegmented neutrophils on peripheral smear.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which mechanism underlies pernicious anemia, a specific cause of vitamin B12 deficiency?
o: Excess dietary intake of vitamin B12
Excess folate intake competitively inhibiting B12 absorption
Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells leading to loss of intrinsic factor and impaired B12 absorption
Increased renal excretion of vitamin B12
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Pernicious anemia results from autoimmune-mediated destruction of gastric parietal cells (or anti-intrinsic factor antibodies), causing loss of intrinsic factor production, which is required for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which inherited hemoglobinopathy results from a single point mutation causing substitution of valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the beta-globin chain, leading to red cell sickling under hypoxic conditions?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Sickle cell disease results from a point mutation (GAG to GTG) causing substitution of valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of beta-globin, producing hemoglobin S, which polymerizes and distorts red cells into a sickle shape under hypoxic conditions.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which inherited disorder results from reduced or absent synthesis of one or more globin chains, leading to an imbalance of alpha and beta chain production and ineffective erythropoiesis?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Thalassemias result from reduced or absent synthesis of alpha- or beta-globin chains due to gene deletions or mutations, causing an imbalance between chain production, ineffective erythropoiesis, and hemolysis.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which inherited red cell membrane defect, resulting from mutations in proteins such as spectrin or ankyrin, produces spherical, osmotically fragile red cells prone to splenic sequestration?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Hereditary spherocytosis results from defects in red cell membrane proteins (spectrin, ankyrin, band 3), producing spherical, less deformable red cells that are trapped and destroyed in the spleen, causing hemolytic anemia.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which enzyme deficiency, X-linked and common in certain populations, predisposes red cells to oxidative hemolysis, classically triggered by fava beans, certain drugs (e.g., primaquine), or infection?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: G6PD deficiency impairs the hexose monophosphate shunt, reducing NADPH and glutathione regeneration, leaving red cells vulnerable to oxidative stress from certain drugs, fava beans, or infections, precipitating hemolysis.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which type of hemolytic anemia is characterized by the presence of Heinz bodies and 'bite cells' on peripheral smear following an oxidative stress?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: In G6PD deficiency, oxidative damage causes denaturation of hemoglobin, forming Heinz bodies, which are subsequently removed by splenic macrophages, producing characteristic 'bite cells' on peripheral smear.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which term describes a bone marrow failure syndrome characterized by pancytopenia due to hypocellular marrow, which can be idiopathic, drug-induced, or associated with viral infection?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Aplastic anemia is a bone marrow failure syndrome resulting in pancytopenia due to markedly hypocellular bone marrow, caused by immune-mediated destruction of hematopoietic stem cells, drugs, radiation, or viral infections, or occurring idiopathically.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which clonal hematologic disorder is characterized by ineffective hematopoiesis, dysplastic blood cell morphology, and a risk of progression to acute myeloid leukemia?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Myelodysplastic syndromes are clonal stem cell disorders characterized by dysplastic, ineffective hematopoiesis leading to cytopenias, with variable but significant risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukemia.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which leukemia is characterized by a proliferation of immature lymphoblasts, most common in children, and generally has a favorable prognosis with treatment?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia, characterized by proliferation of immature lymphoblasts, is the most common childhood malignancy and generally has a favorable prognosis with modern combination chemotherapy, particularly in children.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which leukemia is characterized by proliferation of mature-appearing but functionally incompetent B lymphocytes, typically affecting older adults, often with smudge cells on peripheral smear?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia involves clonal proliferation of mature, small, but immunologically dysfunctional B lymphocytes, typically affecting older adults, with characteristic fragile cells forming 'smudge cells' on blood smear preparation.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which leukemia is characterized by proliferation of myeloid precursor cells and is classically associated with the Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL fusion)?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Chronic myeloid leukemia is characterized by clonal proliferation of myeloid cells driven by the BCR-ABL fusion gene resulting from the t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome translocation, treatable with tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which acute leukemia subtype is characterized by the presence of Auer rods within blast cells on peripheral smear or bone marrow examination?
o: Chronic myeloid leukemia in chronic phase
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Auer rods are needle-like cytoplasmic inclusions composed of fused primary granules, characteristically seen in myeloblasts of acute myeloid leukemia, particularly the acute promyelocytic leukemia (M3) subtype.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which malignant lymphoma is characterized by the presence of Reed-Sternberg cells and typically spreads in a predictable, contiguous nodal fashion?
o: Burkitt lymphoma exclusively classified as non-contiguous
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Hodgkin lymphoma is defined by the presence of characteristic Reed-Sternberg cells (large, binucleate cells with prominent 'owl-eye' nucleoli) within a reactive inflammatory background, and typically spreads contiguously from one lymph node group to adjacent ones.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which malignant plasma cell disorder is characterized by monoclonal immunoglobulin (M protein) production, lytic bone lesions, hypercalcemia, renal impairment, and anemia (the 'CRAB' features)?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of plasma cells producing a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M protein), classically presenting with the CRAB features: hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, and lytic Bone lesions.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which laboratory/urine finding is characteristic of multiple myeloma, reflecting excretion of free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains?
o: Proteinuria of nephrotic range exclusively from albumin
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Bence Jones proteins are free monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains (kappa or lambda) excreted in the urine, characteristically found in multiple myeloma and other plasma cell dyscrasias, and can contribute to renal tubular damage.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which coagulation disorder results from a deficiency of factor VIII and is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern, predominantly affecting males?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Hemophilia A results from deficiency or dysfunction of coagulation factor VIII, inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern, predominantly affecting males, and presenting with deep tissue and joint bleeding.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which coagulation disorder is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, resulting from deficiency or dysfunction of a protein that mediates platelet adhesion and stabilizes factor VIII?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Von Willebrand disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder, results from deficiency or dysfunction of von Willebrand factor, which mediates platelet adhesion to damaged endothelium and stabilizes circulating factor VIII.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which acquired coagulopathy is characterized by widespread activation of the coagulation cascade, leading to consumption of clotting factors and platelets, with resultant bleeding despite an initial hypercoagulable trigger?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: DIC is a consumptive coagulopathy triggered by conditions such as sepsis, obstetric complications, or malignancy, in which widespread activation of coagulation depletes platelets and clotting factors, paradoxically leading to both thrombosis and bleeding.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which inherited hypercoagulable disorder results from a point mutation in the factor V gene rendering it resistant to inactivation by activated protein C?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited hypercoagulable disorder, resulting from a point mutation making factor V resistant to degradation by activated protein C, increasing thrombotic risk.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which laboratory test primarily assesses the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways, used to monitor warfarin therapy?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Prothrombin time assesses the extrinsic (factor VII) and common coagulation pathways, and its standardized form (INR) is used to monitor warfarin (vitamin K antagonist) therapy.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which laboratory test primarily assesses the intrinsic and common coagulation pathways, used to monitor unfractionated heparin therapy?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: aPTT assesses the intrinsic (factors VIII, IX, XI, XII) and common coagulation pathways, and is used to monitor and adjust unfractionated heparin dosing.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which condition, resulting from immune-mediated destruction of platelets, presents with isolated thrombocytopenia, mucocutaneous bleeding, and a normal bone marrow with increased megakaryocytes?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura results from autoantibody-mediated destruction of platelets, causing isolated thrombocytopenia with compensatory increased megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, presenting with petechiae and mucosal bleeding.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which microangiopathic disorder is characterized by the pentad of thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, renal dysfunction, neurological symptoms, and fever, classically due to ADAMTS13 deficiency?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: TTP classically results from severe deficiency of ADAMTS13 (a von Willebrand factor-cleaving protease), causing formation of platelet microthrombi throughout the microvasculature and producing the classic pentad of symptoms, though not all features are always present.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which myeloproliferative neoplasm is characterized by clonal proliferation of erythroid precursors, resulting in an absolute increase in red cell mass, often associated with a JAK2 mutation?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by clonal proliferation of erythroid (and often myeloid/megakaryocytic) precursors, causing an absolute increase in red cell mass, strongly associated with an activating JAK2 V617F mutation.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which myeloproliferative neoplasm is characterized by progressive replacement of bone marrow by fibrous tissue, leading to extramedullary hematopoiesis and a characteristic 'teardrop' red cell morphology?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Primary myelofibrosis involves progressive fibrotic replacement of the bone marrow, causing extramedullary hematopoiesis (notably in the spleen, producing marked splenomegaly) and characteristic teardrop-shaped red cells (dacrocytes) on peripheral smear.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which lymphoma subtype is classically associated with a translocation involving the MYC oncogene, is highly aggressive, and demonstrates a characteristic 'starry sky' appearance on histology due to interspersed macrophages?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Burkitt lymphoma is characterized by translocations involving MYC (classically t(8;14)), a very high proliferation rate, and a 'starry sky' histological appearance from tingible-body macrophages phagocytosing apoptotic tumor cells scattered among sheets of lymphoma cells.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which lymphoma subtype is associated with the t(14;18) translocation, resulting in overexpression of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL2?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Follicular lymphoma is characteristically associated with the t(14;18) translocation, juxtaposing the BCL2 gene with the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus, resulting in BCL2 overexpression and inhibition of apoptosis, contributing to indolent lymphoma growth.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which of the following best describes the reticulocyte count's clinical utility in evaluating anemia?
o: It has no clinical utility in anemia workup
A low reticulocyte count always indicates hemolysis
Reticulocyte count is only useful in leukemia, not anemia
An elevated reticulocyte count suggests appropriate bone marrow response (e.g., to hemolysis or blood loss), while a low count suggests inadequate marrow production
Reticulocyte count reflects white blood cell production, not red cell production
