general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: The reticulocyte count reflects marrow erythropoietic activity; an appropriately elevated count in the setting of anemia suggests a peripheral cause (hemolysis, blood loss) with adequate marrow compensation, while a low count suggests a primary marrow production defect.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which peripheral blood finding, consisting of red cell fragments (schistocytes), is characteristic of microangiopathic hemolytic processes such as TTP, HUS, or DIC?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Schistocytes, or fragmented red cells (often helmet-shaped), result from mechanical shearing of red cells as they pass through partially occluded, fibrin-strand-containing microvasculature, characteristic of microangiopathic hemolytic anemias.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which nutritional deficiency, in addition to vitamin B12, is a common cause of megaloblastic anemia, particularly relevant in pregnancy due to increased demand?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Folate deficiency, like vitamin B12 deficiency, impairs DNA synthesis and causes megaloblastic anemia; increased demand during pregnancy makes folate deficiency a particularly important and preventable cause in that setting.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which of the following blood film findings, small, round, densely staining red cell remnants representing nuclear fragments, are classically seen after splenectomy or in functional hyposplenism?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants normally removed by the spleen; their presence on peripheral smear indicates splenic dysfunction or absence (e.g., post-splenectomy, sickle cell disease with autosplenectomy).

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which coagulation factor deficiency, X-linked recessive, is responsible for hemophilia B (also known as Christmas disease)?
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Hemophilia B results from deficiency of factor IX, inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern, clinically similar to hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) but less common.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which of the following is the most common cause of anemia of chronic disease, involving elevated hepcidin leading to functional iron sequestration despite adequate body iron stores?
o: Chronic inflammatory states (e.g., chronic infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy) elevating hepcidin, which reduces iron absorption and release from stores
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Anemia of chronic disease results from chronic inflammation elevating hepcidin, which downregulates ferroportin, trapping iron within macrophages and enterocytes and limiting its availability for erythropoiesis despite normal or increased total body iron stores.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which sickle cell trait (heterozygous HbAS) confers relative protection against severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria?
o: Complete absence of any hemoglobin S effect
Sickle trait eliminates the malaria parasite directly via antibody-mediated destruction
Sickling of parasitized red cells under the relatively hypoxic, acidic conditions within the parasitized cell promotes their early clearance from circulation, limiting parasite proliferation
Sickle trait prevents mosquito transmission of the parasite
Sickle trait causes complete resistance to all forms of malaria
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: In sickle cell trait, parasitized red cells experience more sickling under the altered intracellular conditions created by the parasite, promoting their earlier splenic clearance, which is thought to provide partial protective advantage against severe falciparum malaria, an example of balancing selection.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which of the following best describes the mechanism underlying the anemia typically seen in chronic renal failure?
o: Decreased renal production of erythropoietin, reducing bone marrow stimulation for red cell production
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Chronic kidney disease impairs the kidney's ability to produce erythropoietin, reducing stimulation of erythroid progenitors in the bone marrow, producing a normocytic, normochromic anemia proportional to the degree of renal impairment.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of anemia in chronic lead poisoning, relevant to interference with heme synthesis?
o: Lead has no effect on heme synthesis
Lead inhibits enzymes of the heme synthesis pathway (notably ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase), causing a microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling on peripheral smear
Lead causes anemia only through direct hemolysis via complement activation
Lead poisoning causes polycythemia, not anemia
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Lead inhibits key enzymes in the heme biosynthetic pathway, including ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, impairing hemoglobin synthesis and producing a microcytic, hypochromic anemia often accompanied by basophilic stippling of red cells.

general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.s: Which of the following best describes the pathophysiological basis of anemia of prematurity in newborns?
o: Excessive erythropoietin production overwhelming the marrow
A combination of shortened red cell lifespan, rapid growth diluting red cell mass, and relatively low erythropoietin production by the immature kidney
general-and-systemic-pathology/hematopat.e: Anemia of prematurity results from a combination of factors including a shorter neonatal red cell lifespan, rapid somatic growth diluting red cell mass, and relatively low erythropoietin production, since the switch to renal erythropoietin production is not yet fully established in preterm infants.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which type of arteriosclerosis is characterized by lipid-laden plaques within the intima of large and medium-sized arteries, the underlying pathology of most ischemic heart disease?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Atherosclerosis is characterized by formation of intimal fibrofatty plaques (atheromas) containing lipid, inflammatory cells, and fibrous tissue, underlying the majority of ischemic heart disease, stroke, and peripheral vascular disease.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which cell type, after migrating into the arterial intima and accumulating lipid, becomes a foam cell, a key early component of the atherosclerotic fatty streak?
o: Macrophage (via LDL uptake through scavenger receptors)
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Monocyte-derived macrophages migrate into the arterial intima, take up oxidized LDL cholesterol via scavenger receptors, and transform into lipid-laden foam cells, a hallmark of early atherosclerotic fatty streaks.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of an acute myocardial infarction in the majority of cases?
o: Chronic, stable narrowing of a coronary artery without any acute event
Embolism from a cardiac valve, unrelated to atherosclerosis, in virtually all cases
Acute rupture or erosion of an atherosclerotic plaque with superimposed thrombosis causing sudden coronary occlusion
Coronary artery spasm alone, without any underlying atherosclerosis, in the vast majority of cases
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Most acute myocardial infarctions result from sudden disruption (rupture or erosion) of an atherosclerotic plaque, exposing thrombogenic material and triggering superimposed thrombus formation that acutely occludes the coronary artery.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which serum cardiac biomarker is most specific and sensitive for diagnosing acute myocardial infarction, remaining elevated for up to 7-10 days?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Cardiac troponins (I and T) are highly sensitive and specific biomarkers of myocardial injury, rising within hours of infarction and remaining elevated for 7-10 days, making them the preferred diagnostic marker over CK-MB.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which type of myocardial infarction involves the full thickness of the ventricular wall, typically resulting from complete, prolonged coronary occlusion?
o: Silent infarction exclusively without any ECG changes
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Transmural infarction involves the full thickness of the ventricular wall, typically resulting from complete and prolonged occlusion of a coronary artery, usually corresponding to ST-elevation myocardial infarction on ECG.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which valvular heart disease is most commonly caused by rheumatic fever, resulting from prior group A streptococcal pharyngitis and molecular mimicry-mediated autoimmune damage?
o: Isolated aortic stenosis in young patients
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Rheumatic heart disease, resulting from molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens and cardiac tissue following group A streptococcal pharyngitis, most classically causes mitral stenosis due to chronic valvular scarring and fusion.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which type of endocarditis is characterized by small, sterile, non-bacterial thrombotic vegetations classically associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (Libman-Sacks endocarditis) or malignancy?
o: Marantic endocarditis is unrelated to malignancy
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis produces small, sterile fibrin-platelet vegetations, classically the Libman-Sacks lesions in systemic lupus erythematosus, and also occurs in hypercoagulable states associated with malignancy (marantic endocarditis).

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which organism is most commonly implicated in subacute infective endocarditis affecting previously damaged or abnormal heart valves?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Viridans group streptococci, part of normal oral flora, are the most common cause of subacute infective endocarditis, typically affecting previously damaged or abnormal heart valves after transient bacteremia (e.g., from dental procedures).

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which organism is most classically associated with acute infective endocarditis, often affecting previously normal heart valves and following a fulminant clinical course?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Staphylococcus aureus is a highly virulent organism capable of infecting previously normal heart valves, causing acute, rapidly progressive infective endocarditis, often associated with intravenous drug use.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which type of cardiomyopathy is characterized by ventricular dilation and impaired systolic (contractile) function, often idiopathic but also caused by alcohol, viral myocarditis, or peripartum state?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by ventricular chamber dilation and systolic dysfunction, with causes including idiopathic, genetic, alcohol-related, viral myocarditis, and peripartum cardiomyopathy.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which type of cardiomyopathy is characterized by asymmetric septal hypertrophy, often genetically inherited (commonly due to sarcomeric protein gene mutations), and a leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, frequently caused by autosomal dominant mutations in sarcomeric protein genes, causes asymmetric ventricular (often septal) hypertrophy that can obstruct left ventricular outflow and is a significant cause of sudden cardiac death in young, otherwise healthy athletes.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which type of cardiomyopathy is characterized by impaired ventricular filling due to increased myocardial stiffness, with preserved systolic function, classically caused by infiltrative diseases such as amyloidosis?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Restrictive cardiomyopathy results from increased myocardial stiffness impairing diastolic filling, with relatively preserved systolic function, classically caused by infiltrative processes such as amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, or hemochromatosis.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which type of shock results from an overwhelming systemic inflammatory response to infection, characterized by widespread vasodilation and distributive hypotension?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Septic shock is a form of distributive shock resulting from an overwhelming inflammatory response to infection, causing widespread vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and often myocardial depression, producing severe hypotension despite normal or increased cardiac output initially.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which of the following best describes the pathophysiology of left-sided heart failure leading to pulmonary edema?
o: Increased left ventricular output causing decreased pulmonary venous pressure
Right ventricular failure causing pulmonary edema directly
Impaired left ventricular function increases pulmonary venous and capillary hydrostatic pressure, forcing fluid into the alveolar spaces
Increased plasma oncotic pressure causing edema
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Left-sided heart failure impairs forward flow, causing blood to back up into the pulmonary venous system, raising pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure and driving fluid transudation into the alveolar spaces, producing pulmonary edema.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which of the following best describes cor pulmonale?
o: Left ventricular failure caused by systemic hypertension
A congenital cardiac malformation unrelated to the lungs
Right ventricular hypertrophy and/or failure resulting from a primary disorder of the lung, pulmonary vasculature, or chest wall causing pulmonary hypertension
A form of infective endocarditis affecting the tricuspid valve
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Cor pulmonale refers to right ventricular hypertrophy and/or failure secondary to pulmonary hypertension caused by a primary disorder of the lung parenchyma, pulmonary vasculature, or chest wall (e.g., COPD, pulmonary fibrosis, or chronic pulmonary embolism).

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which respiratory disease is characterized by irreversible dilation of bronchi due to chronic infection and inflammation, resulting in chronic cough, purulent sputum, and recurrent infections?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Bronchiectasis is characterized by permanent, abnormal dilation of bronchi due to destruction of the bronchial wall from chronic infection and inflammation, presenting with copious purulent sputum production and recurrent respiratory infections.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which obstructive lung disease is defined by chronic productive cough for at least three months in at least two consecutive years, after excluding other causes?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Chronic bronchitis is a clinical diagnosis defined by chronic productive cough for at least 3 months in at least 2 consecutive years, resulting from mucous gland hyperplasia and chronic airway inflammation, typically due to cigarette smoking.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which obstructive lung disease is characterized pathologically by permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole with destruction of alveolar walls, without significant fibrosis?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Emphysema is defined pathologically by permanent enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchiole, with destruction of alveolar walls, resulting from an imbalance between proteases (elastase) and antiproteases (alpha-1 antitrypsin), classically related to smoking or antitrypsin deficiency.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which inherited condition, associated with panacinar emphysema (especially affecting the lower lung zones) at a young age, results from deficiency of a protease inhibitor normally protecting lung elastin?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency reduces inhibition of neutrophil elastase, allowing unchecked proteolytic destruction of lung elastin, causing early-onset panacinar emphysema, particularly affecting the lower lung zones, in contrast to the upper-zone predominant centriacinar emphysema of smoking.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which reversible obstructive airway disease is characterized by episodic bronchospasm, airway hyperresponsiveness, and inflammation, often triggered by allergens, exercise, or cold air?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Bronchial asthma is characterized by reversible airway obstruction due to bronchospasm, mucosal edema, and mucus hypersecretion, driven by chronic airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness to various triggers.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which type of hypersensitivity reaction underlies the pathogenesis of atopic (allergic) asthma?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Atopic asthma is mediated by a type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction, in which allergen-specific IgE bound to mast cells triggers degranulation and release of mediators (histamine, leukotrienes) upon allergen re-exposure, causing bronchoconstriction and inflammation.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which restrictive lung disease is characterized by progressive interstitial fibrosis of unknown cause, with a 'usual interstitial pneumonia' pattern on histology and a poor prognosis?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a chronic, progressive interstitial lung disease of unknown etiology, characterized histologically by a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern (patchy fibrosis with fibroblastic foci), generally carrying a poor prognosis.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which occupational lung disease results from inhalation of silica dust, classically seen in miners and sandblasters, and is associated with an increased risk of tuberculosis?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Silicosis results from chronic inhalation of crystalline silica dust, causing nodular pulmonary fibrosis, and is associated with an increased susceptibility to tuberculosis, thought to be related to silica's inhibitory effect on macrophage function.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which occupational lung disease is caused by inhalation of asbestos fibers and is associated with pleural plaques, pulmonary fibrosis, and increased risk of both bronchogenic carcinoma and malignant mesothelioma?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Asbestosis results from chronic asbestos fiber inhalation, causing progressive pulmonary interstitial fibrosis, pleural plaques, and significantly increased risk of bronchogenic carcinoma (particularly with concurrent smoking) and malignant mesothelioma.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which pulmonary vascular condition results from occlusion of a pulmonary artery, most commonly by a thromboembolus originating from deep leg veins?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Pulmonary embolism most commonly results from thromboembolism originating in the deep veins of the lower extremities (deep vein thrombosis), traveling to and occluding pulmonary arterial branches, potentially causing infarction, hypoxemia, or acute right heart strain.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which lung carcinoma histological subtype is most strongly associated with cigarette smoking, typically arising centrally near the hilum, and often produces cavitation?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is strongly associated with cigarette smoking, typically arises centrally from bronchial epithelium (often preceded by squamous metaplasia and dysplasia), and characteristically shows a tendency to cavitate.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which lung carcinoma histological subtype is currently the most common overall, often arising peripherally, and does not require as strong an association with smoking as squamous cell carcinoma?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Adenocarcinoma is currently the most common histological subtype of lung cancer overall, tends to arise peripherally, and occurs more frequently in never-smokers compared to other lung cancer subtypes, though smoking remains a risk factor.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which lung carcinoma subtype is strongly associated with smoking, arises centrally, shows neuroendocrine differentiation, and is characteristically associated with several paraneoplastic syndromes including SIADH and Lambert-Eaton syndrome?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Small cell (oat cell) carcinoma of the lung is a highly aggressive neuroendocrine tumor strongly linked to smoking, typically arising centrally, and is classically associated with paraneoplastic syndromes such as SIADH, ectopic ACTH (Cushing syndrome), and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which term describes the collapse of previously expanded lung tissue, which can result from airway obstruction (resorption atelectasis), external compression, or loss of surfactant?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Atelectasis refers to incomplete expansion or collapse of previously inflated lung tissue, which can result from airway obstruction, external compression (e.g., pleural effusion, pneumothorax), or surfactant deficiency, reducing effective gas exchange.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which type of pneumonia is characterized by patchy areas of consolidation centered around bronchi and bronchioles, commonly seen in young children and elderly, often with multiple organisms?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Bronchopneumonia presents as patchy areas of acute inflammation and consolidation distributed around bronchi and bronchioles, in contrast to lobar pneumonia's diffuse consolidation of an entire lobe; it is common in infants, the elderly, and those with underlying illness.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which classic pathological stages describe the progression of lobar pneumonia (e.g., due to Streptococcus pneumoniae)?
o: Consolidation, liquefaction, abscess, chronic scarring exclusively
Congestion, red hepatization, gray hepatization, resolution
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Classic lobar pneumonia progresses through four stages: congestion (vascular engorgement and edema), red hepatization (neutrophilic and fibrinous exudate with red cells giving a liver-like consistency), gray hepatization (degradation of red cells, persistent fibrinosuppurative exudate), and resolution (enzymatic digestion and clearance of exudate).

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which granulomatous lung disease of unknown etiology is characterized by noncaseating granulomas, commonly affecting young adults, with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on chest imaging?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Sarcoidosis is a systemic granulomatous disease of unknown cause, characterized by noncaseating granulomas most commonly affecting the lungs and lymph nodes, with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy being a classic radiographic finding.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which type of pulmonary hypertension results primarily from chronic left heart disease causing passive backward transmission of elevated pressure into the pulmonary venous system?
o: Group 2 (pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease)
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Group 2 pulmonary hypertension arises from left-sided heart disease (e.g., left ventricular failure, mitral valve disease), causing passive elevation of pulmonary venous and then arterial pressure due to backward transmission.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which vasculitis, a small-vessel ANCA-associated condition, classically involves the upper and lower respiratory tract along with necrotizing glomerulonephritis?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a small-vessel, ANCA-associated (c-ANCA/anti-PR3) necrotizing vasculitis classically affecting the upper respiratory tract (sinusitis, nasal septal perforation), lungs (nodules, cavitation), and kidneys (rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis).

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which type of aneurysm results from weakening of the aortic wall by atherosclerosis, most commonly involving the infrarenal abdominal aorta?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Abdominal aortic aneurysms most commonly result from atherosclerotic weakening of the aortic wall, characteristically involving the infrarenal segment, and carry significant risk of rupture as diameter increases.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which condition results from a tear in the aortic intima allowing blood to dissect into and along the aortic media, creating a false lumen, often associated with hypertension or connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome?
o: Aortic regurgitation exclusively due to endocarditis
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Aortic dissection occurs when a tear in the intima allows blood under arterial pressure to enter and dissect through the weakened medial layer, creating a false lumen, classically associated with hypertension and, in younger patients, connective tissue disorders like Marfan syndrome affecting the media's structural integrity.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which type of hypertensive vascular change, characterized by concentric, laminated thickening of small arteriolar walls ('onion-skinning'), is characteristic of malignant hypertension?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, characterized by concentric, laminated ('onion-skin') thickening of the arteriolar wall due to smooth muscle cell proliferation, is characteristic of malignant (severely elevated) hypertension, often accompanied by fibrinoid necrosis.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which type of hypertensive vascular change, characterized by homogeneous, pink hyaline thickening of arteriolar walls, is typically seen in benign, long-standing hypertension and diabetes mellitus?
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis produces homogeneous, eosinophilic thickening of the arteriolar wall due to leakage and deposition of plasma proteins and increased matrix production, typically seen in chronic, benign hypertension and diabetes mellitus, narrowing the vessel lumen.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which of the following best explains the pathophysiological basis of high-altitude pulmonary edema?
o: Decreased pulmonary arterial pressure at high altitude reducing capillary pressure
Complete absence of any hypoxic pulmonary vascular response
Hypoxia-induced pulmonary vasoconstriction leading to uneven perfusion and increased capillary pressure in some regions, causing leakage of fluid into alveoli
Decreased permeability of pulmonary capillaries at altitude
Exclusively a cardiac, not pulmonary, phenomenon
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: High-altitude pulmonary edema results from hypoxia-induced pulmonary vasoconstriction, which is uneven, leading to overperfusion and increased capillary pressure in some lung regions, causing a high-permeability-type edema.

general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.s: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of pink, frothy sputum production in acute pulmonary edema due to left heart failure?
o: Bronchial gland hypersecretion of mucus alone
Direct bleeding from a bronchial tumor
Transudation of fluid (with some red cells) from pulmonary capillaries into alveolar spaces, which mixes with air during breathing to form a frothy, blood-tinged fluid
general-and-systemic-pathology/systemic-.e: In acute pulmonary edema, elevated pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure forces fluid transudate (sometimes with red cells) into the alveolar spaces; this mixes with air during respiration to form the characteristic pink, frothy sputum.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which pharmacokinetic parameter describes the fraction of an administered drug dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Bioavailability refers to the fraction of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation in unchanged, active form; intravenous administration has 100% bioavailability by definition, while oral drugs may have reduced bioavailability due to incomplete absorption or first-pass metabolism.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which pharmacokinetic parameter relates the amount of drug in the body to its plasma concentration, providing a theoretical measure of the extent of drug distribution into tissues?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Volume of distribution is a theoretical value relating total drug amount in the body to plasma concentration; a high Vd suggests extensive tissue distribution (e.g., lipophilic drugs), while a low Vd suggests the drug remains largely within the vascular compartment.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which term describes the metabolism of an orally administered drug by the liver (or gut wall) before it reaches the systemic circulation, reducing its bioavailability?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: First-pass metabolism refers to the hepatic (and sometimes intestinal) metabolism of an orally absorbed drug before it reaches the systemic circulation via the portal vein, which can substantially reduce the bioavailability of drugs with high hepatic extraction ratios.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which type of elimination kinetics describes a constant fraction of drug eliminated per unit time, resulting in a constant half-life regardless of drug concentration?
o: Nonlinear kinetics exclusively at all doses
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: First-order kinetics describes elimination of a constant fraction (not amount) of drug per unit time, resulting in an exponential decline in plasma concentration and a constant half-life independent of dose, characteristic of most drugs at therapeutic concentrations.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which type of elimination kinetics describes a constant amount of drug eliminated per unit time, occurring when metabolic or elimination pathways become saturated, as classically seen with phenytoin and ethanol at higher doses?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Zero-order kinetics occurs when drug elimination pathways become saturated, resulting in a constant amount (not fraction) of drug eliminated per unit time; the half-life is not constant and increases with increasing dose, exemplified by phenytoin, ethanol, and aspirin at high/toxic doses.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Approximately how many half-lives are required for a drug given by constant infusion (following first-order kinetics) to reach steady-state plasma concentration?
o: Steady state is never reached with continuous infusion
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: With first-order kinetics, a drug given at a constant rate approaches steady-state plasma concentration after approximately 4-5 half-lives, regardless of the infusion rate or dose (which determine the steady-state level itself, not the time to reach it).

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which term describes the initial higher dose of a drug given to rapidly achieve therapeutic plasma concentration, calculated based on volume of distribution and desired plasma concentration?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: A loading dose is calculated to rapidly achieve a target therapeutic plasma concentration, based on the drug's volume of distribution and the desired concentration, particularly useful for drugs with a long half-life where reaching steady state via maintenance dosing alone would take too long.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which phase of hepatic drug metabolism involves oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis reactions, commonly mediated by cytochrome P450 enzymes, generally producing a more polar (though not always inactive) metabolite?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Phase I metabolism involves oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis reactions (predominantly via cytochrome P450 enzymes), which typically increase drug polarity and can produce active, inactive, or even toxic metabolites.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which phase of hepatic drug metabolism involves conjugation reactions (e.g., glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation) that typically inactivate a drug and increase its water solubility for excretion?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Phase II metabolism involves conjugation of a drug (or its phase I metabolite) with an endogenous substrate (glucuronic acid, sulfate, glycine, acetyl group), generally increasing water solubility and promoting renal or biliary excretion, and usually inactivating the compound.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which cytochrome P450 enzyme induction phenomenon explains why rifampin can reduce the efficacy of concurrently administered oral contraceptives?
o: Rifampin induces CYP3A4 (and other enzymes), increasing metabolism and clearance of estrogen/progestin components, reducing contraceptive efficacy
Rifampin inhibits CYP3A4, increasing contraceptive levels
Rifampin has no effect on hepatic enzymes
Rifampin directly inactivates the contraceptive hormones in the gut
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Rifampin is a potent inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes (notably CYP3A4), increasing the metabolic clearance of many co-administered drugs including oral contraceptive steroids, thereby reducing their contraceptive efficacy.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which pharmacodynamic term describes the concentration (or dose) of a drug required to produce 50% of its maximal effect?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: EC50 (or ED50 for dose) represents the concentration or dose of a drug producing 50% of its maximal possible effect, and is used as a measure of drug potency when comparing different agents.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which pharmacodynamic term describes the maximal effect a drug can produce, regardless of further dose increases?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Efficacy refers to the maximal effect (Emax) achievable by a drug, an important distinction from potency (which reflects the dose required to achieve a given effect), since a drug can be highly potent but have low efficacy, or vice versa.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which term describes the ratio between the toxic dose (or lethal dose) and the effective therapeutic dose of a drug, used as a measure of drug safety?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: The therapeutic index is the ratio of the toxic (or lethal) dose to the effective therapeutic dose; a higher therapeutic index indicates a wider margin of safety between therapeutic and toxic doses.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which type of drug antagonism occurs when two drugs act on completely different receptor systems but produce opposing physiological effects?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Physiological (functional) antagonism occurs when two drugs act through different receptors or mechanisms but produce opposite physiological effects (e.g., histamine causing bronchoconstriction countered by epinephrine causing bronchodilation via different receptors).

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which type of receptor antagonism can be overcome by increasing the concentration of agonist, since the antagonist binds reversibly to the same site as the agonist?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Competitive antagonists bind reversibly to the same receptor site as the agonist; their effect can be overcome (surmounted) by sufficiently increasing agonist concentration, shifting the dose-response curve to the right without reducing maximal efficacy.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which type of receptor antagonism cannot be overcome by increasing agonist concentration, because the antagonist binds irreversibly or to a different (allosteric) site, reducing the maximal achievable effect?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Noncompetitive antagonists bind irreversibly or to an allosteric site distinct from the agonist binding site, reducing the maximal effect (Emax) achievable regardless of agonist concentration, distinguishing it from surmountable competitive antagonism.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which term describes a drug that binds to a receptor and produces a submaximal response even at full receptor occupancy, and can act as an antagonist in the presence of a full agonist?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: A partial agonist binds to the receptor but produces a submaximal response even at full receptor occupancy; in the presence of a full agonist, it can act as a functional antagonist by competing for receptor binding while producing less overall effect.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which term describes an agent that binds to a receptor and produces an effect opposite to that of the endogenous agonist, by stabilizing the receptor's inactive conformation?
o: Competitive antagonist with no intrinsic activity
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: An inverse agonist binds to a receptor with some constitutive (baseline) activity and stabilizes the inactive conformation, producing an effect opposite to that of the agonist, in contrast to a neutral antagonist which has no effect on baseline activity.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which drug interaction mechanism describes a change in the pharmacological effect of one drug caused by another drug altering its absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Pharmacokinetic interactions involve one drug altering the absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion of another, changing its plasma concentration, as opposed to pharmacodynamic interactions, which involve altered effect at the same or related receptor/target sites without a change in plasma concentration.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which term describes an unexpected, often genetically determined abnormal reaction to a drug that occurs in only a small subset of the population, unrelated to the drug's known pharmacological action?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Idiosyncratic drug reactions are unusual, often genetically determined responses that occur in a small subset of patients, unrelated to the drug's known pharmacology, such as hemolysis with certain drugs in G6PD-deficient individuals.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which term describes a reduced response to a drug that develops gradually over repeated administration, requiring increased doses to achieve the original effect?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Tolerance refers to a diminished pharmacological response to a drug developing gradually over repeated administrations (days to weeks), necessitating increased doses to achieve the original therapeutic effect, as seen classically with opioids and benzodiazepines.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which term describes a rapid, acute decrease in response to a drug occurring after only one or a few doses, in contrast to the more gradual development of tolerance?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Tachyphylaxis refers to a rapidly developing, acute decrease in drug responsiveness after repeated administration over a short time period, often due to receptor desensitization or depletion of a mediator, as seen with repeated ephedrine dosing (via norepinephrine depletion).

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which route of drug administration bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism, achieving 100% bioavailability by definition?
o: Sublingual administration exclusively achieves full first-pass bypass
Rectal administration exclusively achieves full bypass
Transdermal administration only partially bypasses first-pass
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Intravenous administration delivers drug directly into the systemic circulation, bypassing absorption and first-pass hepatic metabolism entirely, resulting in 100% bioavailability by definition, serving as the reference standard for calculating the bioavailability of other routes.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which term describes the phenomenon where a drug is absorbed into the bile, secreted into the intestine, and then reabsorbed back into the systemic circulation, prolonging its duration of action?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Enterohepatic recirculation occurs when a drug (or its metabolite) excreted in bile is reabsorbed from the intestine back into the portal circulation, effectively prolonging the drug's duration of action and half-life.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which factor primarily determines whether a weak acid or weak base drug is more readily absorbed across a lipid membrane in a given body compartment, according to the pH-partition hypothesis?
o: Its route of administration exclusively, regardless of chemical properties
The degree of ionization, with the non-ionized (lipid-soluble) form crossing membranes more readily, determined by the drug's pKa relative to the local pH
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: According to the pH-partition hypothesis, the non-ionized form of a weak acid or base is more lipid-soluble and crosses biological membranes more readily; the proportion of non-ionized drug depends on the relationship between the drug's pKa and the local pH (Henderson-Hasselbalch equation).

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which of the following best explains why aspirin overdose can be treated in part by alkalinizing the urine?
o: Alkalinization has no effect on aspirin excretion
Alkalinization increases aspirin's lipid solubility, promoting reabsorption
Alkalinization inactivates aspirin directly within the kidney
Aspirin (a weak acid) becomes more ionized in alkaline urine, trapping it within the tubular lumen and enhancing its renal elimination ('ion trapping')
Alkalinization increases hepatic metabolism of aspirin
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Alkalinizing the urine increases ionization of aspirin (a weak acid) within the renal tubule, trapping the ionized form (which cannot easily diffuse back across the tubular membrane) and enhancing its urinary excretion, a clinically useful strategy in salicylate overdose.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which pharmacogenomic phenomenon explains why some individuals metabolize certain drugs (e.g., isoniazid) much faster than others, due to genetic variation in an acetylation enzyme?
o: N-acetyltransferase (NAT2) polymorphism, producing 'fast' and 'slow' acetylator phenotypes
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Genetic polymorphism in N-acetyltransferase (NAT2) produces 'fast' and 'slow' acetylator phenotypes, affecting the metabolism of drugs such as isoniazid, hydralazine, and certain sulfonamides, with slow acetylators at higher risk of toxicity (e.g., isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy).

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which pharmacogenomic condition, resulting from deficient plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase), causes prolonged neuromuscular blockade after administration of succinylcholine?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Individuals with atypical or deficient plasma pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) cannot efficiently metabolize succinylcholine, leading to prolonged neuromuscular paralysis and delayed recovery of spontaneous respiration after its administration.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which of the following best describes the concept of drug clearance?
o: The total amount of drug remaining in the body at any time
The volume of plasma (or blood) from which a drug is completely removed per unit time, reflecting the efficiency of eliminating organs (primarily liver and kidney)
The time required for plasma drug concentration to fall by half
The fraction of drug bound to plasma proteins
The peak plasma concentration achieved after a single dose
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Clearance is defined as the volume of plasma (or blood) from which a drug is completely and irreversibly removed per unit time, reflecting the combined efficiency of eliminating organs, and is a key determinant of maintenance dosing rate.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which of the following best explains why drugs with a high degree of plasma protein binding can have clinically significant drug-drug interactions when displaced by another highly protein-bound drug?
o: Displacement has no clinical significance for any drug

Displacement transiently increases the free (unbound, pharmacologically active) fraction of the displaced drug, which can transiently increase its effect or toxicity, particularly for drugs with a narrow therapeutic index and high protein binding
Protein binding displacement only affects drug absorption, not its effect
Displaced drugs are immediately and completely eliminated
Protein binding displacement always decreases drug effect
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: When a highly protein-bound drug is displaced from plasma protein-binding sites by another drug, the free (unbound) fraction transiently increases, potentially increasing pharmacological effect or toxicity, particularly relevant for drugs with high protein binding, a narrow therapeutic index, and a small volume of distribution (e.g., warfarin).

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which term describes the additive or greater-than-additive effect produced when two drugs with similar mechanisms are combined, exceeding the effect predicted by simple addition?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Synergism describes a combined drug effect that is greater than the sum of the individual effects of each drug given alone, often exploited therapeutically (e.g., combination antihypertensive or antimicrobial regimens) but also a source of increased toxicity risk.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which enzyme system, located primarily in the liver's smooth endoplasmic reticulum, is responsible for the majority of oxidative phase I drug metabolism reactions?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: The cytochrome P450 enzyme superfamily, located predominantly in the hepatic smooth endoplasmic reticulum, is responsible for the majority of phase I oxidative drug metabolism reactions, with numerous isoforms (e.g., CYP3A4, CYP2D6) exhibiting substrate specificity and susceptibility to induction/inhibition.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which of the following is a classic example of a potent inhibitor of cytochrome P450 enzymes, increasing plasma levels of many co-administered drugs?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Cimetidine, along with certain azole antifungals (e.g., ketoconazole) and macrolide antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin), are well-known inhibitors of cytochrome P450 enzymes, increasing plasma concentrations and potential toxicity of co-administered substrate drugs.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which of the following is a classic example of a potent inducer of cytochrome P450 enzymes, potentially reducing the efficacy of co-administered drugs?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Rifampin, along with certain anticonvulsants (phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine), is a potent inducer of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes, increasing metabolism and reducing plasma levels of many co-administered drugs, potentially reducing their therapeutic efficacy.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which term describes the phase of a drug's action during which the plasma concentration falls exponentially after absorption and distribution are essentially complete, and which is used to calculate the elimination half-life?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: The elimination (beta) phase of a plasma concentration-time curve represents the period after distribution equilibrium is achieved, during which concentration falls primarily due to elimination processes, and is used to calculate the terminal elimination half-life.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which of the following best explains the clinical rationale for therapeutic drug monitoring of drugs such as digoxin, phenytoin, and lithium?
o: These drugs have narrow therapeutic indices, such that small changes in plasma concentration can result in either therapeutic failure or toxicity, making monitoring clinically valuable
These drugs have wide therapeutic indices, making monitoring unnecessary
Monitoring is done purely for research purposes with no clinical benefit
These drugs are never associated with toxicity
Therapeutic drug monitoring is only relevant for antibiotics
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Drugs such as digoxin, phenytoin, and lithium have a narrow therapeutic index, meaning the therapeutic and toxic plasma concentration ranges are close together, making regular monitoring of plasma levels clinically important to optimize efficacy while minimizing toxicity.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which term describes drug elimination that occurs via a combination of hepatic metabolism and renal excretion, requiring dose adjustment in either hepatic or renal impairment depending on the dominant route?
o: Total body clearance (sum of hepatic and renal clearance, among other routes)
Half-life exclusively, unrelated to organ function
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Total body clearance represents the sum of clearance contributions from all eliminating organs, chiefly hepatic (metabolic) and renal (excretory) clearance; impairment of the dominant eliminating organ necessitates dose adjustment to avoid drug accumulation and toxicity.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which of the following best describes a 'prodrug'?
o: A drug that is pharmacologically active in its administered form and requires no metabolic conversion
A drug that has no therapeutic use
A drug used only in veterinary medicine
An inactive or less active compound that requires metabolic conversion (often hepatic) to its active form to exert its pharmacological effect
A drug that acts exclusively on cell surface receptors
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: A prodrug is administered in an inactive or less active form and undergoes metabolic conversion (commonly hepatic) to generate the active drug, sometimes used to improve bioavailability, reduce toxicity, or target specific tissues (e.g., enalapril to enalaprilat, codeine to morphine).

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which of the following best describes the therapeutic window and its clinical relevance for drug dosing?
o: The window has no clinical relevance
A term describing only the time of day a drug should be given
The range of plasma concentrations between the minimum effective concentration and the minimum toxic concentration, within which a drug is both effective and reasonably safe
The time required for a drug to reach peak plasma concentration
The interval between successive maintenance doses, unrelated to concentration
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: The therapeutic window refers to the range of plasma drug concentrations that produces the desired therapeutic effect without significant toxicity; a narrow therapeutic window necessitates more careful dosing and monitoring.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.s: Which of the following best describes the concept of drug potentiation, as distinct from synergism?
o: Potentiation and synergism are identical in every respect
Potentiation refers to one drug enhancing the effect of a second drug, even though the first drug has little or no effect of its own when given alone at that dose
Potentiation always requires both drugs to act on the same receptor
Potentiation refers exclusively to antagonistic interactions
Potentiation cannot occur in clinical pharmacology
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/pharma.e: Potentiation describes a specific case where one drug enhances the effect of another even though it produces little or no effect by itself, distinguishing it from synergism, where both agents individually produce some effect that is enhanced when combined.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which receptor subtype, when activated by acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, mediates skeletal muscle contraction?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Nicotinic Nm receptors at the neuromuscular junction are ligand-gated ion channels that, upon acetylcholine binding, cause depolarization and skeletal muscle contraction, distinct from nicotinic Nn receptors at autonomic ganglia.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which muscarinic receptor subtype, found in gastric parietal cells and other exocrine glands, mediates increased secretion when stimulated?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: M3 muscarinic receptors, coupled to Gq proteins, mediate smooth muscle contraction (e.g., bronchoconstriction, bladder contraction) and increased glandular secretion, including gastric acid and salivary secretion.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which muscarinic receptor subtype, found in the heart (particularly the SA node), mediates decreased heart rate when stimulated by acetylcholine?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: M2 muscarinic receptors, coupled to Gi proteins, are the predominant subtype in the heart, mediating decreased heart rate (negative chronotropy) and decreased conduction velocity (negative dromotropy) via vagal stimulation.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which class of drugs, exemplified by atropine, competitively blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, causing effects such as mydriasis, tachycardia, and decreased secretions?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Atropine and related antimuscarinic drugs competitively block muscarinic receptors, producing mydriasis (pupil dilation), tachycardia, reduced glandular secretions, bronchodilation, and decreased gastrointestinal motility, useful in various clinical contexts including organophosphate poisoning treatment.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which class of drugs inhibits acetylcholinesterase, prolonging the action of acetylcholine at both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors, used in myasthenia gravis and Alzheimer disease?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Cholinesterase inhibitors prevent breakdown of acetylcholine at the synapse, prolonging and enhancing cholinergic transmission at both muscarinic and nicotinic sites, used therapeutically in myasthenia gravis (neostigmine/pyridostigmine) and Alzheimer disease (donepezil, rivastigmine).

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which toxidrome, characterized by salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI distress, and emesis (SLUDGE), along with muscle fasciculations and CNS depression, results from organophosphate (irreversible cholinesterase inhibitor) poisoning?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Organophosphate poisoning causes irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase, producing excessive cholinergic stimulation manifesting as the SLUDGE syndrome (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI upset, emesis) along with miosis, bradycardia, muscle fasciculations, and potentially respiratory failure.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which drug is the antidote of choice for organophosphate poisoning, acting as a competitive muscarinic antagonist to counteract excessive cholinergic stimulation?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Atropine, a competitive muscarinic antagonist, is used as first-line treatment for organophosphate poisoning to counteract the excessive muscarinic effects (bradycardia, bronchorrhea, secretions), often combined with pralidoxime to reactivate acetylcholinesterase before it becomes permanently inhibited (aging).

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which adjunct drug, used alongside atropine in organophosphate poisoning, works by reactivating acetylcholinesterase if administered before the enzyme-inhibitor complex undergoes 'aging'?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Pralidoxime (2-PAM) reactivates acetylcholinesterase by displacing the organophosphate from the enzyme's active site, but is only effective if administered before the enzyme-inhibitor complex undergoes an irreversible chemical change called aging.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which adrenergic receptor subtype, when stimulated, causes vasoconstriction of vascular smooth muscle, mediating the pressor response to norepinephrine?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, coupled to Gq proteins, mediate vascular smooth muscle contraction (vasoconstriction) upon stimulation by norepinephrine and epinephrine, increasing peripheral resistance and blood pressure.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which adrenergic receptor subtype, predominant in cardiac tissue, mediates increased heart rate and contractility when stimulated?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Beta-1 adrenergic receptors, coupled to Gs proteins, are the predominant adrenergic receptor in cardiac tissue, mediating increased heart rate (positive chronotropy), contractility (positive inotropy), and conduction velocity when stimulated by catecholamines.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which adrenergic receptor subtype, predominant in bronchial and vascular smooth muscle, mediates smooth muscle relaxation (bronchodilation and vasodilation) when stimulated?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Beta-2 adrenergic receptors, coupled to Gs proteins, mediate smooth muscle relaxation, causing bronchodilation and vasodilation in skeletal muscle vasculature; selective beta-2 agonists (e.g., albuterol) are used to treat bronchospasm in asthma.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which sympathomimetic drug, a nonselective beta-agonist (also with alpha activity at higher doses), is the drug of choice for treating anaphylactic shock?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Epinephrine, acting on alpha-1 (vasoconstriction, reducing edema), beta-1 (increased cardiac output), and beta-2 (bronchodilation) receptors, is the first-line drug for treating anaphylaxis, rapidly reversing hypotension, bronchospasm, and mucosal edema.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which beta-blocker is described as 'cardioselective,' preferentially blocking beta-1 over beta-2 receptors at usual clinical doses, making it relatively safer in patients with reactive airway disease?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Metoprolol and atenolol are considered cardioselective beta-1 blockers, preferentially blocking beta-1 receptors at usual clinical doses, reducing (though not eliminating) the risk of bronchospasm compared to nonselective beta-blockers like propranolol, in patients with asthma or COPD.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which nonselective beta-blocker is used in the management of essential tremor, migraine prophylaxis, and performance anxiety, in addition to cardiovascular indications?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Propranolol, a nonselective beta-blocker with good CNS penetration, has additional uses including essential tremor, migraine prophylaxis, and performance/situational anxiety, beyond its cardiovascular indications.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which selective alpha-1 adrenergic antagonist is used to relieve symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia by relaxing prostatic and bladder neck smooth muscle?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Tamsulosin, a selective alpha-1A adrenergic antagonist with relative uroselectivity, relaxes smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck, improving urinary flow symptoms in benign prostatic hyperplasia with less systemic hypotensive effect than nonselective alpha-1 blockers.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which class of antihypertensive drugs, exemplified by prazosin, blocks alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, causing vasodilation, but carries a risk of significant first-dose orthostatic hypotension?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Alpha-1 blockers such as prazosin cause vasodilation by blocking postsynaptic alpha-1 receptors, but are associated with a notable 'first-dose phenomenon' of pronounced orthostatic hypotension, requiring dose titration starting at bedtime.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which centrally acting antihypertensive drug reduces sympathetic outflow by stimulating alpha-2 adrenergic receptors in the brainstem, and is notably used in pregnancy-associated hypertension?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Methyldopa, a centrally acting alpha-2 agonist (via its active metabolite alpha-methylnorepinephrine), reduces sympathetic outflow from the brainstem, and has a long track record of safety in hypertension during pregnancy.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which class of drugs mimics the action of acetylcholine directly at muscarinic receptors, used to treat urinary retention (e.g., bethanechol) or glaucoma (e.g., pilocarpine)?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Direct-acting muscarinic agonists such as bethanechol (used for urinary retention, increasing detrusor contraction) and pilocarpine (used in glaucoma, causing miosis and increased aqueous outflow) directly stimulate muscarinic receptors without requiring endogenous acetylcholine.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which ganglionic blocking agent, historically used to produce controlled hypotension during surgery, blocks nicotinic receptors at both sympathetic and parasympathetic autonomic ganglia?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Trimethaphan is a ganglionic blocker that acts at nicotinic Nn receptors in both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia, historically used to produce controlled hypotension during surgery, though largely replaced by other agents due to its broad, unselective autonomic effects.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which neuromuscular blocking drug, a depolarizing agent, initially causes muscle fasciculations before producing paralysis, and is metabolized by plasma pseudocholinesterase?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that initially causes transient muscle fasciculations by persistent depolarization of the motor endplate before producing flaccid paralysis; it is rapidly metabolized by plasma pseudocholinesterase, and its action is prolonged in patients with atypical or deficient enzyme.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which class of neuromuscular blocking drugs competes with acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors without causing initial depolarization, and can be reversed by cholinesterase inhibitors?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers competitively antagonize acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors without causing initial depolarization, and their effect can be reversed (antagonized) by cholinesterase inhibitors, which increase acetylcholine available to outcompete the blocker.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which adrenergic agonist, acting predominantly on dopamine receptors at low doses and beta-1/alpha-1 receptors at progressively higher doses, is used in the management of cardiogenic shock?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Dopamine exhibits dose-dependent receptor selectivity: at low doses it activates D1 receptors (renal/splanchnic vasodilation), at moderate doses beta-1 receptors (increased cardiac output), and at high doses alpha-1 receptors (vasoconstriction), making it useful in various shock states depending on the dose used.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which selective beta-1 agonist, with relatively less chronotropic effect compared to its inotropic effect, is used to increase cardiac contractility in acute decompensated heart failure or cardiogenic shock?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Dobutamine is a relatively selective beta-1 agonist with a predominant positive inotropic effect (increased contractility) and comparatively less chronotropic (heart rate) effect, useful for increasing cardiac output in cardiogenic shock or acute decompensated heart failure.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which of the following best describes the pharmacological basis for using a nonselective alpha-blocker such as phenoxybenzamine before surgical removal of a pheochromocytoma?
o: To directly destroy the tumor cells
To block alpha-1-mediated vasoconstriction from catecholamine surges, preventing hypertensive crisis during tumor manipulation
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Preoperative alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine (an irreversible, nonselective alpha antagonist) prevents severe hypertensive crises from catecholamine surges released during surgical manipulation of a pheochromocytoma, and is typically followed by beta-blockade only after adequate alpha-blockade is established to avoid unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which of the following best explains why beta-blockers should not be given to a pheochromocytoma patient before adequate alpha-blockade has been established?
o: Unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction (from blocking the counterbalancing beta-2-mediated vasodilation) can precipitate a severe hypertensive crisis
Beta-blockade alone has no cardiovascular effect in this setting
Beta-blockers directly stimulate catecholamine release from the tumor
Beta-blockers have no interaction with catecholamine excess
Alpha-blockade always follows beta-blockade in standard preoperative protocols
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Administering a beta-blocker before adequate alpha-blockade removes the counterbalancing beta-2-mediated vasodilation, leaving unopposed alpha-1-mediated vasoconstriction from high catecholamine levels, which can precipitate a severe, potentially life-threatening hypertensive crisis.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which drug, a selective beta-2 agonist with a short onset and duration of action, is used as a rescue inhaler for acute bronchospasm in asthma?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Albuterol (salbutamol) is a short-acting beta-2 agonist providing rapid bronchodilation, used as a rescue inhaler for acute asthma exacerbations, in contrast to long-acting beta-2 agonists like salmeterol and formoterol used for maintenance therapy.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which inhaled anticholinergic drug, blocking muscarinic receptors in the airway, is used as a bronchodilator in asthma and COPD, particularly useful when beta-agonists are poorly tolerated?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Ipratropium bromide is an inhaled short-acting muscarinic antagonist that blocks bronchoconstrictor cholinergic tone, providing bronchodilation, particularly useful in COPD and as an adjunct in acute severe asthma.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism of action of botulinum toxin, used therapeutically for conditions like blepharospasm and cosmetic wrinkle reduction?
o: Blocking presynaptic release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction by cleaving SNARE proteins required for vesicle fusion
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins required for synaptic vesicle fusion, preventing presynaptic release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, producing flaccid paralysis of the affected muscle, exploited therapeutically for focal dystonias and cosmetically for wrinkle reduction.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which class of drugs, acting on alpha-2 adrenergic autoreceptors presynaptically, reduces norepinephrine release through negative feedback, providing the rationale for clonidine's antihypertensive effect?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Alpha-2 adrenergic receptors act as presynaptic autoreceptors that, when stimulated (e.g., by clonidine), inhibit further norepinephrine release via negative feedback, contributing both to clonidine's centrally mediated antihypertensive effect and to reduced peripheral sympathetic outflow.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which mydriatic (pupil-dilating) mechanism is produced by muscarinic antagonists such as atropine, relevant to their use (and side effects) in ophthalmology?
o: Contraction of the sphincter pupillae muscle
Direct stimulation of the dilator pupillae muscle via muscarinic receptors
Paralysis of the ciliary muscle exclusively, without effect on the iris
Relaxation of the sphincter pupillae muscle (which is normally maintained in a state of partial contraction by parasympathetic tone), allowing unopposed dilator pupillae action
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Muscarinic antagonists block parasympathetic tone to the sphincter pupillae muscle, which normally maintains partial pupillary constriction; blocking this tone allows the sympathetically innervated dilator pupillae muscle to act unopposed, producing mydriasis.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which of the following best explains the mechanism of cycloplegia (paralysis of accommodation) produced by muscarinic antagonists such as atropine or cyclopentolate?
o: Stimulation of the ciliary muscle causing lens flattening
Direct paralysis of the optic nerve
Blockade of muscarinic receptors on the ciliary muscle, preventing its contraction and thus preventing the lens from becoming more convex for near vision
Contraction of the lateral rectus muscle
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Normally, muscarinic stimulation of the ciliary muscle causes it to contract, relaxing the zonular fibers and allowing the lens to become more convex for near vision (accommodation); muscarinic antagonists block this contraction, producing cycloplegia (loss of accommodation) for distance-fixed vision.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which drug class, exemplified by physostigmine, is a lipid-soluble, tertiary amine cholinesterase inhibitor capable of crossing the blood-brain barrier, historically used to treat anticholinergic toxicity?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Physostigmine, a tertiary amine, crosses the blood-brain barrier (unlike quaternary compounds such as neostigmine), allowing it to reverse central anticholinergic toxicity symptoms in addition to peripheral effects.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which receptor subtype mediates the vasodilatory, renal blood flow-increasing effect of low-dose dopamine infusion?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: At low doses, dopamine preferentially activates D1 receptors in renal, mesenteric, and coronary vascular beds, causing vasodilation and increased blood flow to these organs.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which adrenergic agonist is relatively selective for alpha-1 receptors, used as a nasal decongestant and to treat hypotension, with minimal beta-adrenergic activity?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Phenylephrine is a relatively pure alpha-1 adrenergic agonist, producing vasoconstriction useful as a nasal decongestant and for treating hypotension, with minimal direct effect on beta-adrenergic receptors.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which of the following best explains why nonselective beta-blockers should be used cautiously in patients with asthma or COPD?
o: They have no effect on airway receptors
They exclusively affect cardiac tissue with no pulmonary effects
They enhance bronchodilation in these patients
They have no clinically significant receptor selectivity concerns
Blockade of beta-2 receptors in bronchial smooth muscle can precipitate bronchoconstriction and worsen airway disease
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Nonselective beta-blockers block both beta-1 and beta-2 receptors; beta-2 blockade in the bronchi removes a bronchodilating influence and can precipitate bronchospasm, making cardioselective agents generally preferred in patients with reactive airway disease when a beta-blocker is required.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which class of drugs used to treat glaucoma, exemplified by timolol, reduces intraocular pressure by decreasing aqueous humor production via beta-adrenergic receptor blockade in the ciliary epithelium?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Topical beta-blockers such as timolol reduce aqueous humor production by blocking beta-adrenergic receptors in the ciliary body epithelium, lowering intraocular pressure, a mainstay treatment for open-angle glaucoma.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which term describes the compensatory reflex tachycardia that can occur following administration of a pure alpha-1 agonist (such as phenylephrine) causing acute hypertension?
o: Baroreceptor-mediated reflex bradycardia (not tachycardia) in this scenario
Baroreceptor reflex mechanism, in which acute hypertension leads to reflex bradycardia via vagal stimulation, opposite to the tachycardia seen with vasodilators causing hypotension
No reflex response occurs with alpha agonists
Direct beta-1 stimulation by phenylephrine causing tachycardia
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: When a pure alpha-1 agonist raises blood pressure, the baroreceptor reflex is engaged, producing reflex bradycardia (via increased vagal tone) rather than tachycardia, in contrast to vasodilators, which lower pressure and elicit reflex tachycardia.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which drug, a direct-acting muscarinic agonist relatively resistant to acetylcholinesterase degradation, is used topically to treat open-angle and angle-closure glaucoma by increasing aqueous humor outflow?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Pilocarpine, a direct muscarinic agonist resistant to acetylcholinesterase breakdown, causes ciliary muscle contraction and miosis, opening the trabecular meshwork and increasing aqueous humor outflow, used in glaucoma management, particularly acute angle-closure glaucoma.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which adverse effect is characteristic of nonselective alpha-blockers such as phenoxybenzamine, resulting from unopposed baroreceptor-mediated reflex tachycardia when peripheral alpha-1 receptors are blocked?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Alpha-1 blockade reduces peripheral vascular resistance, lowering blood pressure and triggering baroreceptor-mediated reflex tachycardia as a compensatory response, a recognized adverse effect of nonselective alpha-blockers like phenoxybenzamine.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.s: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of cocaine at adrenergic synapses, relevant to its cardiovascular toxicity?
o: Cocaine has no effect on catecholamine signaling

Cocaine blocks presynaptic reuptake of norepinephrine (and dopamine), increasing synaptic catecholamine concentration and enhancing adrenergic stimulation, contributing to vasoconstriction, tachycardia, and hypertension
Cocaine depletes norepinephrine stores, causing hypotension
Cocaine acts exclusively on nicotinic receptors
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/autono.e: Cocaine blocks presynaptic norepinephrine (and dopamine) reuptake transporters, increasing synaptic catecholamine levels and prolonging adrenergic receptor stimulation, contributing to its cardiovascular effects including vasoconstriction, tachycardia, hypertension, and increased risk of myocardial ischemia.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.s: Which class of antihypertensive drugs inhibits the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.e: ACE inhibitors block the enzyme responsible for converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II, reducing angiotensin II-mediated vasoconstriction and aldosterone secretion, and also reduce bradykinin degradation, contributing to their characteristic dry cough side effect.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.s: Which side effect is characteristic of ACE inhibitors, resulting from decreased breakdown of bradykinin?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.e: ACE inhibitors reduce bradykinin degradation (since ACE also breaks down bradykinin), and accumulated bradykinin is thought to cause the characteristic dry cough and, rarely, angioedema associated with this drug class.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.s: Which class of antihypertensive drugs blocks the angiotensin II type 1 (AT1) receptor directly, avoiding the bradykinin-related cough seen with ACE inhibitors?
o: Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs, e.g., losartan, valsartan)
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.e: ARBs selectively block the AT1 receptor, preventing angiotensin II's vasoconstrictive and aldosterone-stimulating effects without affecting bradykinin metabolism, generally avoiding the dry cough associated with ACE inhibitors.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.s: Which class of calcium channel blockers is relatively selective for vascular smooth muscle, causing potent vasodilation with less cardiac depressant effect, exemplified by amlodipine?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.e: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (e.g., amlodipine, nifedipine) are relatively selective for vascular smooth muscle, producing potent vasodilation with comparatively less direct effect on cardiac contractility and conduction than nondihydropyridines.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.s: Which class of calcium channel blockers has significant cardiac depressant effects (negative inotropy, chronotropy, and dromotropy), making verapamil particularly useful for rate control in supraventricular tachyarrhythmias?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.e: Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, verapamil and diltiazem, have more prominent direct cardiac effects (reducing heart rate, contractility, and AV nodal conduction), making verapamil especially useful for rate control in atrial fibrillation/flutter and supraventricular tachycardia.

general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.s: Which class of diuretics acts on the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, inhibiting the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter, producing the most potent diuresis?
general-and-systemic-pharmacology/cardio.e: Loop diuretics such as furosemide inhibit the Na+/K+/2Cl- cotransporter in the thick ascending limb, producing the most potent diuretic effect among available diuretic classes, useful in conditions like acute pulmonary edema and severe fluid overload.
