microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.e: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis is most effective when started as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours of exposure, and continued for 28 days.

microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.s: Proper specimen collection for blood culture requires which of the following to minimize contamination?
o: Collection immediately after antibiotics are given
Refrigeration of the sample before inoculation into culture bottles
Aseptic skin antisepsis before venipuncture and collection before antibiotic administration
Use of a single blood culture set regardless of suspected bacteremia
Collection through an existing intravenous line only
microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.e: Blood cultures require strict aseptic skin preparation and should ideally be drawn before antibiotics are started, with paired sets from separate sites to distinguish true bacteremia from contamination.

microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.s: For suspected pulmonary tuberculosis, which specimen collection practice maximizes diagnostic yield on sputum smear microscopy?
o: Collecting a single random saliva sample
Collecting sputum only in the evening
Collecting three separate sputum samples including an early morning sample
Using a throat swab instead of sputum
microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.e: Collection of multiple (traditionally three) sputum specimens, including an early morning sample with the highest bacillary concentration, increases the sensitivity of acid-fast smear microscopy.

microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.s: Which automated blood culture identification method uses matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization to rapidly identify bacterial and fungal species?
microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.e: MALDI-TOF (matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight) mass spectrometry rapidly identifies microorganisms by their unique protein mass spectra, significantly reducing turnaround time compared to biochemical methods.

microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.s: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is defined as resistance to at least which combination of first-line drugs?
microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.e: MDR-TB is defined as Mycobacterium tuberculosis resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin, the two most potent first-line anti-tuberculous drugs, requiring longer, more toxic second-line regimens.

microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.s: Extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing Enterobacteriaceae confer resistance primarily to which class of antibiotics?
microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.e: ESBL enzymes hydrolyze the beta-lactam ring of penicillins, cephalosporins, and monobactams (but not carbapenems), necessitating carbapenem therapy for serious ESBL infections.

microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.s: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae (CRE) are of major public health concern primarily because of which characteristic?
o: Resistance to nearly all beta-lactam antibiotics including last-resort carbapenems, with limited treatment options
They only cause mild self-limiting infections
They are exclusively found in animals
They are always susceptible to first-generation cephalosporins
They cannot be transmitted between patients
microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.e: CRE produce carbapenemases (e.g., KPC, NDM) that inactivate carbapenems, historically the last-resort beta-lactams, leaving very few effective treatment options and posing a serious nosocomial threat.

microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.s: Antimicrobial stewardship programs in hospitals are primarily designed to achieve which goal?
o: Increase the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics for all patients
Eliminate the need for microbiology culture testing
Optimize antibiotic use to improve outcomes and limit resistance
microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.e: Antimicrobial stewardship programs promote appropriate antibiotic selection, dosing, and duration to optimize clinical outcomes while minimizing the emergence of antimicrobial resistance and adverse effects.

microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.s: Universal precautions in infection control were originally developed primarily in response to the risk of transmission of which pathogens?
o: Bloodborne pathogens such as HIV and hepatitis B/C
microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.e: Universal precautions were introduced to prevent transmission of bloodborne pathogens (HIV, hepatitis B and C) by treating all blood and certain body fluids as potentially infectious.

microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.s: Which waste category classification is used for sharps (needles, scalpel blades) in healthcare waste management?
microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.e: Sharps waste must be segregated into dedicated puncture-resistant, leak-proof containers to prevent needlestick injuries and safe disposal, typically via autoclaving or incineration.

microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.s: Fecal-oral transmission of Salmonella typhi in a community outbreak is most effectively interrupted at the public health level by which measure?
o: Mass administration of antibiotics to the general population
Ensuring safe drinking water and proper sanitation/sewage disposal
microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.e: Since typhoid fever spreads via the fecal-oral route through contaminated water and food, safe water supply and sanitation infrastructure are the most effective community-level control measures.

microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.s: Surgical site infection surveillance classifies infections occurring within how many days of a procedure without an implant, per standard definitions?
microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.e: Standard surveillance definitions (e.g., CDC/NHSN) classify surgical site infections occurring within 30 days of the procedure (or up to 90 days/1 year if an implant is left in place) as related to that surgery.

microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.s: Which infection control measure is most important in preventing central line-associated bloodstream infections during catheter insertion?
o: Daily catheter replacement regardless of need
Use of topical antibiotic ointment only
Placing the catheter in the femoral vein preferentially
Avoiding hand hygiene to save time in emergencies
Maximal sterile barrier precautions and chlorhexidine skin antisepsis
microbiology-and-immunology/clinical-mic.e: Bundled practices including maximal sterile barrier precautions, chlorhexidine skin preparation, and optimal catheter site selection significantly reduce central line-associated bloodstream infection rates.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Which is the earliest postmortem change observable in a body, typically noted within minutes to a few hours after death?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Algor mortis, the postmortem cooling of the body toward ambient temperature, begins immediately after death and is one of the earliest measurable changes.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Rigor mortis typically begins approximately how many hours after death and follows which classical sequence?
o: 24 hours, starting in large muscles only
Immediately at death, in all muscles simultaneously
1-2 hours, starting in small muscles (face/jaw) and progressing to larger muscles
72 hours, starting in the lower limbs only
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Rigor mortis begins in small muscle groups (jaw, face) 1-2 hours after death and progresses in a craniocaudal direction (Nysten's law), fully developing by about 12 hours.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Rigor mortis is caused by which underlying biochemical mechanism?
o: Loss of blood supply causing muscle infarction
Depletion of ATP leading to persistent actin-myosin cross-bridge formation
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: After death, ATP depletion prevents the dissociation of actin-myosin cross-bridges, causing sustained muscle contraction (rigor), which resolves only as putrefactive enzymes begin to degrade muscle proteins.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Livor mortis (postmortem hypostasis) results from which process and becomes 'fixed' after approximately how many hours?
o: Gravitational pooling of blood in dependent vessels, fixing by about 8-12 hours
Active bleeding from wounds, fixing within 1 hour
Bacterial gas production, fixing within 24 hours
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Livor mortis develops from passive gravitational settling of blood in dependent capillaries and typically becomes fixed (non-blanching, non-shifting with repositioning) after 8-12 hours.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: In a body found lying face down, pale (blanched) areas of skin corresponding to points of contact with the ground are due to which mechanism?
o: Pressure preventing blood from pooling in compressed capillaries (contact pallor)
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Areas of the body in direct contact with a firm surface are compressed, preventing blood from pooling there, producing pale contact-pallor patches amid surrounding lividity.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Putrefaction, the destruction of soft tissue by bacterial and autolytic processes, characteristically first appears as which visible sign?
o: Greenish discoloration of the abdominal wall (right iliac fossa)
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Putrefaction typically first manifests as a greenish discoloration over the right iliac fossa (overlying the cecum, rich in bacteria), due to bacterial breakdown producing sulfhemoglobin.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Adipocere ('grave wax') formation, a waxy preservation of body fat, is favored by which environmental condition?
o: Moist, warm, and relatively anaerobic conditions such as burial in wet soil or water
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Adipocere forms through hydrolysis and hydrogenation of body fat into a firm, soap-like substance, favored by moist, warm, anaerobic conditions typically found in damp burial or submersion.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Mummification of a body, a form of preservation rather than putrefaction, is favored by which environmental condition?
o: Hot, dry, well-ventilated environment promoting rapid desiccation
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Mummification occurs when rapid loss of body moisture in a hot, dry, well-ventilated environment outpaces bacterial decomposition, preserving skin and other tissues in a dried, leathery state.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Estimation of time since death using vitreous humor potassium levels relies on which principle?
o: Potassium concentration in vitreous humor rises progressively and predictably after death
Vitreous potassium decreases linearly after death
Vitreous humor becomes sterile after death
Vitreous glucose rises rapidly after death
Vitreous humor volume increases after death
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: After death, cellular breakdown and diffusion cause vitreous potassium to rise in a relatively linear, predictable fashion, making it a useful biochemical method for estimating postmortem interval.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Forensic entomology, using insect colonization patterns on a corpse, is most useful for estimating which parameter?
o: Postmortem interval, especially in advanced decomposition
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: The succession and developmental stage of necrophagous insects (e.g., blowfly larvae) colonizing a body follow predictable patterns, allowing estimation of postmortem interval, particularly useful once early signs (rigor, livor) have resolved.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Which of the following best distinguishes an antemortem wound from a postmortem wound on examination?
o: Presence of vital reaction (hemorrhage, inflammation, clot formation) at the wound margins
Presence of any wound edge at all
Location of the wound on the body
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Vital reaction — infiltration of blood into tissue, clot formation, and early inflammatory changes — indicates the wound occurred while the person was alive; postmortem wounds show pale, gaping edges without significant bleeding or vital reaction.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: In forensic medicine, 'manner of death' refers to which classification?
o: The specific organ system that failed
The exact biochemical cause of death
The circumstances of death, such as natural, accidental, suicidal, or homicidal
The legal verdict of a criminal trial
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Manner of death is a medico-legal classification (natural, accident, suicide, homicide, or undetermined) distinct from the 'cause of death,' which is the specific disease or injury that led to death.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: A death certificate's 'cause of death' section should record which of the following as the underlying cause?
o: Only the immediate mode of death such as cardiac arrest
The manner of death (natural, accident, suicide, homicide)
The name of the treating physician
The disease or injury that initiated the chain of events leading directly to death
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: The underlying cause of death is the disease or injury that initiated the sequence of events culminating in death, distinguished from the immediate cause (the final physiological event, e.g., cardiac arrest) and mode/mechanism of death.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: A medico-legal autopsy is mandated in which of the following scenarios?
o: All deaths occurring in a hospital under medical care from a known chronic illness
Deaths in patients over age 90 with a clear terminal diagnosis
Deaths from a well-documented terminal cancer under hospice care
Sudden, unexpected, or unnatural death, including suspected homicide or suicide
Routine deaths with a clearly signed natural-cause certificate
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Medico-legal (forensic) autopsies are required for sudden, unexpected, suspicious, unnatural, or unexplained deaths to establish the cause and manner of death for legal purposes.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: The presence of Tardieu spots (petechial hemorrhages) in the conjunctivae and face is most characteristically associated with which mechanism of death?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Tardieu spots are petechial hemorrhages caused by increased venous pressure and capillary rupture above the point of venous obstruction, classically seen in asphyxial deaths such as strangulation and hanging.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: In hanging, the typical ligature mark is classically described as which shape and position?
o: Horizontal mark below the thyroid cartilage, complete circumferentially
Inverted V-shaped mark above the thyroid cartilage, non-continuous at the point of suspension
A deep, straight mark crossing the trachea only
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: In hanging, the ligature mark classically forms an inverted V (oblique, non-continuous) above the level of the thyroid cartilage, with the mark being absent or faint at the point of suspension due to loss of pressure there.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: The ligature mark in cases of manual/ligature strangulation (as opposed to hanging) typically differs by being which of the following?
o: Oblique and incomplete, above the thyroid cartilage
Horizontal and complete around the neck, usually below the thyroid cartilage
Located only on the back of the neck
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Strangulation by ligature typically produces a horizontal, complete mark encircling the neck at or below the level of the thyroid cartilage, unlike the oblique, incomplete mark of hanging.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Diatoms found in the bone marrow, lungs, and other internal organs are considered supportive evidence of which cause of death?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Diatoms (microscopic algae present in natural water) reaching the bone marrow and distant organs via the circulation suggest the person was alive and breathing at the time of submersion, supporting a diagnosis of drowning.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: 'Cutis anserina' (goose-flesh skin) and washerwoman's skin (bleached, wrinkled skin) are findings classically associated with which cause of death?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Cutis anserina and washerwoman's skin (maceration from prolonged water immersion) are classic external postmortem findings in bodies recovered from water, supportive of drowning as the cause of death.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: A firearm wound with a surrounding zone of blackening, tattooing (stippling), and singeing of hair/skin suggests which range of fire?
o: Contact firing with muzzle pressed against skin exclusively
Cannot be determined from these findings
Firing through an intermediate barrier only
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Blackening (soot deposition), tattooing (embedded unburned powder particles), and singeing indicate close-range firing (typically within about 60 cm depending on weapon and ammunition), distinguishing it from distant gunshot wounds.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: A contact gunshot wound to the head classically produces which additional finding due to gases entering the wound?
o: A clean, small, round entrance wound with no gas effect
A wound identical in every way to a distant gunshot wound
Stellate (star-shaped) wound with muzzle imprint and skin splitting from gas expansion
Multiple small wounds without gas effect
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: In contact wounds over bone (e.g., skull), expanding gases entering the wound cause the skin to split in a stellate pattern, often with a muzzle-shaped imprint (contusion ring) and grey-blackened wound margins.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: In forensic firearm injuries, the entrance wound is typically distinguished from the exit wound by which characteristic?
o: Exit wound is always smaller than the entrance wound
Entrance wound always has everted margins
Entrance wound is usually smaller, round, with an inverted margin and abrasion collar
There is no reliable distinguishing feature
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: The entrance wound is typically smaller and round with inverted (inward-turned) margins and a surrounding abrasion collar from the bullet's friction, while the exit wound is often larger, irregular, and everted, without an abrasion collar.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: A wound caused by a heavy, blunt object with irregular, contused, non-clean-cut margins and tissue bridging within the wound is best classified as which type of injury?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Lacerated wounds result from blunt trauma causing tissue to tear rather than cut cleanly; they show irregular, contused, ragged margins with tissue bridging (nerves and vessels crossing the wound base), unlike clean-cut incised wounds.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: An incised wound caused by a sharp-edged weapon is characteristically distinguished from a lacerated wound by which feature?
o: Presence of tissue bridging across the wound
Clean, straight edges without bruising or tissue bridging
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Incised wounds from sharp weapons have clean, straight, well-defined edges without contusion or tissue bridging, in contrast to the ragged, bridged margins of lacerated wounds from blunt trauma.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: A stab wound, produced by a pointed weapon, is distinguished by which characteristic in relation to its length and depth?
o: Depth typically exceeds the length of the external wound
It never penetrates beyond the skin
It cannot be caused by a single-edged weapon
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Stab wounds are produced by the penetrating action of a pointed weapon, so wound depth (into the body) usually exceeds the length of the external skin wound, unlike incised wounds where length exceeds depth.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Defense wounds in a homicide victim are typically located on which body part, indicating an attempt to ward off an attack?
o: Palms, forearms, and ulnar border of the hands
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Defense wounds occur on the palms, forearms, and ulnar aspects of the hands as the victim instinctively raises the arms or grasps at a weapon to protect against an assault.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: First-degree (superficial) burns are characterized by which histological/clinical extent of injury?
o: Limited to the epidermis, presenting as erythema without blistering
Involvement of underlying muscle and bone
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: First-degree burns involve only the epidermis, presenting as painful erythema without blister formation, and typically heal without scarring, as in mild sunburn.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Postmortem burns, as opposed to antemortem burns, characteristically lack which feature?
o: Vital reaction such as a line of redness/inflammation and blister fluid containing protein and inflammatory cells
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Because postmortem tissue lacks circulation and an inflammatory response, burns inflicted after death show no vital reaction (no inflammatory line, no protein-rich blister fluid), unlike antemortem burns.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Pugilistic attitude (boxer's stance) seen in bodies recovered from fires results from which mechanism?
o: Heat-induced coagulation and shortening of flexor muscles, which are stronger than extensors
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Heat causes coagulation and shortening of muscle protein; since flexor muscle groups are generally more powerful than extensors, the limbs are drawn into a characteristic flexed 'pugilistic' posture after severe heat exposure.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Cadaveric spasm, an instantaneous form of rigidity occurring at the moment of death, is most classically seen in which forensic scenario?
o: A suicide victim's hand still grasping a weapon or object
Deaths from drowning without a weapon involved
Routine natural deaths in elderly patients
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Cadaveric spasm is an immediate, intense muscular rigidity affecting a single muscle group at the moment of death (often from intense emotion or physical exertion), classically causing a suicide victim's hand to remain firmly clutching a weapon, useful in distinguishing suicide from staged homicide.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Exhumation of a buried body for forensic investigation is legally permitted under which general condition?
o: Court or magistrate order when new evidence or suspicion of foul play arises
Only with the unanimous consent of all relatives regardless of legal process
At any time without judicial oversight
Never permitted once burial has occurred
Only for bodies buried within the last 24 hours
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Exhumation is a legal procedure requiring authorization from a court or competent magistrate, usually undertaken when fresh evidence, suspicion, or a legal requirement necessitates re-examination of the remains.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Which finding on skeletal examination is most useful in forensic age estimation of a young individual?
o: Degree of epiphyseal fusion at long bone growth plates
Bone density measured by DEXA alone
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: The sequential and predictable fusion of epiphyses with diaphyses at specific ages is one of the most reliable skeletal indicators for estimating age in children, adolescents, and young adults.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Determination of sex from a skeleton relies most reliably on which bone due to its marked sexual dimorphism?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: The pelvis shows the most pronounced sexual dimorphism (e.g., wider subpubic angle, larger pelvic inlet in females), making it the most reliable skeletal element for sex determination in forensic anthropology.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Superimposition and facial reconstruction techniques in forensic anthropology are primarily used for which purpose?
o: Establishing identity from skeletal remains, especially the skull
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Craniofacial superimposition (comparing a skull to an antemortem photograph) and facial reconstruction are identification techniques used when skeletal remains cannot be identified by other means such as fingerprints or DNA.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: DNA profiling for forensic identification most commonly analyzes which type of genetic marker?
o: Mitochondrial ribosomal RNA exclusively in all cases
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Short tandem repeats (STRs), highly polymorphic repetitive DNA sequences, are the standard genetic markers used in forensic DNA profiling due to their high discriminatory power between individuals.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Mitochondrial DNA analysis is particularly useful in forensic identification of which type of sample?
o: Highly degraded remains or samples lacking nuclear DNA, such as old bones or hair shafts
Fresh blood samples with abundant nuclear DNA
Buccal swabs from a living suspect
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Mitochondrial DNA, present in high copy number per cell and more resistant to degradation, is especially valuable for identification from severely degraded, old, or nuclear-DNA-poor samples like hair shafts and old skeletal remains.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: A body showing extensive skeletonization with no soft tissue remaining suggests a postmortem interval of at least approximately how long, under temperate conditions?
o: Several months to years, depending on environmental conditions
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Complete skeletonization generally requires an extended postmortem interval (commonly many months to years under temperate conditions), though the exact timing is highly variable depending on climate, burial, and scavenger activity.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: The medico-legal significance of identifying 'coup and contrecoup' brain injuries is most relevant in which type of case?
o: Blunt head trauma, particularly from falls or assault
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Coup (at the site of impact) and contrecoup (opposite the site of impact) brain contusions result from the brain's movement within the skull following blunt head trauma, important in reconstructing the mechanism of head injury in assault or fall cases.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: The 'three-stage' rigor mortis progression (onset, full development, resolution) is important forensically because resolution of rigor typically occurs in which order?
o: In the exact reverse order of onset
Same order as onset, resolving first in the muscles where it appeared first
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Rigor mortis typically resolves (due to onset of putrefactive proteolysis) in the same order it developed, disappearing first from the small muscles of the face/jaw and last from larger muscle groups.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: In forensic practice, the term 'presumption of death' after prolonged unexplained absence is typically established through which mechanism?
o: Automatic declaration after exactly 24 hours of absence
Only through DNA testing of a recovered body
Immediate declaration by any family member without legal process
A legal/judicial process based on statutory time periods and circumstantial evidence, in the absence of a body
It is never legally recognized in any jurisdiction
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: When a person has been missing for a legally defined period under circumstances suggesting death, courts can issue a legal presumption of death based on statute and evidence, even without physical recovery of remains.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: An abrasion is defined as an injury limited to which anatomical layer of the skin?
o: Epidermis, without penetration into the dermis
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: An abrasion is a superficial injury caused by friction or scraping that damages only the epidermis, without breaching into the dermis, though minor bleeding may occur from exposed dermal papillae.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: A 'grazed' or 'brush' abrasion, showing heaped-up epidermis at one end, is forensically useful for determining which of the following?
o: Direction of the force causing the injury
Identity of the assailant's weapon material only
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: In a sliding/brush abrasion, epithelial tags and heaping of skin occur at the end where the object left the skin, allowing determination of the direction of the applied force.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: A contusion (bruise) results from which underlying mechanism?
o: Complete laceration of the epidermis and dermis
Rupture of small blood vessels with extravasation of blood into surrounding tissue without breach of skin surface
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: A contusion is caused by blunt force rupturing small vessels, with blood leaking into the surrounding interstitial tissue while the overlying skin remains intact.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Estimating the age of a bruise based on its color change is useful because bruises typically evolve through which general color sequence?
o: No reliable color sequence exists at all
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: As hemoglobin breaks down over time (into biliverdin and bilirubin), a bruise typically evolves from red/purple in the first days to green and yellow over 1-3 weeks, though timing is variable and only an approximate guide.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: A 'patterned' contusion or abrasion that reproduces the shape of the weapon (e.g., a rod, belt buckle, or tire tread) is forensically significant primarily because it helps do what?
o: Identify the type or specific object used to inflict the injury
Determine the exact time of death
Rule out any possibility of homicide
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: A patterned injury reproduces the surface characteristics of the causative object, which can help investigators match the wound to a specific weapon or implement used in the assault.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: In road traffic accident victims, a 'bumper fracture' of the tibia/fibula at a fairly constant height above the ground is most useful forensically for determining which of the following?
o: Blood alcohol concentration of the driver
Exact speed of the vehicle at collision
Type of vehicle involved and whether the victim was standing when struck
Whether the death was a suicide
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: The height of a 'bumper fracture' on the lower limb corresponds to the height of the vehicle's bumper, helping to identify the type of vehicle involved and confirm the victim was upright/pedestrian at impact.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: 'Coning' or beveling of a fracture in a gunshot wound to the skull, where the outer table shows a smaller defect than the inner table, is diagnostic of which of the following?
o: Exit wound of a bullet through the skull
Entry wound of a bullet through the skull
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: At a bullet entrance site in bone, the outer table shows a smaller, cleaner defect while the inner table is beveled outward (larger), a pattern (internal beveling) diagnostic of an entrance wound; exit wounds show the reverse (external beveling).

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: A 'chop wound,' produced by a heavy-edged weapon such as an axe or sword, characteristically shares features of which two other wound types?
o: Incised wound and lacerated wound combined with underlying bone injury
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Chop wounds are produced by heavy sharp-edged weapons delivering a combination of cutting force (incised component) and crushing force (lacerated component), often with underlying fracture of bone.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Pattern of injury in a 'railway spine/limb' accident, where a limb is severed with characteristic crushing and tearing plus grease/soot staining, is diagnostic of which mechanism?
o: Run-over injury by a train/heavy vehicle wheel
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Crush-avulsion amputation with associated grease, soot, and rail/track pattern marks on the skin is characteristic of run-over injuries by trains or heavy vehicles.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Second-degree (partial-thickness) burns are characterized by which clinical feature that distinguishes them from first-degree burns?
o: Blister formation with a painful, moist, erythematous base due to dermal involvement
Full-thickness skin loss with a leathery eschar
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Second-degree (partial-thickness) burns involve the epidermis and part of the dermis, producing painful blisters with a moist, red base, in contrast to first-degree (epidermis-only) or third-degree (full-thickness) burns.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Third-degree (full-thickness) burns are characteristically associated with which clinical finding?
o: Painless, leathery, charred skin due to destruction of nerve endings
Blistering with a moist red base
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Third-degree burns destroy the full thickness of skin including nerve endings, producing a painless, dry, leathery, charred (eschar) appearance requiring surgical grafting for healing.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: The 'Rule of Nines' is a clinical tool used for which purpose in burn victims?
o: Estimating the total body surface area affected by burns
Determining the depth of a single burn
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: The Rule of Nines divides the adult body into regions each representing approximately 9% (or multiples thereof) of total body surface area, allowing rapid estimation of burn extent for fluid resuscitation planning.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: In a case of death from a house fire, finding soot particles in the trachea, bronchi, and evidence of carbon monoxide in the blood indicates which conclusion?
o: The victim was already dead before the fire started
The fire was accidental in nature
The victim died of an unrelated cause
The victim was alive and breathing during the fire
The fire started after the victim's death
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: The presence of soot deep in the airways along with significant carboxyhemoglobin in the blood indicates the victim was alive and breathing (vital reaction) during the fire, supporting antemortem fire exposure.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Death from electrocution characteristically produces which skin finding at the point of electrical contact?
o: Electric mark: a firm, grey-white, painless burn resembling a small crater with raised margins
A large, diffuse thermal burn with no distinct border
Multiple small petechiae only, without any local skin mark
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: An electric mark (Joule burn) is a characteristic firm, painless, greyish-white crater-like lesion with raised, everted margins at the point of electrical current entry into the skin.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: The most common immediate cause of death in low-voltage domestic electrocution is which mechanism?
o: Direct thermal destruction of the brain
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Low-voltage alternating current, especially at frequencies used in domestic supply, can induce ventricular fibrillation by disrupting the heart's electrical conduction during the vulnerable phase of the cardiac cycle, the most common cause of death in domestic electrocution.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Lightning strike injuries characteristically produce which distinctive cutaneous pattern?
o: Multiple small entrance/exit wounds resembling gunshot
Symmetrical full-thickness burns of both palms only
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Lichtenberg figures are transient, fern-like or arborescent erythematous skin patterns caused by electron shower effects from a lightning strike, considered pathognomonic when present.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: A body recovered from a fire showing a fracture line at the base of the skull with extradural hemorrhage, in the absence of soot in the airway, most likely suggests which sequence of events?
o: The victim was alive and burned to death with no head injury
The fire caused the skull fracture directly through heat alone
The victim sustained head trauma and died before the fire started, with the body subsequently burned
The findings are consistent with a natural death unrelated to the fire
It confirms an accidental fire in every case
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Absence of soot in the airway together with an antemortem-pattern skull fracture and extradural hemorrhage suggests the victim died from head trauma before the fire started, and the fire was a secondary event affecting an already-dead body.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Heat hematoma, a postmortem artifact found in the extradural space of fire victims, is distinguished from a true antemortem extradural hematoma by which feature?
o: Heat hematoma always shows an underlying skull fracture
Heat hematoma is indistinguishable from antemortem hematoma in every respect
Heat hematoma occurs only in the subdural space
Heat hematoma is typically frothy, honeycombed, and not adherent to the dura, without associated fracture or vital reaction
Heat hematoma is always accompanied by soot in the airway
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Heat hematoma is a postmortem artifact from heat causing blood to boil and expand within the skull, appearing frothy/honeycombed and not firmly adherent to the dura, unlike a true antemortem extradural hematoma associated with fracture and vital reaction.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: A drowning death in freshwater versus saltwater primarily differs in the underlying pathophysiology due to which mechanism?
o: Saltwater drowning cannot cause cardiac arrhythmia
There is no physiological difference between the two
Freshwater drowning always takes longer to cause death
Osmotic gradient causing hemodilution in freshwater drowning versus hemoconcentration in saltwater drowning
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Classic drowning physiology describes freshwater aspiration causing hypotonic fluid absorption into the circulation (hemodilution, hemolysis) while hypertonic saltwater aspiration draws fluid into the alveoli (hemoconcentration), though in practice electrolyte differences are often less clinically significant than the hypoxia itself.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: 'Dry drowning,' in which laryngospasm prevents significant water entry into the lungs, is estimated to account for what proportion of drowning deaths?
o: None; dry drowning does not exist
Exactly half of all drowning deaths
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: In a minority of drowning deaths, severe laryngospasm prevents significant water aspiration into the lungs ('dry drowning'), while the majority show typical aspiration findings ('wet drowning').

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Froth (fine, white, lathery froth) at the mouth and nostrils of a body recovered from water is considered supportive evidence of which finding?
o: Postmortem submersion of an already-dead body
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Fine, persistent froth results from the mixing of water, air, mucus, and surfactant during the struggle to breathe while submerged, and is considered a supportive (though not conclusive) sign of antemortem drowning.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: The forensic significance of 'washerwoman's hands and feet' (skin maceration) after prolonged water immersion is primarily to help estimate which parameter?
o: The duration of submersion in water
The exact time of day of death
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Progressive skin maceration (wrinkling, whitening) with prolonged water immersion follows a roughly predictable timeline, helping estimate the duration the body has been submerged.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: A blast injury from an explosion is classified as 'primary blast injury' when damage results from which mechanism?
o: Direct effect of the blast overpressure wave on gas-containing organs (lungs, ear, bowel)
Injury from flying debris and fragments
Victims being thrown against solid structures
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Primary blast injury results directly from the pressure wave itself, causing barotrauma to air-containing organs like the tympanic membrane, lungs (blast lung), and gastrointestinal tract.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: 'Secondary blast injury' from an explosion refers to injury caused by which mechanism?
o: Direct pressure wave effect on the lungs
The victim being physically displaced by the blast wind
Flying debris, shrapnel, and fragments propelled by the explosion
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Secondary blast injury results from penetrating or blunt trauma caused by fragments and debris (shrapnel, glass, bomb casing) propelled by the explosion, often a major cause of morbidity and mortality in bombings.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: A gunshot wound demonstrating a 'wad mark' or 'cookie-cutter' pattern around the entrance is most characteristic of which type of firearm?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Shotgun wounds at close-to-intermediate range can show a wad mark from the plastic/felt wad that travels with the shot pellets before dispersing, useful in estimating range of fire.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: As firing range increases in a shotgun injury, the pattern of pellet spread on the skin typically changes in which way?
o: The pellets converge into a single tighter wound at greater distances
The pellets scatter over a progressively wider area with increasing distance
There is no change in pellet spread with distance
The wound size decreases with increasing range
Pellet spread only depends on the victim's clothing, not distance
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: As range increases, shotgun pellets progressively disperse from the choke of the barrel, producing an increasingly wide scatter pattern used forensically to help estimate the firing distance.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: A 'tandem' or 'graze' gunshot wound occurs when a bullet does which of the following?
o: Strikes the skin obliquely/tangentially, producing an elongated, gutter-shaped wound
Enters and exits at the exact same point
Passes completely through the body without deviation
Only causes injury to bone, not soft tissue
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: A graze (tangential) gunshot wound occurs when the bullet strikes the skin at an oblique angle, producing an elongated, furrow-like, gutter-shaped wound rather than a typical round entrance.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: In a case of suicidal firearm injury to the head, the most common site of entrance wound is classically which location?
o: Temple (temporal region) or under the chin
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Suicidal gunshot wounds to the head are most commonly located at the temple or submental (under the chin) region, sites easily accessible to the victim's own hand, and typically show contact or near-contact range findings.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Distinguishing a suicidal from a homicidal gunshot wound relies most heavily on which combination of findings?
o: The caliber of the bullet alone
Range of fire, site of wound, presence of a single accessible wound, and scene/circumstantial evidence
The time of day the shooting occurred
The manufacturer of the firearm alone
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Differentiating suicide from homicide requires correlating the range of fire (contact/near-contact favors suicide), wound site accessibility, single versus multiple wounds, and full scene investigation rather than any single finding in isolation.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: A 'hesitation cut' or 'tentative wound,' consisting of multiple shallow parallel incised wounds near a fatal, deeper wound, is most characteristic of which manner of death?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Hesitation cuts are shallow, superficial, closely-spaced incised wounds typically found adjacent to a fatal wound in self-inflicted (suicidal) sharp-force injuries, reflecting initial tentative attempts before the fatal cut.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Frostbite injury, a form of cold-related tissue damage, primarily results from which pathophysiological mechanism?
o: Ice crystal formation in tissue with vascular injury and thrombosis on rewarming
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Frostbite results from extracellular and intracellular ice crystal formation causing direct cell damage, along with vasoconstriction and microvascular thrombosis, with further reperfusion injury occurring on rewarming.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Systemic hypothermia leading to death is most classically associated with which characteristic postmortem finding in the gastric mucosa?
o: Wischnewski spots (hemorrhagic erosions of the gastric mucosa)
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Wischnewski spots — multiple small hemorrhagic erosions on the gastric mucosa — are a characteristic (though not universal) postmortem finding in deaths due to severe hypothermia.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: A 'paradoxical undressing' phenomenon observed in some hypothermia deaths, where victims are found partially or fully undressed, is thought to result from which mechanism?
o: Terminal vasodilation causing a false sensation of warmth as hypothermia progresses
Robbery at the scene of death
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: As hypothermia advances, a paradoxical failure of the vasomotor center can cause peripheral vasodilation, producing a false sensation of warmth that leads victims to remove their own clothing shortly before death.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Injuries caused by acid (corrosive) attacks on the skin characteristically produce which pathological change?
o: Liquefactive necrosis with a soft, slippery ulcer
Coagulative necrosis with a firm, dry eschar
Immediate charring identical to flame burns
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Strong acids typically cause coagulative necrosis, denaturing proteins to form a firm, dry eschar that can limit further penetration, in contrast to alkalis which cause liquefactive necrosis and deeper tissue penetration.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Alkali (caustic) burns, compared to acid burns, tend to cause deeper tissue injury primarily because of which mechanism?
o: Liquefactive necrosis allows continued penetration into deeper tissue layers
Alkalis are always more dilute than acids
Alkalis do not react with skin proteins
Alkali burns are always more painful, limiting exposure time
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Alkalis cause liquefactive necrosis, dissolving tissue proteins and lipids and allowing the caustic agent to penetrate progressively deeper, generally resulting in more severe injury than acids of comparable strength.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: A pattern of parallel linear abrasions/contusions on the back with intervening normal skin, consistent with a cane or rod, is described using which forensic term?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Tramline (railway-line) bruising describes two parallel linear contusions with a pale central strip, characteristically produced by a blow from a rod-shaped object such as a cane or stick, due to lateral tissue displacement.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Fabricated or self-inflicted wounds, sometimes seen in cases of false allegation, are suggested by which combination of features?
o: A single deep wound to a vital organ
Wounds located exclusively on the back
Wounds inconsistent with any weapon at the scene only
Superficial, multiple, parallel wounds in accessible areas sparing vital structures
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Self-inflicted or fabricated wounds tend to be superficial, multiple, roughly parallel, and confined to accessible, non-vital areas the person can easily reach, in contrast to genuine assault injuries.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: The presence of singeing of eyebrows/eyelashes and soot in the nostrils in a fire victim, together with elevated carboxyhemoglobin, supports which conclusion regarding manner and timing?
o: The fire started after death occurred
The person had no exposure to smoke
Carboxyhemoglobin is irrelevant to this determination
The findings only occur in postmortem burning
The person was alive and breathing during the fire (antemortem exposure)
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Singed facial hair together with soot deep in the airway and significantly elevated carboxyhemoglobin collectively indicate the victim was alive and actively breathing in the smoke-filled environment during the fire.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: A 'sucked wound' or bite mark left on a victim's skin can be forensically valuable primarily for which purpose?
o: Comparison with dental impressions of a suspect for identification
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Bite marks can retain the pattern of a perpetrator's dentition, allowing forensic odontologists to compare the pattern with dental impressions of a suspect as a form of identification evidence.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.s: Injuries described as 'antemortem' versus 'postmortem' based on wound characteristics are important in forensic practice primarily to help establish which of the following?
o: The exact identity of the victim
The blood type of the assailant
The sequence of events and whether an injury contributed to the cause of death
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/mechani.e: Differentiating antemortem from postmortem injuries helps reconstruct the sequence of events, determine which injuries were sustained while the victim was alive, and establish their contribution to the cause of death.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Which organ is the primary site of biotransformation (metabolism) for most poisons and drugs in the body?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: The liver, rich in cytochrome P450 enzymes and other metabolic pathways, is the principal organ responsible for biotransformation of most xenobiotics and poisons into more water-soluble, excretable forms.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: In cases of suspected poisoning, which viscera are classically preserved and sent for chemical (toxicological) analysis at autopsy?
o: Stomach with contents, a portion of liver, kidney, and blood/urine
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Standard forensic protocol preserves stomach and contents, intestine, liver, kidney, and blood/urine samples in appropriate preservatives (e.g., saturated saline) for toxicological analysis, as these best reflect ingested poison and its metabolism.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Which preservative is classically used for viscera samples sent for toxicological analysis when alcohol-based preservatives must be avoided?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Saturated saline solution is preferred as a preservative for viscera intended for toxicological analysis (especially for volatile poisons like alcohol) since alcohol-based preservatives would interfere with detection of ingested ethanol or other volatiles.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Organophosphate poisoning (e.g., from agricultural pesticides) produces toxicity primarily through which mechanism?
o: Direct hepatotoxicity via free radical formation
Blockade of sodium channels in cardiac myocytes
Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase leading to cholinergic excess
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Organophosphates irreversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing accumulation of acetylcholine at synapses and neuromuscular junctions, producing a cholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE symptoms, miosis, bradycardia, muscle fasciculations).

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: The classic antidote regimen for organophosphate poisoning includes which two drugs?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Atropine reverses muscarinic cholinergic effects, while pralidoxime (2-PAM) reactivates acetylcholinesterase if given before 'aging' of the enzyme-organophosphate complex occurs, together forming the standard antidotal regimen.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Cyanide poisoning causes cellular death primarily through which mechanism?
o: Direct hemolysis of red blood cells
Inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase, blocking oxidative phosphorylation
Direct corrosive injury to the gastrointestinal mucosa
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Cyanide binds and inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV) in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, halting oxidative phosphorylation and causing cellular (histotoxic) hypoxia despite adequate oxygen delivery.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: A characteristic smell of 'bitter almonds' on the breath at autopsy is classically associated with poisoning by which substance?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Cyanide poisoning is classically associated with a bitter almond odor on the breath and in the stomach contents, though the ability to detect this smell is genetically variable among examiners.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes tissue hypoxia primarily through which mechanism?
o: Direct destruction of red blood cell membranes
Corrosive injury to the respiratory tract
High-affinity binding to hemoglobin forming carboxyhemoglobin, impairing oxygen transport
Direct suppression of the respiratory center only
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin with roughly 200-250 times the affinity of oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin and shifting the oxygen dissociation curve leftward, severely impairing oxygen delivery to tissues.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: At autopsy, carbon monoxide poisoning classically produces which characteristic finding in the blood and postmortem lividity?
o: No color change in blood at all
Cherry-red discoloration of blood and postmortem lividity
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Carboxyhemoglobin imparts a bright cherry-red color to the blood and postmortem lividity, a classic and useful autopsy finding suggesting carbon monoxide poisoning.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Methemoglobinemia, causing 'chocolate-brown' colored blood, is classically caused by exposure to which type of agent?
o: Oxidizing agents such as nitrites/nitrates or certain aniline-derived compounds
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Oxidizing agents like nitrites, nitrobenzene, and certain aniline dyes convert hemoglobin iron from ferrous to ferric state, forming methemoglobin, which imparts a characteristic chocolate-brown color to the blood and impairs oxygen delivery.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Arsenic poisoning, when chronic, classically produces which characteristic finding on the nails?
o: Beau's lines from unrelated illness only
Mees' lines (transverse white bands on the nails)
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Mees' lines are transverse white bands across the nail plate classically associated with chronic arsenic poisoning (and other heavy metal toxicities), reflecting temporary disruption of nail matrix keratinization.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Acute arsenic poisoning classically presents with which gastrointestinal symptom complex, historically termed 'rice water stools'?
o: Severe vomiting and profuse watery diarrhea mimicking cholera
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Acute arsenic poisoning classically produces severe gastroenteritis with vomiting and profuse, watery 'rice-water' stools, historically leading to confusion with cholera in poisoning cases.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Chelation therapy with dimercaprol (BAL) or succimer is the standard treatment for poisoning with which class of substances?
o: Heavy metals such as arsenic, lead, and mercury
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Dimercaprol and succimer are chelating agents that bind heavy metals (arsenic, lead, mercury), forming stable, water-soluble complexes that can be excreted, forming the mainstay treatment for significant heavy metal poisoning.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Chronic lead poisoning classically produces which characteristic finding along the gum margins?
o: White plaques on the buccal mucosa
Burton's line (blue-black line at the gingival margin)
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Burton's line, a blue-black discoloration at the gum margin caused by deposition of lead sulfide, is a classic sign of chronic lead poisoning, alongside microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling of red cells.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Lead poisoning classically causes which type of anemia, associated with basophilic stippling of red blood cells?
o: Microcytic, hypochromic anemia due to impaired heme synthesis
Anemia of chronic disease with normal iron studies
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Lead inhibits several enzymes in the heme biosynthetic pathway (e.g., ALA dehydratase, ferrochelatase), producing a microcytic, hypochromic anemia with characteristic basophilic stippling of erythrocytes.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Mercury poisoning, particularly from organic mercury compounds, classically produces toxicity primarily affecting which organ system?
o: Central nervous system, causing symptoms such as ataxia, tremor, and visual field constriction
The reproductive system exclusively with no neurological involvement
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Organic mercury (e.g., methylmercury) is highly neurotoxic, causing ataxia, sensory disturbances, tremor, and constriction of visual fields, classically illustrated by Minamata disease from contaminated fish consumption.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Aluminum phosphide (commonly used as a grain fumigant and a common suicidal poison in South Asia) is toxic primarily through release of which gas after contact with moisture/gastric acid?
o: Phosphine gas, which inhibits cytochrome c oxidase and causes profound cardiotoxicity
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Aluminum phosphide reacts with moisture and gastric acid to liberate phosphine gas, which inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome c oxidase and causes severe cardiotoxicity (refractory hypotension, arrhythmias), a leading cause of fatal poisoning in some regions.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Barbiturate poisoning classically causes death primarily through which mechanism?
o: Direct hepatotoxicity causing fulminant liver failure
Central respiratory depression leading to hypoxia and cardiovascular collapse
Acute renal failure from tubular necrosis
Cardiac arrhythmia from sodium channel blockade as the primary mechanism
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Barbiturates potentiate GABA-mediated inhibition, causing dose-dependent CNS and respiratory depression; death in overdose most commonly results from respiratory failure and subsequent hypoxic cardiovascular collapse.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Opioid overdose classically presents with which triad of clinical findings?
o: Miosis (pinpoint pupils), respiratory depression, and altered/depressed consciousness
Blurred vision, dry mouth, and urinary retention
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: The classic opioid overdose triad consists of pinpoint pupils (miosis), respiratory depression, and depressed level of consciousness, reversible with the opioid antagonist naloxone.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Naloxone, the standard antidote for opioid overdose, acts through which mechanism?
o: Direct stimulation of the respiratory center independent of opioid receptors
Osmotic diuresis to enhance renal excretion
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist that rapidly displaces opioids from mu-receptors, reversing respiratory depression and sedation in overdose, though its short half-life may require repeat dosing.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Alcohol (ethanol) poisoning is metabolized in the liver primarily via which enzyme to produce acetaldehyde?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Alcohol dehydrogenase catalyzes the first step of ethanol metabolism, oxidizing ethanol to the toxic intermediate acetaldehyde, which is subsequently metabolized to acetate by acetaldehyde dehydrogenase.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Methanol poisoning causes characteristic ocular toxicity (blindness) primarily due to accumulation of which toxic metabolite?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Methanol is metabolized via alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde and then formic acid, which is directly toxic to the retina and optic nerve, causing characteristic blindness and severe metabolic acidosis.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Ethylene glycol (antifreeze) poisoning classically produces which characteristic finding in the urine due to its toxic metabolites?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Ethylene glycol is metabolized to glycolic and oxalic acid; oxalic acid combines with calcium to form calcium oxalate crystals, which deposit in renal tubules and appear in the urine, associated with severe anion-gap metabolic acidosis and renal failure.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Fomepizole is used as an antidote in poisoning with which two substances by inhibiting alcohol dehydrogenase?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Fomepizole competitively inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, preventing the conversion of methanol and ethylene glycol into their highly toxic metabolites (formic acid and glycolic/oxalic acid respectively).

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose causes hepatotoxicity primarily through accumulation of which toxic metabolite once glutathione stores are depleted?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: In paracetamol overdose, the minor CYP-mediated metabolite NAPQI accumulates once glutathione conjugation pathways are saturated, causing centrilobular hepatic necrosis unless treated promptly with N-acetylcysteine.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: N-acetylcysteine, the antidote for paracetamol overdose, works primarily through which mechanism?
o: Replenishing hepatic glutathione stores to detoxify NAPQI
Enhancing renal excretion via osmotic diuresis
Blocking hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes completely
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: N-acetylcysteine acts as a glutathione precursor/substitute, replenishing depleted hepatic glutathione stores that are needed to conjugate and detoxify the toxic metabolite NAPQI, preventing hepatocellular necrosis.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Salicylate (aspirin) poisoning classically produces which acid-base disturbance pattern in adults?
o: Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic (anion-gap) acidosis
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Salicylates directly stimulate the respiratory center causing hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis, while also uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation and accumulating organic acids, producing a concurrent anion-gap metabolic acidosis — a classic mixed picture.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Datura (Jimson weed) poisoning, containing anticholinergic alkaloids, classically produces which toxic syndrome?
o: Cholinergic toxidrome with excessive salivation and miosis
Opioid toxidrome with pinpoint pupils and respiratory depression
Sympathomimetic toxidrome with diaphoresis and normal pupils
Anticholinergic toxidrome: mydriasis, dry flushed skin, urinary retention, delirium, hyperthermia
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Datura contains atropine-like anticholinergic alkaloids (atropine, scopolamine, hyoscyamine), producing the classic anticholinergic toxidrome remembered as 'red as a beet, dry as a bone, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, hot as a hare.'

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Snake venom of the elapid family (e.g., cobra, krait) is predominantly which type of toxin, causing paralysis?
o: Hemotoxin causing widespread hemorrhage as the predominant effect
Cytotoxin causing local tissue necrosis exclusively
Cardiotoxin causing only direct myocardial infarction
Neurotoxin, causing descending flaccid paralysis via neuromuscular blockade
Nephrotoxin causing isolated renal failure without paralysis
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Elapid venoms (cobras, kraits, coral snakes) are predominantly neurotoxic, blocking neuromuscular transmission and causing a descending flaccid paralysis that can progress to fatal respiratory failure.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Viper snake envenomation (family Viperidae) classically produces toxicity primarily through which mechanism?
o: Pure neurotoxic paralysis without any local reaction
Selective cardiotoxicity with no hemorrhagic component
Exclusively renal toxicity without coagulation abnormality
Hemotoxic/vasculotoxic effects causing coagulopathy, hemorrhage, and local tissue necrosis
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Viper venoms are predominantly hemotoxic, causing local swelling and necrosis at the bite site along with systemic coagulopathy, spontaneous hemorrhage, and potential acute kidney injury.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: The Widmark formula in forensic toxicology is used for which purpose?
o: Back-calculating blood alcohol concentration at an earlier time point (e.g., at the time of an accident)
Calculating the lethal dose of arsenic
Estimating time since death from body temperature
Determining the postmortem interval from potassium levels
Estimating the age of a bruise
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: The Widmark formula estimates blood alcohol concentration at a prior time point (e.g., at the time of driving) based on a later measured BAC, body weight, sex-specific distribution factor, and elimination rate.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: In forensic toxicology, 'postmortem redistribution' refers to which phenomenon that complicates interpretation of drug levels at autopsy?
o: The complete absence of drug metabolism before death
Immediate degradation of all drugs at the moment of death
Uniform drug distribution throughout the body at all times
Enhanced drug absorption from the gut after death
Diffusion of drugs from tissue reservoirs into central blood after death, altering measured concentrations
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Postmortem redistribution describes the movement of drugs (especially those with large volumes of distribution) from tissue depots such as the lungs and liver into central blood after death, which can falsely elevate postmortem blood drug concentrations.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Which toxicological screening test is commonly used as an initial, rapid, qualitative method to detect classes of drugs of abuse in urine?
o: Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) as the initial screen
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Immunoassay-based screening tests provide rapid, relatively inexpensive qualitative detection of drug classes in urine, typically followed by confirmatory testing (e.g., GC-MS) for definitive identification and quantification.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) is considered the gold-standard confirmatory test in forensic toxicology primarily because of which feature?
o: Its extremely low cost compared to immunoassay
Its ability to be performed without any laboratory equipment
High specificity and sensitivity for definitive identification and quantification of substances
Its use exclusively for detecting heavy metals
Its complete independence from sample preparation
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: GC-MS separates and identifies compounds based on their mass spectral fragmentation pattern with very high specificity and sensitivity, making it the confirmatory reference method in forensic toxicology.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Corrosive poisoning from a strong acid such as sulfuric acid characteristically produces which finding on oral/esophageal examination?
o: Complete absence of any mucosal change
Isolated dental erosion without mucosal injury
Bright red, non-necrotic mucosal hyperemia only
Multiple discrete ulcers resembling herpetic lesions
Coagulative necrosis with a grey-white, leathery eschar at contact sites
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Strong acid ingestion produces coagulative necrosis of the mucosa, forming a firm, grey-white to brown-black leathery eschar at points of contact (lips, mouth, esophagus, stomach).

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Kerosene (hydrocarbon) poisoning, common in accidental childhood ingestion, poses its greatest danger through which complication?
o: Direct cardiotoxicity as the primary concern
Hepatic failure as the most immediate life-threatening risk
Renal failure as the most immediate life-threatening risk
Aspiration pneumonitis from low viscosity and high volatility
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Kerosene's low viscosity and high volatility make it prone to aspiration into the lungs (either during ingestion or with vomiting), causing chemical pneumonitis, which is the primary danger rather than systemic absorption.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Which forensic toxicology principle states that 'the dose makes the poison,' emphasizing that toxicity is fundamentally dependent on which factor?
o: The route of administration exclusively, regardless of amount
The legal classification of the substance
The quantity/concentration of a substance absorbed relative to body response
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: This foundational toxicological principle (attributed to Paracelsus) holds that virtually any substance can be toxic at a sufficient dose, and conversely, that dose (not identity alone) is the key determinant of whether a substance produces a toxic effect.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Which classification describes poisons whose primary toxic action is on the central nervous system, such as strychnine and cocaine?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Neurotoxic poisons exert their primary toxic effect on the central or peripheral nervous system; strychnine causes convulsions via glycine receptor antagonism, while cocaine has stimulant CNS effects.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Strychnine poisoning classically produces which distinctive clinical picture?
o: Painless progressive paralysis with preserved consciousness
Pure sedation without any motor activity
Violent, painful generalized convulsions with the patient remaining conscious between episodes
Isolated visual disturbances without other symptoms
Selective cardiac toxicity without neuromuscular involvement
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Strychnine antagonizes inhibitory glycine receptors in the spinal cord, causing intensely painful, violent generalized convulsions with hyperextension (opisthotonus) while the patient typically remains conscious between episodes.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.s: Irritant poisons, a toxicological classification that includes agents like arsenic and mercuric chloride, primarily produce toxicity through which mechanism at the site of contact?
o: Selective blockade of neuromuscular transmission only
Local inflammation, corrosion, or irritation of mucous membranes and the gastrointestinal tract
Direct action limited to cardiac tissue exclusively
Pure central nervous system depression without any local effect
Exclusive renal toxicity with no gastrointestinal involvement
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/forensi.e: Irritant poisons act locally to inflame, corrode, or irritate tissues they contact (particularly the gastrointestinal mucosa), producing symptoms such as vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, in addition to any systemic absorption effects.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: In the medico-legal definition, 'rape' is fundamentally classified as which type of offence rather than a purely medical diagnosis?
o: A medical diagnosis established solely by the physical examination
A legal offence, determined by the court based on evidence including but not limited to medical findings
A psychiatric diagnosis requiring a mental health evaluation
A finding that can be established purely by laboratory tests
An offence that can only be confirmed by DNA evidence
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Rape is ultimately a legal determination made by the court based on the totality of evidence; the medical examiner's role is to document findings and provide an opinion, not to declare a legal verdict of rape.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: The medico-legal examination of an alleged sexual assault survivor should ideally be conducted with which of the following as a foundational principle?
o: Examination without consent if the police request it
Examination only in the presence of the alleged accused
Informed consent, privacy, and a trained, sensitive, ideally same-sex or survivor's-choice examiner
Mandatory examination by a male physician exclusively regardless of preference
A public examination for evidentiary transparency
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Ethical and medico-legal guidelines require informed consent, a private setting, and a sensitive, trained examiner (with the survivor given a choice of examiner's gender where possible) throughout sexual assault examination.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: The 'two-finger test' for assessing vaginal laxity in sexual assault examinations is regarded by current medico-legal and human rights standards as which of the following?
o: The current gold-standard diagnostic test for confirming rape
A mandatory legal requirement in every jurisdiction
A reliable indicator of a woman's sexual history relevant to the case
An unscientific, invasive, and unethical practice that should be discontinued
An accurate predictor of consent at the time of the incident
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: The two-finger test has been widely condemned by courts, medical bodies, and human rights organizations as unscientific, degrading, and irrelevant to establishing whether sexual assault occurred, and its use has been discontinued in updated guidelines.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: In an alleged sexual assault examination, the term 'hymen' findings should be interpreted with which important caveat?
o: An intact hymen definitively excludes any sexual contact
A torn hymen definitively proves recent sexual assault
Hymenal appearance alone (including an intact hymen) cannot reliably confirm or exclude a history of penetration
Hymenal shape is identical in all individuals
Hymenal findings are the only evidence required for a legal verdict
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Hymenal tissue is highly variable in shape and elasticity, may not tear with penetration, and can heal without visible signs; therefore, hymenal findings alone are unreliable for confirming or excluding sexual contact, an important point in contemporary forensic guidelines.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Collection of forensic evidence in a sexual assault examination (a 'rape kit') is most useful when performed within which general time frame after the incident?
o: As soon as possible, ideally within 72-96 hours
Only if the survivor has not bathed within the past month
There is no time sensitivity to evidence collection
Only within the first hour and never afterward
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Biological evidence such as semen, hair, and DNA degrades and is lost over time (through washing, urination, defecation), so evidence collection is most valuable when performed as soon as possible, generally within 72-96 hours, though some evidence may persist longer.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: The presence of motile spermatozoa in vaginal swabs taken from a sexual assault survivor provides evidence most useful for estimating which parameter?
o: The identity of the assailant with certainty
Recency of the sexual contact (since motility is typically lost within hours)
The exact age of the survivor
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Sperm motility is generally lost within a few hours after deposition in the vagina (though non-motile sperm and DNA may persist longer), so finding motile sperm suggests very recent sexual contact.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Acid phosphatase testing on vaginal swabs in a sexual assault examination is used as a presumptive test for the presence of which substance?
o: Vaginal secretions of the survivor only
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Acid phosphatase is present in high concentration in seminal fluid; a positive test on vaginal swabs serves as a presumptive (not definitive) indicator of recent seminal fluid deposition, to be confirmed by more specific tests.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Confirmatory identification of semen in forensic samples is most specifically achieved by detecting which substance/marker?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA, also called p30) is a highly specific marker for seminal fluid, used as confirmatory evidence of semen presence in forensic samples, distinct from the presumptive acid phosphatase test.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: The legal age of consent and the definition of statutory rape are primarily determined by which of the following?
o: Universal international medical consensus applicable everywhere identically
The physical maturity (puberty status) of the minor exclusively
The applicable law of the jurisdiction, which varies by country/region
The opinion of the examining physician alone
The marital status of the accused only
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: The age of consent and definitions of statutory offences are established by each jurisdiction's specific legislation, and vary considerably between countries and regions; the physician documents findings but the legal age threshold is set by law.
