forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: In medico-legal examination of a child suspected of sexual abuse, which principle should guide the approach to the physical examination?
o: Repeated examinations by multiple untrained examiners for corroboration
Examination should always be deferred regardless of urgency
The child should be examined without any parent/guardian support present
A gentle, non-traumatic examination by a trained specialist, minimizing repeated examinations
General anesthesia is mandatory for every child examination
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Best practice for suspected child sexual abuse emphasizes minimizing trauma through examination by a trained specialist, limiting repeat examinations, and providing appropriate psychological support throughout the process.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Anal findings such as fissures or scarring in a suspected case of sexual abuse must be interpreted with caution because they may also result from which non-abusive cause?
o: They are always specific and diagnostic of abuse with no other explanation possible
They can never occur in the absence of abuse
They only occur following surgical intervention
They are exclusively seen in cases of confirmed abuse
Chronic constipation or other benign anorectal conditions
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Anal fissures, dilatation, and other findings can arise from benign causes such as chronic constipation, so a thorough medical history and correlation with other findings are essential before attributing such signs to abuse.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Determination of virginity based solely on physical examination findings is considered by modern forensic medicine to be which of the following?
o: A precise and universally reliable determination
Medically and scientifically unreliable, and its use is discouraged
Legally mandatory in every jurisdiction before marriage
Achievable with 100% accuracy using the two-finger test
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Modern forensic and medical consensus holds that 'virginity testing' via physical examination lacks scientific validity, as hymenal and other findings cannot reliably confirm or exclude prior sexual activity; such practices are increasingly condemned internationally.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: In cases of alleged male sexual assault (of a male survivor), which examination site is typically most relevant for evidence of anal penetration?
o: The vaginal region exclusively, which is not applicable
The perianal and anal region for injury and biological evidence
The oral cavity exclusively in every case
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: In male sexual assault involving anal penetration, examination should focus on the perianal and anal region for signs of trauma, along with collection of relevant swabs for biological evidence, in addition to a general physical examination.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: 'Consent' in the context of sexual offence law is generally invalidated by law when obtained under which circumstance?
o: A prior long-term relationship between the parties
Force, fear, fraud, intoxication incapacitating judgment, or from a person below the legal age of consent
Financial transaction between consenting adults, which is a separate legal matter
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Legally valid consent requires voluntary agreement free from coercion, fraud, or incapacitating intoxication, and cannot be given by a person below the legal age of consent or one lacking mental capacity, regardless of apparent agreement.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Medical documentation in a suspected sexual assault case should include which essential element for legal purposes?
o: Only the examiner's personal opinion on guilt or innocence
A detailed, objective, contemporaneous record of history, examination findings, and evidence collected with a clear chain of custody
Handwritten notes without any signature or date
A summary omitting details of injuries to spare the survivor distress
Verbal reporting only, without any written record
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Thorough, objective, and contemporaneous documentation with a properly maintained chain of custody for collected evidence is essential for the medico-legal report to hold evidentiary value in subsequent legal proceedings.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: The term 'chain of custody' in forensic evidence handling refers to which concept?
o: A documented, unbroken trail accounting for the location, handling, and control of evidence from collection to court presentation
The order in which witnesses testify in court
The sequence of medical treatments given to a survivor
The hierarchy of hospital staff performing an examination
The list of possible suspects in a case
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Chain of custody documents every individual who has handled evidence, when, and under what conditions, ensuring the integrity and admissibility of evidence is not compromised or challenged in legal proceedings.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: In cases of suspected drug-facilitated sexual assault, which biological sample is most useful for detecting common sedative agents if collected promptly?
o: Hair sample only, useful for acute detection
Urine, due to its longer detection window for many sedatives compared to blood
Skin swab from an unaffected area
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Urine generally provides a longer detection window than blood for many sedative-hypnotics and other drugs used in facilitated sexual assault, making prompt urine collection valuable, though blood may also be collected for concurrent analysis.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Which examination finding is considered supportive, but not solely diagnostic, of recent forceful penetrative sexual contact in an adult female?
o: Presence of a normal-appearing hymen only
Presence of any vaginal discharge unrelated to trauma
Fresh lacerations or bruising of the genital/perianal region correlating with the history
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Fresh genital or perianal injuries consistent temporally and mechanistically with the reported history provide supportive medical evidence, though the absence of such injuries does not exclude assault, since many cases show no visible trauma.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: The examination and reporting of an alleged sexual assault case should avoid which of the following, per current ethical and legal standards?
o: Commenting on the survivor's moral character or past sexual history as evidence of consent
Collecting appropriate forensic samples with consent
Referring the survivor for psychological support
Recording the time and date of examination
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Modern legal and ethical standards prohibit using a survivor's past sexual history or character as evidence bearing on the veracity of the assault allegation or on consent in the specific incident being investigated.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: In determining the age of a survivor for medico-legal purposes when documentary evidence is unavailable, which method is commonly used?
o: Radiological assessment of bone age (ossification centers) and dental examination
Height measurement alone without further assessment
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: In the absence of birth records, forensic age estimation commonly relies on radiographic assessment of ossification centers/epiphyseal fusion and dental development, since these follow reasonably predictable age-related patterns, though with an inherent margin of error.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Medico-legal examination findings that are 'not consistent with' a history of assault should be communicated by the examining physician in which manner?
o: As definitive proof that no assault occurred
By refusing to complete the examination report
By altering the survivor's stated history to match examination findings
As an objective statement of medical findings, without definitively ruling out the occurrence of assault
By omitting any mention of the discrepancy from the report
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Since many genuine sexual assaults leave no visible physical findings, examiners should report objective findings without over-interpreting a normal examination as proof that no assault took place, leaving the ultimate determination to the judicial process.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Medico-legal examination of the accused in a sexual offence case may include which of the following, subject to legal authorization?
o: No examination of the accused is ever permissible under any circumstances
Examination for injuries, potency, and collection of biological samples for comparison
Only a verbal interview without any physical examination
Examination without any legal order or consent process
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: With appropriate legal authorization, the accused may be medically examined for injuries (e.g., scratch marks), assessment of sexual potency where relevant, and collection of biological samples (e.g., DNA) for forensic comparison.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: In the context of forensic gynecological examination, 'genital injury' correlating with a history of sexual assault is most commonly located in which region for adult female survivors?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: In adult female sexual assault survivors, genital injuries most frequently involve the posterior fourchette and fossa navicularis, areas of the vulva that are most susceptible to trauma during forceful penetration.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: The use of a colposcope in sexual assault forensic examination provides which advantage over unaided visual examination?
o: Magnified visualization and photographic documentation of subtle genital injuries
Detection of internal organ injuries unrelated to the genital exam
Replacement of the need for any laboratory testing
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Colposcopy provides magnification and photographic/video documentation capability, improving detection and objective recording of subtle genital injuries that might be missed on unaided visual examination.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Toluidine blue dye application during sexual assault examination is used to highlight which finding?
o: Subtle lacerations of the posterior fourchette by staining exposed nuclear material in disrupted epithelium
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Toluidine blue selectively stains exposed nuclei in areas where the superficial epithelial layer has been disrupted (as in lacerations), improving detection of subtle posterior fourchette injuries not visible to the naked eye.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Which statement best reflects current medico-legal understanding regarding the absence of genital injury in a reported case of forceful sexual assault?
o: Absence of injury conclusively proves that no assault occurred
Absence of injury is only possible if the survivor consented
Absence of injury means the history must be false
Genital injury is present in all cases of assault without exception
Absence of injury does not exclude sexual assault, as many cases (even forceful ones) show no visible trauma
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Multiple studies have shown that a substantial proportion of confirmed sexual assault cases, including forceful ones, show no visible genital injury due to tissue elasticity, examination timing, and other factors, so absence of injury does not exclude assault.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Pregnancy resulting from sexual assault raises which important medico-legal and clinical consideration in the examination and follow-up?
o: No action is required regarding pregnancy risk
Pregnancy testing should never be offered to survivors
Only termination of pregnancy should be discussed, with no other options
Offering emergency contraception where appropriate and timely, and discussing further reproductive health options
Pregnancy risk is irrelevant to the medico-legal examination
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Comprehensive care for sexual assault survivors includes timely counseling and offering of emergency contraception where clinically appropriate, pregnancy testing, and follow-up reproductive health support as part of holistic post-assault care.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Screening for sexually transmitted infections after an alleged sexual assault is recommended primarily for which reason?
o: To determine legal guilt of the accused
To detect and treat infections potentially transmitted during the assault and establish a baseline
It is never medically indicated after assault
Only to satisfy police requirements with no clinical value
To replace the need for any other forensic evidence collection
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: STI screening and, where indicated, prophylactic treatment are recommended as part of comprehensive post-assault medical care, both to address potential transmission during the assault and to establish a clinical baseline.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: In medico-legal terminology, 'unnatural offences' historically referenced in some legal codes typically refer to which acts?
o: Any consensual heterosexual intercourse between adults
Non-consensual or criminalized forms of anal or oral intercourse as defined by the applicable penal code
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Historical/legal terminology such as 'unnatural offences' in various penal codes has referred to specific criminalized sexual acts (varying by jurisdiction and evolving with legal reform), typically involving non-consensual anal or oral intercourse.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: The medico-legal report in a sexual assault case should be provided to which party through the proper legal channel?
o: The investigating police/legal authority, following the applicable jurisdiction's procedure
Directly to media outlets for public disclosure
Posted publicly on social media by the examining physician
Given only informally with no written record
Withheld indefinitely from all legal authorities
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: The medico-legal report is a formal legal document that must be transmitted through proper official/legal channels to the investigating authority, maintaining confidentiality and legal integrity throughout the process.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Which of the following best describes the appropriate physician's role when a survivor of sexual assault declines forensic examination or evidence collection?
o: Force the examination regardless of the survivor's wishes
Refuse to provide any medical care until the survivor consents to forensic examination
Report the survivor to police for non-cooperation
Respect the survivor's autonomy while providing information about available options and support services
Discharge the survivor immediately without offering any support
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Respecting patient autonomy is a fundamental ethical principle; survivors have the right to decline forensic examination while still being offered medical care, counseling, and information about their options, without coercion.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: In suspected cases of child sexual abuse, mandatory reporting laws in many jurisdictions require healthcare providers to do which of the following?
o: Maintain absolute confidentiality even from child protection authorities
Only report if the child explicitly requests it
Report reasonable suspicion of abuse to the appropriate child protection or legal authority
Wait for definitive proof before any reporting action
Report only to the family without involving authorities
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Many jurisdictions have mandatory reporting laws requiring healthcare professionals to report reasonable suspicion of child abuse to child protective services or law enforcement, overriding standard confidentiality in this specific context.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: In forensic examination following alleged sexual assault, clothing worn at the time of the incident should be handled in which manner?
o: Washed immediately to remove any offensive odor
Discarded as it has no evidentiary value
Carefully collected, air-dried if wet, and packaged separately in paper bags to preserve trace evidence
Placed together with other survivors' clothing in a single bag
Sealed permanently in plastic bags regardless of moisture content
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Clothing is an important source of trace evidence (fibers, hair, biological fluid) and should be air-dried if damp and packaged individually in paper (not plastic, which promotes mold/degradation) bags to preserve evidentiary integrity.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Photographic documentation of injuries in a sexual assault examination should include which element for proper forensic value?
o: Only close-up images without any reference scale
Photographs taken by the survivor themselves without medical supervision
No photography, as it is never permitted in forensic examination
Photography only if requested by the accused
A scale ruler in the frame along with patient identification and date/time
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Forensic photography should include a scale ruler for accurate size reference, along with proper labeling (case identifiers, date, time) to ensure the images have full evidentiary value in subsequent legal proceedings.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: The examination of a sexual assault survivor should routinely include assessment for which additional non-genital finding relevant to the alleged history?
o: Only the genital area, with no assessment of other body regions
Extragenital injuries such as bruising, bite marks, or restraint marks on other body areas
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: A comprehensive sexual assault examination assesses the entire body for extragenital injuries (bruising, bite marks, restraint marks, defensive wounds) that may corroborate the reported history, not just the genital area.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Pregnancy testing in the context of a sexual assault examination serves which primary clinical purpose?
o: Establishing a baseline pregnancy status before consideration of emergency contraception
Determining the identity of the assailant
Assessing the survivor's fertility for unrelated reasons
Replacing the need for STI screening
Confirming the exact time of the assault
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Baseline pregnancy testing helps guide clinical decision-making regarding emergency contraception and appropriate counseling, and is a standard component of comprehensive post-assault care.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: When a survivor of sexual assault has consumed alcohol or drugs voluntarily prior to the incident, which principle applies regarding consent and culpability?
o: Voluntary intoxication of the survivor does not imply consent to sexual activity and does not diminish the criminal culpability of an assailant
The survivor is always considered legally at fault
Consent is automatically presumed if any substance was consumed
The assault cannot be prosecuted if either party had consumed alcohol
Intoxication of the survivor invalidates all forensic evidence collected
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Voluntary substance use by a survivor does not constitute consent to sexual activity nor reduce the assailant's legal culpability; in many jurisdictions, incapacitation from intoxication in fact negates the possibility of valid consent.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: The medico-legal examiner's opinion in a sexual assault case should be phrased with which appropriate level of certainty?
o: An absolute, unqualified statement of 'confirmed rape' in every case with any finding
A definitive statement of the accused's guilt
No opinion should ever be offered, only raw data
A statement based solely on the survivor's demeanor during history-taking
Findings are 'consistent with,' 'not inconsistent with,' or provide no support for the alleged history, without overstating certainty
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Examiners should offer carefully qualified opinions correlating objective findings with the reported history, avoiding overstated conclusions of certainty, since the final legal determination rests with the court considering all evidence.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV should be considered in sexual assault cases under which circumstance?
o: In every case regardless of exposure risk or timing
Only if the assailant's HIV status is confirmed positive with certainty
Never, as it is not part of sexual assault care
When there is a plausible risk of HIV exposure and the survivor presents within the effective treatment window (ideally within 72 hours)
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis should be offered when there is a plausible risk of exposure and the survivor presents within the window during which prophylaxis remains effective, ideally within 72 hours of the incident.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.s: Which statement best reflects appropriate psychological support in the management of a sexual assault survivor?
o: Psychological support is unnecessary if physical injuries are absent
Only the police, not medical staff, should address psychological needs
Psychological referral should be delayed until after legal proceedings conclude
Referral for counseling and psychological support should be offered as an integral part of comprehensive care
Psychological support should only be offered to survivors under 18
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/sexual-.e: Comprehensive sexual assault care recognizes the psychological impact of trauma and includes timely referral for counseling and mental health support as a standard, integral component of care, regardless of the presence of physical injury.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: Informed consent for a medical or surgical procedure requires that the patient be given information about which of the following?
o: Only the name of the surgeon performing the procedure
Only the cost of the procedure
Only the expected duration of hospital stay
The nature of the procedure, its risks, benefits, and reasonable alternatives
Only the anesthesia type to be used
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Valid informed consent requires disclosure of the nature of the proposed procedure, material risks and benefits, and reasonable alternative options, enabling the patient to make an autonomous, informed decision.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: Which type of consent is legally considered valid for a routine physical examination in an adult patient?
o: Implied consent, inferred from the patient's cooperative behavior
Written consent is mandatory for every physical examination
No consent is required for physical examination
Consent from a family member only, regardless of patient capacity
Consent obtained after the examination is completed
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Implied consent, inferred from a patient's voluntary presentation and cooperative participation, is generally sufficient for routine, low-risk examinations, whereas invasive or higher-risk procedures typically require explicit written consent.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: For consent to be legally valid, the patient must fulfill which basic criterion?
o: Be of legal age and possess the mental capacity to understand the information given
Be accompanied by a lawyer at all times
Have completed at least a secondary school education
Be free of any chronic illness
Provide consent only in the presence of police
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Valid consent requires that the individual has attained the legal age of majority (or consent is obtained from a guardian for minors) and possesses adequate mental capacity to understand the nature and consequences of the decision.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: In an emergency where a patient is unconscious and unable to give consent, and no guardian is immediately available, treatment is generally justified under which legal doctrine?
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: The doctrine of necessity permits healthcare providers to render emergency treatment necessary to preserve life or prevent serious harm when a patient cannot consent and no substitute decision-maker is immediately available.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: 'Medical negligence' is legally established when which combination of elements is proven?
o: Any adverse outcome of treatment regardless of the standard of care provided
The patient's dissatisfaction with the outcome alone
A bad outcome occurring during any surgical procedure
Duty of care, breach of that duty, causation, and resulting damage
Failure to achieve a complete cure
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Medical negligence requires proof of all four elements: the existence of a duty of care, a breach of the accepted standard of care, that breach causing harm, and demonstrable damage to the patient — a bad outcome alone is insufficient.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The legal principle 'res ipsa loquitur' ('the thing speaks for itself') applies in medical negligence cases under which circumstance?
o: Whenever a patient dies during treatment, regardless of circumstances
When the injury is of a type that would not normally occur without negligence, and the instrumentality was under the defendant's control
Only in cases involving surgical instruments left inside a patient exclusively
Never applies in medical negligence cases
Only when the patient explicitly alleges negligence in writing
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Res ipsa loquitur allows an inference of negligence when the harm is of a kind that ordinarily does not occur absent negligence, and the instrumentality causing harm was under the exclusive control of the defendant, shifting the evidentiary burden.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: 'Vicarious liability' in a hospital setting refers to which legal concept?
o: The patient's own responsibility for their illness
A doctor's liability for the actions of another unrelated doctor
The employer/institution's legal responsibility for negligent acts of its employees performed within the scope of employment
Liability that never applies to hospital administration
A form of criminal liability exclusively
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Vicarious liability holds an employer (e.g., a hospital) legally responsible for the negligent acts of its employees (e.g., nurses, resident doctors) committed in the course of their employment duties.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: Professional misconduct by a physician, as distinct from negligence, typically refers to which type of behavior?
o: Any single instance of an unsuccessful treatment outcome
A diagnostic error made despite reasonable care
A complication that is a recognized risk of a properly performed procedure
Any deviation from a patient's personal treatment preference
Violation of ethical or professional standards of conduct, such as fraud or breach of confidentiality
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Professional misconduct involves violations of ethical/professional codes of conduct (e.g., fraud, breach of confidentiality, unethical advertising), which is judged by medical councils and is distinct from negligence, which involves a failure of the standard of clinical care.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The concept of 'privileged communication' in the doctor-patient relationship primarily concerns which of the following?
o: The doctor's right to charge higher fees for confidential consultations
Protection of confidential information shared by the patient from unauthorized disclosure
A patient's right to demand a specific treatment
The doctor's right to refuse treatment for any reason
A hospital's right to share records freely with insurance companies
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Privileged communication refers to the ethical and often legal obligation to maintain confidentiality of information disclosed by a patient during the course of medical care, subject to specific legally recognized exceptions.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: Breach of medical confidentiality may be legally and ethically justified under which of the following circumstances?
o: Whenever a journalist requests patient information
When required by law (e.g., mandatory disease reporting) or to prevent serious harm to identifiable third parties
To share information with the patient's employer without consent
Whenever the treating doctor personally finds it convenient
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Exceptions to confidentiality are narrowly recognized, including legally mandated reporting (e.g., notifiable diseases, certain injuries) and situations where disclosure is necessary to prevent serious, identifiable harm to third parties (duty to warn).

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The ethical principle of 'autonomy' in medical ethics primarily refers to which of the following?
o: The doctor's authority to make all treatment decisions unilaterally
The hospital's independence from government regulation
A patient's right to demand any treatment regardless of medical appropriateness
The right of a doctor to refuse all patients
Respecting a patient's right to make informed decisions about their own care
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Autonomy is the ethical principle that respects a competent patient's right to self-determination, including the right to accept or refuse recommended medical treatment after being adequately informed.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The ethical principle of 'beneficence' in medical practice requires the physician to do which of the following?
o: Avoid all forms of patient contact
Act in the best interest of the patient, promoting their well-being
Prioritize personal financial gain over patient welfare
Follow patient instructions without any professional judgment
Refuse to treat patients with poor prognosis
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Beneficence obligates physicians to act positively to promote the patient's welfare and best interests, balanced alongside respect for autonomy and the principle of non-maleficence.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The ethical principle of 'non-maleficence,' often summarized as 'first, do no harm,' requires which physician obligation?
o: Prioritizing research outcomes over patient safety
Ensuring absolute cure in every case
Ignoring risks if a treatment might be beneficial
Avoiding actions that cause unnecessary harm or risk of harm to the patient
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Non-maleficence obligates physicians to avoid causing unnecessary harm, carefully weighing potential risks against benefits before undertaking any intervention.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The ethical principle of 'justice' in medical ethics primarily concerns which of the following?
o: A doctor's right to charge unlimited fees
Preferential treatment for wealthy patients only
Fair and equitable distribution of healthcare resources and treatment among patients
The legal punishment of patients who violate hospital rules
The right of a hospital to deny care based on nationality
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Justice in medical ethics addresses the fair, equitable, and non-discriminatory allocation of healthcare resources and access to treatment among individuals and populations.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: A 'living will' or 'advance directive' allows a competent individual to do which of the following?
o: Appoint a new physician for another person
Specify in advance their wishes regarding future medical treatment if they become unable to communicate
Mandate a specific surgeon for future procedures
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: An advance directive (living will) allows a person, while still competent, to document their preferences regarding future medical interventions (e.g., life support) in the event they later lose decision-making capacity.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: 'Euthanasia' refers to which of the following medical-ethical concepts?
o: The deliberate act of ending a person's life to relieve suffering, a practice with significant legal and ethical variation across jurisdictions
The routine discontinuation of all medical treatment for any illness
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Euthanasia involves deliberately ending a patient's life (actively or passively) to relieve intractable suffering; its legality and ethical acceptance vary considerably worldwide and remain subjects of ongoing debate.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The distinction between 'active' and 'passive' euthanasia is generally based on which factor?
o: The age of the patient involved
Whether death results from a deliberate act (e.g., lethal injection) versus withholding/withdrawing life-sustaining treatment
Whether the patient is conscious at the time
The location where the act takes place
The specialty of the treating physician
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Active euthanasia involves a deliberate act causing death (e.g., administering a lethal substance), while passive euthanasia involves withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment, allowing the underlying disease to progress to death.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: Organ transplantation from a deceased donor generally requires which prerequisite condition to be legally certified before organ retrieval?
o: Certification of brain death (or cardiac death, per protocol) by qualified physicians per legal criteria
Consent from the organ recipient's family only
A minimum waiting period of one year after death
Payment of a fee by the recipient to the donor's family
No formal death certification is required
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Deceased organ donation requires proper legal certification of death — typically brain death (or, in donation-after-circulatory-death protocols, cardiac death) — determined by qualified physicians following established medical and legal criteria, before organ retrieval can proceed.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: Brain death is legally and medically defined as which of the following?
o: A deep coma from which recovery is still possible
Irreversible cessation of all functions of the entire brain, including the brainstem
Loss of higher cortical function alone with an intact brainstem
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Brain death is defined as the complete and irreversible cessation of all functions of the entire brain, including the brainstem, distinguishing it from a persistent vegetative state where brainstem function may be preserved.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The sale of human organs for transplantation, as opposed to voluntary altruistic donation, is regarded by most national and international ethical frameworks as which of the following?
o: A universally accepted and legal practice
Encouraged as the primary method of organ procurement
Ethically equivalent to blood donation with no special concerns
Ethically problematic and prohibited in most jurisdictions due to exploitation concerns
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Commercial organ trading is widely prohibited and considered ethically problematic due to risks of exploitation of vulnerable donors, commodification of the human body, and inequitable access, with most frameworks endorsing only voluntary, altruistic donation.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: A 'dying declaration' in forensic medico-legal practice refers to a statement made by which person, under which condition?
o: Any witness present at a crime scene, regardless of their own health status
A person who believes death is imminent, regarding the cause or circumstances of their impending death
A physician's opinion about a patient's prognosis
A statement made by a healthy person about a future hypothetical death
A statement recorded only after the person has died
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: A dying declaration is a statement made by a person who has a reasonable belief that death is imminent, concerning the cause or circumstances of their impending death, and is admissible as evidence in many legal systems as an exception to hearsay rules.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: For a dying declaration to hold evidentiary value, which condition regarding the declarant's mental state is essential?
o: The declarant must be unconscious while making the statement
The declarant must be a licensed physician
The declarant must be of sound and conscious mind at the time of making the statement
The declarant's statement must be written by a lawyer
The declarant must survive for at least 24 hours afterward
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: A dying declaration is only considered valid and reliable evidence if the declarant was of sound, conscious mind and capable of accurately perceiving and communicating the relevant facts at the time it was made.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: A physician summoned to give expert testimony in court regarding a medico-legal case is functioning in which specific capacity?
o: Witness of fact only, unable to give any opinion
Judge, deciding the outcome of the case
Expert witness, providing professional opinion based on medical facts
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: A physician called to interpret medical evidence and provide a professional opinion in court functions as an expert witness, distinct from an ordinary witness of fact who can only testify to directly observed events.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: A 'dying deposition,' as distinguished from a 'dying declaration,' is characterized by which feature?
o: It requires no formal recording process at all
It can only be given by a physician
It is inadmissible in every legal system
It is recorded under oath, typically in the presence of a magistrate, with an opportunity for cross-examination
It must be given more than a year before death
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: A dying deposition is a formal statement recorded under oath, usually before a magistrate, with the accused (or their representative) given an opportunity to cross-examine, distinguishing it from the less formal dying declaration.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The doctrine of 'therapeutic privilege' in medical ethics allows a physician to do which of the following, under narrow and justified circumstances?
o: Withhold certain information from a patient if full disclosure would cause serious, demonstrable psychological harm
Withhold information from all patients as a routine practice
Refuse treatment to any patient without justification
Override a competent patient's informed refusal of treatment
Charge additional fees for providing complete information
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Therapeutic privilege is a narrow, ethically controversial exception allowing withholding of specific information when disclosure is judged likely to cause serious harm to the patient; it must be used cautiously and is not a general license to withhold information.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: Medical records are considered legally important documents primarily because they serve which purpose in medico-legal contexts?
o: Providing contemporaneous documented evidence of the patient's condition, treatment, and clinical decision-making
They are useful only for billing purposes
They have no legal standing in court
They are relevant only after the patient's death
They exist solely to satisfy hospital administration requirements
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Accurate, contemporaneous medical records serve as crucial legal evidence of the patient's clinical course, decisions made, and care provided, and are frequently central to resolving medico-legal disputes including negligence claims.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The 'standard of care' against which a physician's conduct is judged in a negligence case is typically defined as which of the following?
o: The highest possible level of care achievable with unlimited resources
What a reasonably competent physician of similar training would do under similar circumstances
Whatever the individual physician personally believes is best
The care given by the most advanced specialist in the world regardless of context
A fixed universal standard identical in every country
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: The standard of care is generally defined as the level of care and skill that a reasonably prudent and competent physician with similar training would provide under similar circumstances, not an idealized or maximal standard.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: Which of the following best describes the medico-legal concept of 'contributory negligence' as a defense?
o: The hospital administration is always fully liable regardless of patient behavior
It applies only in criminal cases, never civil cases
It eliminates all liability of the treating physician entirely in every case
It refers to negligence by a second treating physician only
The patient's own conduct partly contributed to the harm suffered, potentially reducing the defendant's liability
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Contributory negligence is a legal defense asserting that the patient's own actions (e.g., non-compliance with medical advice) contributed to the resulting harm, which may reduce or, in some jurisdictions, bar the defendant's liability.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: Which of the following is an example of 'medical maloccurrence' as distinguished from medical negligence?
o: An unavoidable, recognized complication occurring despite the exercise of reasonable skill and care
A surgeon operating on the wrong body part
A physician prescribing a medication clearly contraindicated for the patient
Failure to obtain consent before an elective procedure
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Medical maloccurrence refers to an adverse outcome or recognized complication that occurs even when the treating physician has exercised due care and skill, distinguishing it from negligence, which requires a breach of the standard of care.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The 'locality rule' historically used in some negligence cases assessed a physician's standard of care based on which comparison?
o: Practice standards of physicians in the same or similar community/locality
A single universal international standard regardless of location
The practices of only the most prestigious academic medical centers
Standards from an unrelated medical specialty
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: The locality rule (now largely superseded in many jurisdictions by a national standard) evaluated a physician's conduct against the practices of similarly situated practitioners in the same or a similar community, historically accounting for differences in resources.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: In pediatric practice, informed consent for a minor's treatment is typically obtained from which party, except in specific legally defined circumstances (e.g., emergencies, emancipated minors)?
o: The treating physician alone, bypassing the family
A random adult relative regardless of legal guardianship
No consent is required for minors under any circumstance
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Except in emergencies or specific legal exceptions (e.g., emancipated minors, certain reproductive health services in some jurisdictions), informed consent for a minor's medical treatment is generally obtained from a parent or legal guardian.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The Hippocratic Oath and modern codes of medical ethics both emphasize which foundational obligation of physicians?
o: Maximizing personal financial gain as the primary goal
Avoiding all forms of patient contact to prevent liability
Prioritizing institutional reputation over patient welfare
Treating only patients who can pay in full upfront
Acting in the patient's best interest and maintaining confidentiality
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Both historical and contemporary medical ethical codes consistently emphasize the physician's core duties to act in the patient's best interest (beneficence) and to safeguard patient confidentiality.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: A physician who continues to treat a patient despite the patient's clear, competent refusal of a specific treatment risks which legal consequence?
o: No legal consequence, as physicians may always override patient wishes
Liability for battery/assault for treating without valid consent
Automatic loss of medical license without any hearing
Criminal liability only if the patient dies
Civil liability only if the treatment is unsuccessful
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Providing treatment against a competent patient's explicit refusal, even with good intentions, can constitute battery/assault in law, since valid consent is a legal prerequisite for most medical interventions on a competent adult.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The 'captain of the ship' doctrine in medical liability historically held which principle regarding surgical teams?
o: The operating surgeon bears overall responsibility for the actions of the surgical team during an operation
Every team member bears entirely independent, unrelated liability
Only the anesthesiologist is liable for any operative complication
Hospital administration alone is liable for surgical outcomes
No one is liable for errors during a team-based operation
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: The 'captain of the ship' doctrine historically assigned overall responsibility to the operating surgeon for the conduct of the surgical team during an operation, though modern law increasingly recognizes individual accountability among team members.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: A 'second opinion' in clinical practice serves which primary ethical and practical purpose?
o: Replacing the need for the primary physician's judgment entirely
Guaranteeing a different, more favorable diagnosis
Eliminating the need for any further treatment
Serving only a legal, not clinical, function
Providing the patient with additional information and perspective to support informed decision-making
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Seeking a second opinion allows a patient to gather additional professional perspective, supporting more informed and confident decision-making about their care, and is an ethically encouraged practice, particularly for major or uncertain diagnoses.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: Falsification of medical records or backdating entries by a physician constitutes which type of violation?
o: Professional misconduct and potential legal/criminal liability for fraud
An acceptable practice if done to correct a simple error promptly
A purely administrative matter with no ethical implications
A protected act under physician confidentiality obligations
An action that strengthens the evidentiary value of the record
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Falsifying or backdating medical records is considered serious professional misconduct and can constitute fraud, undermining the integrity of medical documentation and exposing the physician to disciplinary and legal consequences.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The concept of 'defensive medicine,' where physicians order excessive tests or procedures primarily to avoid litigation, raises which ethical concern?
o: It may not serve the patient's best interest and can increase unnecessary costs/risks
It always improves patient outcomes with no downside
It has no relationship to medico-legal concerns
It is required by law in all jurisdictions
It eliminates the possibility of any negligence claim
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Defensive medicine, driven by fear of litigation rather than clinical necessity, can lead to unnecessary tests, costs, and patient risks, raising ethical concerns about prioritizing legal self-protection over genuine patient welfare.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: A physician's duty to maintain proper medical records serves which important medico-legal function in the event of a negligence claim?
o: Serving no purpose since verbal recollection is always sufficient in court
Providing objective evidence of the care provided and clinical reasoning at the time
Only being relevant if the patient specifically requests copies
Replacing the need for any other form of evidence in litigation
Being legally irrelevant once the patient is discharged
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Complete and accurate medical records serve as the primary objective evidence of the clinical decision-making, consent process, and treatment provided, and are often decisive in defending or establishing a negligence claim.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: The ethical principle of 'veracity' in the physician-patient relationship refers to which obligation?
o: The physician's right to withhold all information indefinitely
A patient's obligation to always agree with the physician's recommendation
The physician's right to guarantee a cure
Truthfulness in communicating with patients about their diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Veracity is the ethical principle obligating physicians to be truthful and honest in their communications with patients regarding diagnosis, prognosis, treatment options, and any errors that may have occurred.

forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.s: Whistleblowing by a healthcare professional regarding unsafe practices within their institution is generally considered which of the following, from an ethics perspective?
o: Always unethical regardless of the circumstances
Legally prohibited in every jurisdiction without exception
An ethically justified action to protect patient safety, though it may carry professional risk
Only appropriate if approved in advance by hospital administration
forensic-medicine-and-toxicology/medical.e: Whistleblowing to expose unsafe or unethical practices that threaten patient safety is generally regarded as ethically justified, reflecting the primacy of patient welfare, even though it may expose the reporting professional to institutional or professional risk; many jurisdictions provide legal protections for good-faith whistleblowers.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Which epidemiological study design begins by selecting subjects based on exposure status and follows them forward in time to determine outcome incidence?
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: A cohort study selects participants based on exposure status and follows them prospectively (or retrospectively) to compare disease incidence between exposed and unexposed groups.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Which epidemiological study design begins by selecting subjects based on disease status (cases and controls) and looks backward for prior exposure?
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Case-control studies select cases (with disease) and controls (without disease) and retrospectively compare the frequency of prior exposure between the two groups, making them efficient for studying rare diseases.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Which study design measures exposure and outcome simultaneously in a population at a single point in time, useful for determining disease prevalence?
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: A cross-sectional study assesses both exposure and outcome at a single point in time within a defined population, providing a 'snapshot' most useful for estimating prevalence rather than incidence or causal timing.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: The randomized controlled trial is considered the strongest study design for establishing causality primarily because randomization achieves which effect?
o: Eliminating the need for a control group
Removing the need for informed consent
Balancing known and unknown confounding variables between comparison groups
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Randomization distributes both known and unknown confounding factors evenly between intervention and control groups, minimizing selection bias and allowing more confident causal inference regarding the intervention's effect.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: The odds ratio is the appropriate measure of association calculated directly in which type of study design?
o: Cohort study (where relative risk is preferred)
Randomized controlled trial (where relative risk is preferred)
Cross-sectional study exclusively (where prevalence ratio is preferred)
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Because case-control studies do not measure disease incidence directly (cases are selected first), the odds ratio is the appropriate measure of association, and it approximates the relative risk when the disease is rare.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Relative risk (risk ratio) is defined as which of the following?
o: The odds of exposure among cases divided by odds of exposure among controls
The absolute difference in risk between two groups
The total number of new cases in a population over a year
The ratio of incidence of disease in the exposed group to incidence in the unexposed group
The proportion of the population currently affected by disease
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Relative risk is calculated as the incidence of disease among the exposed divided by the incidence among the unexposed, directly quantifying how many times more (or less) likely the exposed group is to develop disease.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: 'Attributable risk' (risk difference) is best used to communicate which type of public health information?
o: The relative strength of an association between two variables
The prevalence of a disease in a population
The absolute excess risk of disease due to exposure, useful for estimating the public health impact of removing that exposure
The specificity of a diagnostic test
The statistical power of a study
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Attributable risk (exposed incidence minus unexposed incidence) quantifies the absolute excess disease burden attributable to an exposure, informing how much disease could be prevented by eliminating that exposure in the population.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: The 'basic reproduction number' (R0) of an infectious disease represents which concept?
o: The total number of people currently infected
The case fatality rate of the disease
The average number of secondary infections produced by one infected individual in a fully susceptible population
The proportion of the population that is immune
The incubation period of the disease in days
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: R0 quantifies the expected number of secondary cases generated by a single infectious individual in an entirely susceptible population, with R0 greater than 1 indicating potential for sustained transmission/epidemic spread.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: 'Herd immunity' refers to which epidemiological concept?
o: Immunity acquired only through natural infection, never through vaccination
Indirect protection of susceptible individuals when a sufficient proportion of the population is immune, reducing disease transmission
A phenomenon that only applies to livestock diseases
Complete elimination of a pathogen from the environment
Immunity present in a single individual only
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Herd immunity occurs when a sufficiently high proportion of a population is immune (via vaccination or prior infection), reducing the probability of transmission and indirectly protecting susceptible individuals who are not immune.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: The 'incubation period' of an infectious disease is defined as which time interval?
o: The interval between symptom onset and recovery
The interval during which a person remains infectious to others
The interval between exposure to an infectious agent and the onset of clinical symptoms
The interval between diagnosis and treatment initiation
The total duration of an epidemic
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: The incubation period spans from the time of exposure/infection to the appearance of the first clinical symptoms, a key parameter in outbreak investigation and quarantine period determination.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: The 'infectious period,' distinct from the incubation period, refers to which interval?
o: The time from vaccination to development of immunity
The time during which an infected individual can transmit the pathogen to others
The time from birth to disease onset
The time from symptom resolution to hospital discharge
The average lifespan of the pathogen outside a host
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: The infectious (communicable) period is the timeframe during which an infected person can transmit the pathogen to susceptible contacts, which may or may not overlap fully with the period of clinical symptoms.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: An epidemic curve showing a sharp, single peak with cases clustered tightly around a common incubation period suggests which type of outbreak source?
o: Mixed outbreak with two distinct sources
An outbreak with no identifiable pattern
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: A point source outbreak, where all cases are exposed to the same source over a brief period, characteristically produces a single sharp peak on the epidemic curve, clustered around the disease's typical incubation period.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: A propagated (person-to-person) epidemic typically shows which pattern on an epidemic curve?
o: A single sharp peak followed by an abrupt decline
A flat, unchanging line throughout the outbreak
An immediate decline to zero cases after the first case
Multiple successive peaks, each roughly one incubation period apart, of increasing or fluctuating magnitude
A curve identical in shape to a point-source outbreak
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Propagated epidemics, spread through successive person-to-person transmission generations, typically show multiple successive peaks separated by roughly one incubation period, reflecting sequential waves of secondary infection.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: The 'case fatality rate' of a disease is calculated as which of the following?
o: Number of deaths from the disease divided by the total population
Number of new cases divided by the total population at risk
Number of deaths from all causes divided by total population
Number of deaths from the disease divided by the number of diagnosed cases, over a specified period
Number of hospital admissions divided by total cases
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Case fatality rate measures the proportion of diagnosed cases of a specific disease that result in death, providing a measure of disease severity rather than overall population mortality burden.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: 'Sensitivity' of a diagnostic screening test is defined as which of the following?
o: The proportion of true positives correctly identified as positive by the test among all individuals who truly have the disease
The proportion of true negatives correctly identified as negative among all disease-free individuals
The proportion of positive test results that are true positives
The proportion of negative test results that are true negatives
The overall accuracy of the test regardless of disease status
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Sensitivity measures a test's ability to correctly identify individuals who truly have the disease (true positive rate); a highly sensitive test has few false negatives, making it useful for screening/ruling out disease.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: 'Specificity' of a diagnostic screening test is defined as which of the following?
o: The proportion of true positives correctly identified among diseased individuals
The proportion of positive results confirmed by a gold-standard test
The proportion of true negatives correctly identified as negative among all individuals without the disease
The overall proportion of correct test results in the population
The rate of disease occurrence in the tested population
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Specificity measures a test's ability to correctly identify individuals who truly do not have the disease (true negative rate); a highly specific test has few false positives, useful for confirming/ruling in disease.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Positive predictive value of a diagnostic test is most strongly influenced by which additional factor beyond sensitivity and specificity?
o: The prevalence of the disease in the tested population
The age of the laboratory equipment used
The specialty of the ordering physician
The time of day the test is performed
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Positive predictive value (the probability that a positive test result truly reflects disease) is strongly affected by disease prevalence in the tested population; even a highly specific test will have a lower PPV when applied to a low-prevalence population.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: The 'incidence rate' of a disease measures which of the following?
o: The total number of existing cases (new and old) at a single point in time
The proportion of the population that has ever had the disease
The number of deaths from the disease over a specified time period
The number of hospital beds occupied by cases of the disease
The rate of new cases occurring in a population at risk over a specified time period
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Incidence rate quantifies the occurrence of new cases of disease within a defined population over a specified period, reflecting the rate at which new disease events occur (risk of developing disease), as opposed to prevalence.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: 'Prevalence' of a disease is best described as which of the following?
o: The number of new cases occurring over the same time period
The rate at which people recover from the disease
The number of deaths caused by the disease
The number of people vaccinated against the disease
The total number of existing cases (new plus old) in a population at a given point or period in time
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Prevalence represents the total burden of existing disease (both newly diagnosed and previously diagnosed cases) present in a population at a specific point (point prevalence) or period (period prevalence) of time.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: The relationship between incidence and prevalence for a chronic disease with a long duration is best described by which statement?
o: Prevalence and incidence are always numerically identical
Incidence always exceeds prevalence regardless of disease duration
Prevalence and incidence have no mathematical relationship
Prevalence decreases as disease duration increases
Prevalence tends to be higher relative to incidence, since cases accumulate over a longer duration
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: For chronic diseases with long duration, cases accumulate over time, so prevalence tends to be substantially higher than the incidence rate (approximately Prevalence ≈ Incidence × average disease duration, under steady-state conditions).

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: The 'epidemiological triad' model of disease causation consists of which three components?
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: The classic epidemiological triad conceptualizes disease occurrence as resulting from the interaction of an infectious/causal agent, a susceptible host, and the surrounding environment that facilitates or hinders their interaction.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Vertical disease transmission refers to which mode of pathogen spread?
o: Transmission via a vector such as a mosquito
Transmission between unrelated individuals in a community
Transmission through airborne droplets between strangers
Transmission from mother to offspring, such as transplacental or perinatal transmission
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Vertical transmission describes the transfer of an infectious agent from mother to child, occurring transplacentally, during delivery (perinatal), or postnatally through breastfeeding, as with HIV, hepatitis B, and syphilis.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Horizontal disease transmission, as distinguished from vertical transmission, refers to which mode of spread?
o: Transmission exclusively from mother to fetus
Transmission between individuals of the same generation through direct or indirect contact, common vehicle, vector, or airborne routes
Transmission that occurs only in hospitals
Transmission limited strictly to sexual contact
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Horizontal transmission encompasses the range of person-to-person or environment-to-person spread among individuals of the same generation, including direct contact, droplet, airborne, vector-borne, and common-vehicle (food/water) routes.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: A 'vector' in the context of disease transmission is best defined as which of the following?
o: A living organism (typically an arthropod) that transmits an infectious agent from one host to another
Any inanimate object that can harbor pathogens
A person who has recovered from the disease
The geographic location where an outbreak began
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: A vector is a living organism, most often an arthropod (mosquito, tick, flea), that actively transmits an infectious agent between hosts, as distinguished from a fomite (inanimate object) which passively harbors pathogens.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: 'Biological transmission' by a vector, as opposed to 'mechanical transmission,' is characterized by which feature?
o: The pathogen undergoes multiplication or developmental changes within the vector before becoming infective
The pathogen is simply carried on the vector's body surface without any biological change
No vector is involved at all in biological transmission
The vector is destroyed immediately after acquiring the pathogen
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: In biological transmission, the pathogen undergoes essential multiplication and/or developmental changes within the vector (e.g., Plasmodium in the Anopheles mosquito) before it becomes infective to a new host, unlike simple mechanical carriage.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: A 'zoonotic disease' is defined as an infection that is transmitted under which circumstance?
o: Naturally transmitted between vertebrate animals and humans
Transmitted only via contaminated water supplies
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Zoonotic diseases are infections naturally transmissible between vertebrate animals and humans, such as rabies, brucellosis, and various viral hemorrhagic fevers, often requiring specific animal reservoirs or vectors.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: The 'carrier state' in infectious disease epidemiology refers to which condition?
o: A person who has been fully cured and is no longer infectious
A vaccinated individual with complete immunity
A person who has never been exposed to the pathogen
An individual who harbors and can transmit a pathogen without showing overt clinical symptoms
A healthcare worker who treats infected patients
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: A carrier harbors and can potentially transmit an infectious agent while remaining asymptomatic (or after symptom resolution, as a convalescent carrier), posing an important and often underrecognized source of ongoing transmission, as classically illustrated by Typhoid Mary.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: The 'iceberg phenomenon' of disease in epidemiology illustrates which important concept?
o: All cases of a disease are always clinically apparent
Disease severity always correlates with the visible portion of an outbreak
Only severe cases require public health surveillance
Clinically recognized cases represent only a fraction of the total disease burden, with many subclinical or undiagnosed cases remaining hidden
The concept applies only to cold-related illnesses
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: The iceberg phenomenon illustrates that overt, diagnosed clinical cases (the visible 'tip') often represent only a small fraction of total infections, with a much larger, hidden burden of subclinical, undiagnosed, or asymptomatic cases (the submerged bulk).

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Screening for a disease using a highly sensitive test as an initial step is a strategy primarily intended to achieve which goal?
o: Minimize the cost of the screening program regardless of accuracy
Guarantee a definitive diagnosis without further testing
Eliminate the need for any confirmatory testing
Minimize false negatives so that true cases are not missed at the initial screening stage
Maximize the number of false positives intentionally
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: A highly sensitive screening test minimizes false negatives, ensuring that most true cases are captured for further confirmatory testing, even at the cost of generating more false positives that require additional evaluation.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Bias arising when study subjects who volunteer differ systematically from those who do not is best described as which type of bias?
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Selection bias, including volunteer (self-selection) bias, occurs when the process of selecting study participants results in a sample that is systematically different from the target population, distorting the study's findings.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Bias arising when cases more accurately remember past exposures than controls (or vice versa) is best described as which type of bias?
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Recall bias occurs in retrospective studies (notably case-control studies) when there is a systematic difference in the accuracy or completeness of memories retrieved by cases versus controls regarding past exposures.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: 'Confounding' in an epidemiological study occurs when which condition is present?
o: The study sample size is too small
Only one group is followed over time
The study lacks a control group entirely
A third variable is associated with both the exposure and the outcome, distorting the true association between them
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Confounding arises when an extraneous factor is independently associated with both the exposure and the outcome under study, without being an intermediate step in the causal pathway, thereby distorting the observed exposure-outcome association.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: 'Lead-time bias' in the evaluation of a screening program refers to which phenomenon?
o: A genuine improvement in disease outcome from screening
Apparent improvement in survival time due to earlier diagnosis, without any true change in the disease's natural course
Bias arising from inaccurate exposure recall
A statistical error in calculating incidence rates
Bias that only affects randomized controlled trials
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Lead-time bias creates an artificial impression of prolonged survival in screened patients simply because the disease is detected earlier in its course, even if the actual time of death and disease progression remain unchanged.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Herd immunity threshold for a given infectious disease is directly related to which key epidemiological parameter?
o: The basic reproduction number (R0) of the pathogen
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: The herd immunity threshold (the proportion of the population that must be immune to interrupt sustained transmission) is mathematically derived from the pathogen's basic reproduction number (R0): threshold ≈ 1 − 1/R0.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: In outbreak investigation, the first essential step after receiving a report of a suspected outbreak is to do which of the following?
o: Immediately implement mass vaccination regardless of confirmation
Verify the diagnosis and confirm that an outbreak truly exists
Publish findings in a scientific journal before further investigation
Notify the media before verifying any facts
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Standard outbreak investigation methodology begins with confirming the diagnosis and verifying that observed case numbers truly exceed the expected baseline before proceeding to case definition, descriptive epidemiology, and hypothesis generation.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Establishing a 'case definition' early in an outbreak investigation serves which essential purpose?
o: Determining the exact treatment protocol for all patients
Assigning legal liability for the outbreak's cause
Replacing the need for laboratory confirmation entirely
Identifying the specific individual responsible for the outbreak
Standardizing criteria to consistently identify and count cases for the outbreak
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: A clear, standardized case definition (based on clinical, laboratory, and epidemiological criteria) ensures consistency in identifying and counting cases throughout the outbreak investigation, enabling valid comparison and analysis.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Descriptive epidemiology in outbreak investigation characterizes cases according to which three fundamental parameters?
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Descriptive epidemiology organizes outbreak data according to person (who is affected), place (where cases occur), and time (when cases occur), generating hypotheses about the source and mode of transmission for further analytic investigation.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Notifiable diseases are defined as conditions that healthcare providers are legally required to do which of the following?
o: Treat exclusively in specialized isolation hospitals
Withhold from any official reporting to protect patient privacy
Report only if the patient specifically consents to disclosure
Report to public health authorities to enable surveillance and control measures
Manage without any government or public health involvement
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Notifiable disease reporting requirements mandate that healthcare providers report specified conditions (e.g., tuberculosis, cholera, measles) to public health authorities, enabling surveillance, outbreak detection, and timely control interventions.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: Secular trend in disease occurrence refers to which pattern of variation over time?
o: Gradual changes in disease frequency occurring over long periods, such as years or decades
Seasonal variation occurring within a single year
Random day-to-day fluctuation in case counts
Sudden epidemic spikes lasting only days
Variation strictly tied to a single generation of person-to-person spread
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Secular trends describe long-term changes in disease frequency over extended periods (years to decades), often reflecting gradual shifts in risk factors, healthcare access, diagnostic practices, or population demographics, as distinct from short-term seasonal or epidemic variation.

community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.s: 'Herd immunity' protection is generally considered least reliable for interrupting transmission of diseases that spread primarily through which route, due to practical vaccination coverage challenges?
o: Diseases with no human-to-human transmission at all
Diseases that are already eradicated worldwide
Diseases transmitted only through blood transfusion with existing robust screening
Highly contagious airborne diseases requiring very high coverage thresholds (e.g., measles)
community-medicine-and-public-health/epi.e: Highly contagious diseases with a high basic reproduction number (such as measles) require very high vaccination coverage thresholds to achieve herd immunity, making transmission interruption more challenging if coverage gaps exist.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: Which measure of central tendency is most affected by extreme outlier values in a data set?
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: The mean, calculated by summing all values and dividing by the count, is heavily influenced by extreme outliers, whereas the median (middle value) is comparatively resistant to such extreme values.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: The median of a data set is best described as which of the following?
o: The most frequently occurring value in the data set
The middle value when data are arranged in ascending or descending order
The arithmetic average of all values
The difference between the highest and lowest values
The square root of the variance
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: The median is the middle value of an ordered data set (or the average of the two middle values for an even number of observations), making it a robust measure of central tendency less affected by skewed data or outliers.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: For a normally distributed (Gaussian) data set, approximately what percentage of observations fall within one standard deviation of the mean?
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: In a normal distribution, approximately 68% of observations lie within one standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within two standard deviations, and about 99.7% within three standard deviations (the empirical or 68-95-99.7 rule).

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: Standard deviation is best described as a measure of which statistical property of a data set?
o: The central tendency of the data set
The sample size used in the study
The dispersion or spread of individual values around the mean
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Standard deviation quantifies the average amount by which individual data points deviate from the mean, serving as a fundamental measure of variability/dispersion within a data set.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A 'null hypothesis' in statistical hypothesis testing typically states which of the following?
