o: There is no true difference or association between the groups/variables being compared
There is a definite, significant difference between groups
The study will definitely fail to reject the alternative hypothesis
The sample size is inadequate for meaningful analysis
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: The null hypothesis represents the default assumption of no true effect, difference, or association between the variables or groups under study, which the researcher then attempts to test against using collected data.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A 'Type I error' in hypothesis testing occurs when which of the following happens?
o: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis (a false negative finding)
Correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis
Rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false positive finding)
Correctly failing to reject a true null hypothesis
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: A Type I error (false positive) occurs when a study incorrectly concludes that a significant difference or association exists when, in truth, the null hypothesis is correct (no true effect exists); its probability is denoted by alpha.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A 'Type II error' in hypothesis testing occurs when which of the following happens?
o: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis (a false negative finding)
Correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis
Correctly accepting a true null hypothesis
Choosing too large a sample size
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: A Type II error (false negative) occurs when a study fails to detect a true effect or difference that actually exists, incorrectly failing to reject a false null hypothesis; its probability is denoted by beta.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: 'Statistical power' of a study refers to which of the following probabilities?
o: The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis (detecting a true effect)
The probability of committing a Type I error
The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The probability of selecting a biased sample
The probability of obtaining a p-value below 0.05 regardless of a true effect
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Statistical power (equal to 1 minus the Type II error rate, beta) represents a study's probability of correctly detecting a true effect or difference when one genuinely exists, and is influenced by sample size, effect size, and variability.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A 'p-value' of 0.03 in a hypothesis test is generally interpreted as which of the following, using the conventional threshold of 0.05?
o: The probability that the null hypothesis is true is exactly 3%
The result is statistically significant, as the p-value is below the conventional alpha threshold of 0.05
The result is definitely clinically important
The finding is certainly a true positive with no chance of error
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: A p-value of 0.03, being less than the conventional significance threshold of 0.05, indicates statistical significance under that convention — meaning the observed result would be unlikely under the null hypothesis — although it does not represent the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor guarantee clinical importance.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A 95% confidence interval for a mean difference is best interpreted as which of the following?
o: A range that would contain the true population parameter in 95% of repeated samples drawn the same way
The range within which 95% of individual observations in the sample fall
A guarantee that the true value lies exactly at the midpoint
The probability that the null hypothesis is true
A measure of the study's statistical power
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: A 95% confidence interval reflects the range of values that would contain the true population parameter in 95% of repeated samples under identical conditions, providing an estimate of precision around the sample statistic.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: The Student's t-test is appropriately used to compare which of the following?
o: Proportions of more than two categorical groups
Means of two groups, particularly with small sample sizes and normally distributed data
Association between two categorical variables in a contingency table
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: The t-test compares the means of two groups (independent or paired) and is particularly appropriate for smaller samples with approximately normally distributed continuous data and comparable variances.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: Analysis of variance (ANOVA) is the appropriate statistical test when comparing which of the following?
o: Survival times using the log-rank method
Means of three or more groups simultaneously
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: ANOVA tests whether there is a statistically significant difference among the means of three or more independent groups, avoiding the inflated Type I error risk of performing multiple pairwise t-tests.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: The chi-square test is most appropriately used to analyze the association between which types of variables?
o: A continuous outcome across three or more groups
Two categorical variables presented in a contingency table
Paired continuous measurements before and after intervention
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: The chi-square test evaluates whether there is a statistically significant association between two categorical variables by comparing observed versus expected frequencies within a contingency table.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) measures which of the following relationships between two continuous variables?
o: The presence of a causal relationship
The difference between the two variables' means
The strength and direction of a linear relationship
The statistical significance of a proportion difference
The reliability of a diagnostic test
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Pearson's correlation coefficient quantifies the strength and direction of a linear association between two continuous variables, ranging from -1 (perfect negative) to +1 (perfect positive), but does not by itself establish causation.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A correlation coefficient does not, by itself, establish causation between two variables primarily because of which possibility?
o: Correlation coefficients cannot be calculated for continuous variables
Correlation always implies a direct causal pathway
Correlation coefficients are always statistically significant
A third confounding variable may independently influence both variables, creating a spurious association
Causation can only be established using correlation analysis
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: An observed correlation may arise from confounding (a third variable influencing both), reverse causation, or chance, so correlation alone is insufficient to establish a true causal relationship between two variables.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: In survival analysis, the Kaplan-Meier method is used primarily for which purpose?
o: Estimating the survival function over time, accounting for censored observations
Calculating the mean and standard deviation of continuous data
Testing the association between two categorical variables
Estimating a simple linear regression coefficient
Determining sample size for a clinical trial
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: The Kaplan-Meier method estimates the probability of survival (or event-free status) over time from observed data, appropriately incorporating censored observations (participants lost to follow-up or without the event by study end).

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: The 'log-rank test' in survival analysis is used to accomplish which comparison?
o: Compare means of continuous variables between groups
Estimate the correlation between two variables
Compare survival curves between two or more groups
Estimate the standard error of a proportion
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: The log-rank test statistically compares Kaplan-Meier survival curves between two or more groups, testing whether there is a significant difference in the overall survival experience between them.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A study that is 'double-blinded' means which of the following?
o: Only the participants are unaware of their treatment assignment
Only the investigators are unaware of the treatment assignment
The study has two separate control groups
Neither the participants nor the investigators/assessors know which intervention each participant is receiving
The study uses two different statistical tests to confirm results
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: In a double-blind study, both participants and those assessing outcomes (and often those administering treatment) are unaware of group assignment, minimizing bias in both response and outcome assessment.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: Randomization in a clinical trial primarily serves which purpose?
o: Ensuring comparable distribution of known and unknown confounders between study groups
Guaranteeing that the trial will show a statistically significant result
Eliminating the need for informed consent
Ensuring all participants receive the active treatment eventually
Reducing the cost of conducting the trial
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Randomization allocates participants to study groups by chance, helping to balance both known and unknown confounding factors across groups and strengthening the validity of causal inferences drawn from the trial.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: Intention-to-treat analysis in a randomized controlled trial involves analyzing participants according to which principle?
o: Their originally assigned treatment group, regardless of whether they completed or adhered to that treatment
Only the treatment they actually received, regardless of original assignment
Only participants who completed the full trial protocol
Only participants who experienced the primary outcome
Excluding all participants who experienced any side effects
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Intention-to-treat analysis retains participants in their originally randomized group for analysis regardless of adherence, treatment crossover, or dropout, preserving the benefits of randomization and better reflecting real-world effectiveness.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A 'placebo' in a clinical trial serves which primary methodological purpose?
o: Providing an active pharmacological effect equivalent to the study drug
Ensuring that all participants receive the same active dose
Eliminating the need for a control group
Guaranteeing statistical significance in the trial results
Controlling for non-specific effects of receiving treatment, such as the placebo effect and natural disease course
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: A placebo (an inactive substance resembling the active treatment) helps control for non-specific effects — such as the psychological placebo effect, natural disease fluctuation, and regression to the mean — isolating the true pharmacological effect of the study intervention.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A systematic review differs from a traditional narrative review primarily by employing which methodological feature?
o: A pre-defined, reproducible, comprehensive search strategy and explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria
Reliance solely on the reviewer's personal clinical experience
Exclusion of all randomized controlled trials from consideration
A requirement that only a single study be included
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Systematic reviews use explicit, reproducible methodology including comprehensive literature searches and pre-specified inclusion/exclusion criteria to minimize bias, in contrast to traditional narrative reviews which may be more subjective and selective.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A meta-analysis is best described as which of the following?
o: A single large clinical trial conducted at multiple sites
A quantitative statistical technique that combines results from multiple independent studies to derive a pooled estimate of effect
A qualitative summary of expert opinion
A study design that only uses case reports
A test used exclusively for diagnostic accuracy studies
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Meta-analysis statistically combines quantitative results from multiple independent studies addressing a similar research question, producing a pooled effect estimate with greater precision (narrower confidence interval) than any single study alone.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: 'Heterogeneity' in a meta-analysis refers to which concept?
o: Variability in study results and characteristics that goes beyond what would be expected by chance alone
The number of participants included across the combined studies
The overall statistical significance of the pooled estimate
The publication year range of the included studies
The geographic location of the studies included
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Heterogeneity describes the degree of variability among the effect estimates of individual studies included in a meta-analysis, which may arise from differences in populations, interventions, or methodology, and can be assessed statistically (e.g., using the I-squared statistic).

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: 'Publication bias' in the context of a systematic review or meta-analysis refers to which phenomenon?
o: The tendency for studies with statistically significant or 'positive' results to be more likely published than null/negative studies
The tendency of journals to only publish studies with negative results
A bias that only affects randomized controlled trials
A statistical error in calculating confidence intervals
The exclusion of all non-English language studies as standard practice
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Publication bias occurs when studies with statistically significant or favorable results are more likely to be published than those with null or negative findings, potentially skewing the evidence base and inflating apparent treatment effects in reviews.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A 'funnel plot' in meta-analysis is primarily used as a visual tool to detect which of the following?
o: The exact pooled effect size numerically
The statistical power of individual studies
The randomization method used across studies
Potential publication bias or small-study effects
Sample size calculations for future trials
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: A funnel plot graphs individual study effect estimates against a measure of their precision (e.g., standard error); asymmetry in the resulting funnel shape suggests possible publication bias or other small-study effects.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: Sample size calculation for a clinical study depends on which of the following key parameters?
o: Only the researchers' personal preference for study size
The total funding available, regardless of statistical considerations
Expected effect size, desired statistical power, significance level, and variability of the outcome measure
The number of co-investigators involved in the study
The geographic location of the study site alone
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Proper sample size calculation incorporates the anticipated effect size, desired power (commonly 80% or 90%), chosen significance level (commonly 0.05), and expected variability in the outcome measure to ensure the study can reliably detect a true effect if one exists.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A study with inadequate statistical power (a small sample size) primarily increases the risk of which type of error?
o: Type I error (falsely detecting an effect that does not exist)
Type II error (failing to detect a true effect)
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: An underpowered study (typically due to insufficient sample size) has a higher probability of committing a Type II error, failing to detect a true effect or difference that genuinely exists in the population.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: Which measure of dispersion is calculated as the difference between the 75th and 25th percentiles of a data set?
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: The interquartile range (IQR), the difference between the 75th percentile (Q3) and 25th percentile (Q1), captures the spread of the middle 50% of the data, providing a measure of dispersion relatively resistant to outliers.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A skewed distribution with a long tail extending to the right (higher values) is described as which type of skew?
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: A positively (right) skewed distribution has a longer tail extending toward higher values, typically with the mean greater than the median, as commonly seen in income or hospital length-of-stay data.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: In a positively skewed distribution, the relationship between the mean, median, and mode typically follows which order?
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: In a right (positively) skewed distribution, extreme high values pull the mean upward more than the median, giving the typical order: Mean > Median > Mode.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: The choice between using a parametric versus non-parametric statistical test primarily depends on which consideration?
o: Whether the underlying data distribution meets assumptions such as normality
The total number of variables measured in the study
The funding source of the research
The country in which the study was conducted
The specialty of the journal to which the study will be submitted
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Parametric tests (e.g., t-test, ANOVA) assume the data follow a specific distribution (usually normal) and other assumptions like equal variance, while non-parametric tests (e.g., Mann-Whitney U, Kruskal-Wallis) make fewer distributional assumptions and are used when these are violated.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: The Mann-Whitney U test is the non-parametric equivalent of which parametric test?
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: The Mann-Whitney U test (Wilcoxon rank-sum test) is used to compare two independent groups when data are not normally distributed or are ordinal, serving as the non-parametric counterpart to the independent samples t-test.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: Linear regression analysis is primarily used to model which type of relationship?
o: The association between two purely categorical variables
Diagnostic test sensitivity and specificity exclusively
The variance of a single variable alone
The relationship between a continuous dependent variable and one or more independent variables
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Linear regression models the linear relationship between a continuous outcome (dependent variable) and one or more predictor (independent) variables, allowing prediction and quantification of the strength of association while adjusting for other variables.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: Logistic regression is the appropriate statistical technique when the outcome (dependent) variable is of which type?
o: Purely ordinal outcome with more than 5 categories only
Only applicable to normally distributed continuous data
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Logistic regression models the probability of a binary outcome (e.g., disease present/absent) as a function of one or more predictor variables, producing odds ratios that quantify the strength of association while adjusting for confounders.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: Ethical approval from an institutional review board (IRB) or ethics committee is required for research involving human subjects primarily to ensure which protection?
o: Protection of participants' rights, safety, and well-being throughout the research process
Guaranteed publication of the research findings
Automatic funding approval for the study
Elimination of the need for informed consent
Faster completion of the study timeline
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Ethics committee/IRB review is a fundamental safeguard ensuring that research involving human participants adheres to ethical principles protecting their rights, safety, privacy, and well-being, in line with frameworks such as the Declaration of Helsinki.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: The Declaration of Helsinki is an internationally recognized document primarily addressing which topic?
o: Ethical principles for medical research involving human subjects
Standardized diagnostic criteria for infectious diseases
International classification of causes of death
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: The Declaration of Helsinki, developed by the World Medical Association, sets out ethical principles guiding medical research involving human subjects, including informed consent, risk-benefit assessment, and the primacy of participant welfare.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: Sensitivity and specificity of a diagnostic test are properties that remain relatively stable regardless of which factor, unlike predictive values?
o: Disease prevalence in the tested population
The gold-standard reference test used for comparison
The statistical software used for analysis
The country in which testing occurs
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic properties of a diagnostic test in relation to disease status and remain relatively stable regardless of disease prevalence, in contrast to predictive values (PPV, NPV), which are directly influenced by the prevalence of disease in the tested population.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A 'cohort effect' in epidemiological data analysis refers to which phenomenon?
o: A statistical error unrelated to any real population pattern
The effect of a single outlier value on study results
Variations in health outcomes among groups of people born in the same period, reflecting shared exposures across their lifetime
A bias that only occurs in laboratory experiments
An effect limited exclusively to twin studies
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: A cohort effect describes variation in disease risk or outcomes among groups defined by their year or period of birth, reflecting differences in shared exposures, behaviors, or environmental factors experienced by that generation over their life course.

community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.s: A 'crossover study design' in clinical research involves which methodological feature?
o: Each participant receives multiple interventions in sequence, serving as their own control
Participants are permanently assigned to only one treatment group with no switching
Only healthy volunteers are enrolled with no patients
The study has no control group of any kind
Randomization is never used in this design
community-medicine-and-public-health/bio.e: In a crossover study, each participant receives two or more different interventions in a specified sequence (often randomized, with a washout period between), allowing each subject to serve as their own control and reducing between-subject variability.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Primary prevention in the classic levels-of-prevention framework is best exemplified by which of the following interventions?
o: Screening mammography to detect early breast cancer
Vaccination of healthy individuals to prevent disease occurrence
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Primary prevention aims to prevent disease before it occurs, through measures such as vaccination, health promotion, and risk factor reduction, applied to a healthy population prior to disease onset.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Secondary prevention is best exemplified by which of the following activities?
o: Providing health education to prevent smoking initiation
Screening for cervical cancer via Pap smear to detect early or preclinical disease
Administering a vaccine to prevent an infection
Providing palliative care in terminal illness
Public health legislation banning a hazardous substance
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Secondary prevention focuses on early detection and prompt treatment of disease in its preclinical or early clinical stage (before symptoms are apparent or advanced), exemplified by screening programs such as Pap smears or mammography.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Tertiary prevention in the levels-of-prevention framework aims to achieve which of the following?
o: Limit disability and promote rehabilitation in patients with established disease
Prevent disease occurrence in a healthy population
Detect disease at an asymptomatic stage
Eliminate risk factors before exposure occurs
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Tertiary prevention focuses on reducing complications, disability, and promoting rehabilitation and quality of life in individuals who already have established disease, distinct from primary (before disease) and secondary (early detection) prevention.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: 'Health promotion,' as distinguished from disease-specific prevention, focuses primarily on which broader objective?
o: Managing acute emergencies in a hospital setting
Enabling individuals and communities to increase control over and improve their overall health and well-being
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Health promotion, as defined by the WHO Ottawa Charter, encompasses broader efforts enabling individuals and communities to increase control over the determinants of their health, extending beyond disease-specific prevention to overall well-being.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI), a WHO initiative, primarily targets which population for its core vaccination schedule?
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: The Expanded Programme on Immunization was established by WHO to ensure that all children have access to routinely recommended vaccines, forming the backbone of childhood immunization schedules worldwide.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The BCG vaccine, given at or shortly after birth in high-burden tuberculosis settings, primarily protects against which severe pediatric complication of TB?
o: Latent tuberculosis infection with complete prevention of reactivation
Disseminated (miliary) tuberculosis and tuberculous meningitis in young children
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: BCG vaccination provides its most significant protective benefit against severe, disseminated forms of childhood tuberculosis, such as miliary TB and TB meningitis, though its protection against adult pulmonary TB is more variable.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The oral polio vaccine (OPV) provides which additional immunological benefit compared to inactivated polio vaccine (IPV)?
o: Provides immunity against a broader range of unrelated pathogens
Requires no cold chain for storage and transport
Is safer than IPV in all immunocompromised populations
Eliminates the need for any booster doses
Induces strong mucosal (intestinal) immunity that helps interrupt fecal-oral transmission
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: OPV, being a live attenuated vaccine given orally, induces robust mucosal immunity in the gut, helping to interrupt person-to-person fecal-oral transmission of wild poliovirus, an advantage over the injectable inactivated vaccine.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The pentavalent vaccine used in many national immunization programs typically combines protection against which five diseases?
o: Measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, and hepatitis A
Diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus, hepatitis B, and Haemophilus influenzae type b
Polio, rotavirus, pneumococcus, meningococcus, and typhoid
Tuberculosis, tetanus, measles, rubella, and rabies
Yellow fever, cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A, and hepatitis B
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: The commonly used pentavalent vaccine combines diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus (DPT) with hepatitis B and Haemophilus influenzae type b antigens into a single injection, simplifying immunization schedules.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The 'cold chain' in immunization programs refers to which essential system?
o: A legal chain of custody documentation for vaccine batches
A sequence of vaccines given in a specific temporal order
A record-keeping system tracking which children have been vaccinated
A temperature-controlled system for storing and transporting vaccines from manufacture to administration
A method for calculating vaccine efficacy
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: The cold chain is the temperature-controlled supply chain (refrigeration and monitoring at every stage from manufacturer to point of use) essential for maintaining vaccine potency, since many vaccines are sensitive to heat or freezing.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: 'Vaccine efficacy' is defined as which of the following?
o: The percentage of vaccine doses that are administered correctly
The total number of doses distributed in a national program
The proportion of the population that has been vaccinated
The percentage reduction in disease incidence among vaccinated individuals compared to unvaccinated individuals under ideal (trial) conditions
The cost-effectiveness of a vaccination program
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Vaccine efficacy measures the percentage reduction in disease incidence among vaccinated versus unvaccinated groups under controlled (typically randomized trial) conditions, distinct from 'vaccine effectiveness,' which reflects real-world performance.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Which of the following vaccines is contraindicated in a patient with a severe, confirmed immunodeficiency due to the risk of vaccine-derived disease?
o: Live attenuated vaccines such as measles, mumps, rubella (MMR), OPV, and BCG
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Live attenuated vaccines carry a risk of causing vaccine-associated disease in individuals with significant immunodeficiency, since the weakened pathogen may still be able to replicate and cause illness in the absence of adequate immune control.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The concept of 'herd immunity threshold' has direct practical importance for immunization programs because it informs which of the following?
o: The minimum vaccination coverage needed in a population to interrupt sustained disease transmission
The exact dose of vaccine required per individual
The cost of manufacturing a vaccine
The shelf life of a vaccine vial
The color-coding system used for vaccine vial labels
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Understanding the herd immunity threshold allows public health programs to set target vaccination coverage levels sufficient to interrupt sustained transmission of a disease within a community, protecting even unvaccinated individuals indirectly.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Vitamin A supplementation programs for children in developing countries primarily aim to reduce mortality and morbidity from which condition?
o: Measles and other infections through improved immune function, and to prevent xerophthalmia/blindness
Protein-energy malnutrition exclusively without any effect on infection
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Vitamin A supplementation reduces child mortality and morbidity by improving immune function against infections such as measles and diarrheal disease, in addition to preventing vitamin A deficiency-related xerophthalmia and blindness.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Universal salt iodization programs are a public health strategy primarily aimed at preventing which spectrum of disorders?
o: Iodine deficiency disorders, including goiter and cretinism
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Universal salt iodization is a cost-effective public health measure to prevent the spectrum of iodine deficiency disorders, ranging from goiter to severe intellectual disability (cretinism) in children born to iodine-deficient mothers.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Oral rehydration therapy (ORT), a cornerstone intervention in preventing mortality from acute diarrheal disease, works primarily through which physiological mechanism?
o: Direct antimicrobial action against enteric pathogens
Replacement of lost blood volume through the oral route directly into the bloodstream
Sodium-glucose co-transport in the intestine, which remains functional even during diarrheal illness
Stimulation of antibody production against the causative organism
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Oral rehydration solution exploits the sodium-glucose co-transport mechanism in the intestinal brush border, which remains intact during most diarrheal illnesses, allowing effective absorption of water and electrolytes even in the presence of ongoing fluid losses.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended by WHO for the first how many months of an infant's life?
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding (no other foods or liquids, including water) for the first 6 months of life, followed by continued breastfeeding with appropriate complementary feeding up to 2 years or beyond.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Growth monitoring using a 'road to health' chart in child health programs primarily serves which purpose?
o: Determining the child's exact caloric requirement precisely
Replacing the need for immunization records
Early detection of growth faltering or malnutrition through serial weight/height plotting
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Serial plotting of a child's growth parameters (weight, height) on a standardized growth chart allows early identification of growth faltering, wasting, or stunting, prompting timely nutritional intervention.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The concept of 'health for all' articulated in the Alma-Ata Declaration of 1978 emphasized which foundational strategy for achieving global health goals?
o: Exclusive reliance on tertiary care hospitals
Vertical, disease-specific programs exclusively without integration
Complete elimination of traditional/community health workers
Primary health care as the key strategy for achieving health for all
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: The Alma-Ata Declaration (1978) established primary health care — accessible, community-based, and comprehensive — as the central strategy for achieving the WHO goal of 'Health for All,' emphasizing equity and community participation.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Which of the following is considered one of the core elements of primary health care as outlined by the Alma-Ata Declaration?
o: Exclusive focus on curative hospital-based services
Health education about prevailing health problems and their prevention/control
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Core elements of primary health care per Alma-Ata include health education, adequate nutrition, safe water and sanitation, maternal and child health services, immunization, prevention of local endemic diseases, and provision of essential drugs — accessible and community-oriented.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The concept of 'Health impact assessment' of a proposed policy or project primarily aims to evaluate which of the following?
o: The financial profitability of the project
The aesthetic design of a building
The legal liability of the project's investors
The marketing strategy for a new pharmaceutical product
Potential effects of the policy/project on the health of a population before implementation
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Health impact assessment is a systematic process evaluating the potential positive and negative effects of a proposed policy, program, or project on population health before it is implemented, informing decision-making.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: 'Screening' as a secondary preventive strategy is most appropriate for a disease that fulfills which of the following criteria (per Wilson-Jungner principles)?
o: The disease has no early detectable stage and no effective treatment exists
The disease is extremely rare with no significant public health burden
The disease has a recognizable early/latent stage and an effective, acceptable treatment is available if detected early
The screening test is prohibitively expensive with poor accuracy
The disease always resolves spontaneously without any intervention
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: The Wilson-Jungner criteria for screening emphasize that a suitable disease should have a detectable early/latent stage, and that early treatment must confer meaningful benefit, alongside an acceptable, accurate, and cost-effective screening test.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Which of the following best describes 'community-based rehabilitation' as a public health strategy?
o: A hospital-based intensive care program exclusively
A strategy that uses community resources to enhance the quality of life and participation of persons with disabilities within their own communities
A strategy focused solely on curative surgical intervention for disability
A program limited strictly to urban tertiary care centers
An approach that excludes family and community involvement
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Community-based rehabilitation mobilizes local resources, family, and community participation to support the rehabilitation, inclusion, and improved quality of life of persons with disabilities within their own communities, rather than relying solely on centralized institutional care.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The 'sentinel surveillance' method of disease monitoring involves which approach?
o: Mandatory reporting from every single healthcare facility in a country without exception
Random sampling of the general population with no fixed reporting sites
Surveillance limited exclusively to hospital-based inpatient data
Systematic data collection from selected reporting sites chosen to represent the broader population or high-risk groups
A one-time cross-sectional survey with no ongoing data collection
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Sentinel surveillance relies on a selected network of reporting sites (chosen for their representativeness, high-risk population, or capacity for quality data) to monitor disease trends efficiently, rather than attempting universal case reporting.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Passive disease surveillance systems, as distinguished from active surveillance, are characterized by which feature?
o: Public health staff actively visit facilities and communities to search for cases
Surveillance conducted only through household surveys
Data collected exclusively via laboratory testing initiated by public health authorities
Health facilities routinely report cases as part of standard reporting procedures without active case-finding by public health staff
A system that requires no data collection at any level
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Passive surveillance relies on routine reporting from health facilities and providers without active efforts by public health staff to seek out cases, in contrast to active surveillance, which involves proactive case-finding efforts.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The 'demographic transition' theory describes population change through successive stages primarily driven by changes in which two vital rates?
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Demographic transition theory describes the historical shift of populations through stages characterized by changing patterns of birth and death rates, progressing from high birth/high death rates to low birth/low death rates as societies develop.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The 'total fertility rate' (TFR) is defined as which of the following?
o: The total number of live births in a country in one year
The average number of children a woman would bear during her reproductive lifespan under current age-specific fertility rates
The proportion of married women of reproductive age
The number of children born per 1,000 population
The maternal mortality ratio of a population
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Total fertility rate estimates the average number of live births a woman would have during her reproductive years if she experienced the current age-specific fertility rates throughout her childbearing life, a key indicator of population growth potential.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: A total fertility rate of approximately 2.1 in a developed country is often referred to as which of the following?
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Replacement-level fertility (approximately 2.1 in most developed countries, accounting for mortality before reproductive age) is the total fertility rate at which a population exactly replaces itself from one generation to the next, without migration.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Maternal mortality ratio is defined as the number of maternal deaths per how many live births, per WHO convention?
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Maternal mortality ratio is conventionally expressed as the number of maternal deaths occurring during pregnancy, childbirth, or within 42 days postpartum, per 100,000 live births in a given period.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Infant mortality rate is defined as which of the following?
o: Number of deaths of children under 5 years per 1,000 live births
Number of deaths of infants under 1 year of age per 1,000 live births in a given year
Number of stillbirths per 1,000 total births
Number of neonatal deaths per 1,000 population
Number of maternal deaths per 1,000 live births
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Infant mortality rate measures deaths of children before their first birthday per 1,000 live births in a given year, serving as a key indicator of overall population health, healthcare access, and socioeconomic development.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: 'Neonatal mortality rate' specifically measures infant deaths occurring within which time period after birth?
o: The first 7 days of life exclusively
The first year of life entirely
From birth to 5 years of age
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Neonatal mortality rate specifically captures deaths occurring within the first 28 completed days of life, a period that accounts for a substantial proportion of overall infant mortality, often further subdivided into early (0-7 days) and late (8-28 days) neonatal periods.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The under-5 mortality rate is considered a particularly sensitive indicator of which broader aspect of population health and development?
o: Only the quality of a country's surgical services
Exclusively the prevalence of genetic disorders
Only vaccination coverage against a single specific disease
The literacy rate of adult women exclusively
Overall socioeconomic development, nutrition, and access to basic health services in a population
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: The under-5 mortality rate reflects a broad range of factors including nutrition, sanitation, maternal health, healthcare access, and socioeconomic conditions, making it one of the most widely used composite indicators of a population's overall health and development status.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: A national immunization program achieving 'cold chain failure' at a storage facility would most likely result in which consequence?
o: No effect on vaccine quality at all
Reduced vaccine potency/efficacy due to improper temperature exposure
Automatic conversion of live vaccines into inactivated vaccines
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Exposure of vaccines to temperatures outside the recommended range (too hot or too cold, depending on the vaccine) due to cold chain failure can degrade vaccine potency, reducing the immune protection conferred upon administration.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Which of the following best describes the concept of 'health equity' in public health?
o: Providing exactly equal resources to every individual regardless of need
Ensuring all citizens have identical income levels
A focus exclusively on urban populations
Equal distribution of hospitals regardless of population density
The absence of avoidable, unfair, or remediable differences in health status among population groups
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Health equity refers to the absence of unjust and avoidable differences in health outcomes between population groups, requiring resource allocation and interventions tailored to need (which may mean unequal resource distribution) rather than strict numerical equality.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: 'Social determinants of health' refer to which of the following?
o: Only genetic factors influencing disease risk
The conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age, which influence health outcomes
Exclusively the availability of hospital beds
Only an individual's personal lifestyle choices
Purely biological factors unrelated to social context
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Social determinants of health encompass the broader social, economic, and environmental conditions — such as income, education, employment, and living conditions — that significantly shape health outcomes beyond individual behavior or biology alone.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Health education aimed at behavior change is most effective when it incorporates which of the following approaches, per established health promotion theory?
o: A single generic message delivered identically to all populations regardless of context
Exclusive reliance on fear-based messaging without follow-up support
One-time mass communication with no reinforcement
Ignoring existing community health beliefs and practices
Understanding the target community's beliefs, culture, and using participatory, tailored communication strategies
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Effective health education draws on behavioral theories emphasizing culturally sensitive, participatory approaches that consider existing community beliefs and practices, generally proving more successful than generic, one-size-fits-all messaging.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The 'epidemiological transition' describes a population-level shift in the leading causes of morbidity and mortality typically from which pattern to which?
o: Predominantly infectious/communicable diseases to predominantly non-communicable/chronic diseases
Predominantly chronic diseases to predominantly infectious diseases
No change in disease patterns over time
A shift limited only to mental health disorders
Exclusively a shift in maternal mortality causes
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: The epidemiological transition describes the pattern seen with socioeconomic development in which the predominant burden of disease shifts from infectious and communicable diseases toward non-communicable, chronic diseases (e.g., cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes).

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The 'Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative' launched by WHO/UNICEF primarily promotes which practice?
o: Routine formula feeding for all newborns
Early separation of mother and newborn as standard practice
Support for early initiation and exclusive breastfeeding in maternity facilities
Delaying breastfeeding until 24 hours after birth
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: The Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative promotes evidence-based maternity care practices — including early skin-to-skin contact and support for early initiation and exclusive breastfeeding — to improve infant health outcomes.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: Micronutrient deficiency of iodine during pregnancy poses which serious risk to the developing fetus if left uncorrected?
o: Isolated dental caries in the child later in life
Exclusively maternal hair loss with no fetal effect
Irreversible intellectual disability (cretinism) and impaired neurodevelopment
Only mild, fully reversible skin changes in the newborn
No known effect on fetal development
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: Severe maternal iodine deficiency during pregnancy can result in irreversible fetal neurodevelopmental damage, manifesting as cretinism (severe intellectual disability, deaf-mutism, and motor impairment), making iodine sufficiency crucial during pregnancy.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: School health programs commonly include periodic health screening of students primarily to detect which category of conditions early?
o: Only genetic disorders requiring advanced testing
Vision and hearing defects, nutritional deficiencies, and other treatable conditions affecting learning and development
Exclusively dental conditions with no other screening component
Adult-onset chronic diseases irrelevant to the school-age population
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: School health screening programs aim to detect common, often correctable conditions such as vision and hearing impairments, malnutrition, and other health issues that can affect a child's learning and development, enabling timely referral and intervention.

community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.s: The 'catch-up' immunization schedule is used in which clinical scenario?
o: For healthy children who have received all vaccines on time, as a routine booster
Only for adult travelers visiting endemic areas
Exclusively for vaccines administered at birth
When a vaccine has expired and needs replacement with a different product
When a child has missed one or more scheduled vaccine doses and needs a modified schedule to complete the required series
community-medicine-and-public-health/pre.e: A catch-up immunization schedule provides guidance for administering remaining doses to children who have fallen behind on the routine schedule, ensuring they still achieve full protection through an appropriately spaced series of catch-up doses.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: The most important single measure for preventing waterborne diseases in a community is generally considered to be which of the following?
o: Mass antibiotic prophylaxis of the population
Routine vaccination against all enteric pathogens
Individual water boiling only, without infrastructure improvement
Provision of safe drinking water and proper sanitation/sewage disposal
Construction of hospitals in every village
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Ensuring access to safe drinking water combined with adequate sanitation and sewage disposal remains the single most effective public health measure for preventing the transmission of waterborne and fecal-oral diseases at a population level.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Chlorination of drinking water supplies is a widely used method of disinfection primarily effective against which category of microorganisms?
o: All protozoan cysts, including Cryptosporidium, with complete effectiveness
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Chlorination effectively inactivates most bacteria and many viruses in water supplies, though certain protozoan cysts (e.g., Cryptosporidium, Giardia) are relatively resistant to standard chlorine doses and may require filtration or other treatment.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: The 'biological oxygen demand' (BOD) of water is used as an indicator of which of the following?
o: The exact bacterial species present in a water sample
The degree of organic pollution in water, based on oxygen consumed by microorganisms decomposing organic matter
The temperature of a water body
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: BOD measures the amount of dissolved oxygen consumed by microorganisms in decomposing organic matter over a specified period, serving as an indirect indicator of the degree of organic pollution in a water sample.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Fluoridation of community water supplies is a public health measure primarily aimed at preventing which condition?
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Controlled fluoridation of drinking water at an optimal concentration is an established, cost-effective public health measure for reducing the incidence of dental caries in a population, though excessive fluoride intake can itself cause dental/skeletal fluorosis.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: 'Eutrophication' of a water body refers to which environmental process?
o: The natural purification of water through sedimentation
A method of water disinfection using ozone
The natural cooling of surface water temperature
Excessive nutrient enrichment (commonly nitrogen and phosphorus) leading to algal blooms and oxygen depletion
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Eutrophication results from excessive input of nutrients (especially nitrogen and phosphorus, often from agricultural runoff and sewage) into a water body, promoting excessive algal growth that depletes dissolved oxygen upon decomposition, harming aquatic ecosystems.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Air pollution from particulate matter with an aerodynamic diameter of 2.5 micrometers or less (PM2.5) is of particular health concern primarily because of which characteristic?
o: Its complete inability to be inhaled by humans
Its exclusive association with only cosmetic skin effects
Its ability to penetrate deep into the alveoli and enter the bloodstream, contributing to cardiovascular and respiratory disease
Its role solely in causing visible smog with no health effects
Its rapid degradation in the atmosphere within seconds
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: PM2.5 particles are small enough to penetrate deep into the alveolar spaces of the lungs and even enter systemic circulation, contributing significantly to cardiovascular disease, respiratory illness, and increased mortality.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: The 'greenhouse effect' contributing to global climate change is primarily driven by increased atmospheric concentration of which class of gases?
o: Inert noble gases such as argon and neon
Ozone-depleting substances exclusively, unrelated to warming
Water vapor exclusively with no contribution from other gases
Greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Greenhouse gases, notably carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide, trap infrared radiation in the atmosphere, driving the enhanced greenhouse effect responsible for observed global climate change and warming trends.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Depletion of the stratospheric ozone layer, historically linked to chlorofluorocarbon (CFC) emissions, primarily increases human health risk from which exposure?
o: Increased risk of carbon monoxide poisoning
Increased risk of heavy metal toxicity
Increased ultraviolet (UV) radiation reaching the earth's surface, raising skin cancer and cataract risk
Increased risk of waterborne disease transmission
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Ozone layer depletion allows greater penetration of harmful ultraviolet radiation to the earth's surface, increasing the risk of skin cancers, cataracts, and other UV-related health effects in exposed populations.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Municipal solid waste management hierarchies generally prioritize which approach as most preferable from an environmental and public health standpoint?
o: Open dumping as the primary and most preferred method
Indiscriminate incineration without any emission controls
Waste reduction and recycling before disposal methods such as landfilling
Direct discharge of solid waste into rivers
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Modern waste management hierarchies prioritize source reduction and recycling/reuse as the most environmentally sound approaches, with controlled treatment and sanitary landfilling as less preferred but necessary options, and open dumping considered the least acceptable practice.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Biomedical (hospital) waste, including sharps and infectious material, requires specific segregation and disposal primarily to prevent which risk?
o: Reduction in the number of hospital beds
Transmission of infection to waste handlers, the public, and the environment
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Proper segregation, handling, and disposal of biomedical waste (sharps, infectious, pathological, and chemical waste) is essential to prevent transmission of infections to waste handlers, the general public, and to avoid environmental contamination.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Occupational exposure to asbestos fibers is most strongly associated with which serious long-term health consequence?
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Chronic occupational exposure to asbestos fibers is causally linked to mesothelioma (a malignant tumor of the pleura/peritoneum) and asbestosis (progressive pulmonary fibrosis), both with long latency periods after exposure.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: 'Silicosis,' an occupational lung disease affecting miners and stone workers, results from chronic inhalation of which substance?
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Silicosis is a progressive, irreversible fibrotic lung disease caused by chronic inhalation of crystalline silica dust, classically affecting workers in mining, quarrying, sandblasting, and stone-cutting occupations.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: 'Byssinosis,' an occupational respiratory disease historically termed 'Monday fever,' is caused by chronic occupational exposure to which substance?
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Byssinosis results from chronic inhalation of cotton (and related textile fiber) dust, classically causing chest tightness that is most pronounced at the start of the working week ('Monday fever') among textile industry workers.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: 'Coal workers' pneumoconiosis' (black lung disease) results from chronic occupational inhalation of which substance?
o: Silica dust exclusively without coal exposure
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis results from long-term inhalation of coal dust, leading to characteristic pulmonary nodules and, in advanced cases, progressive massive fibrosis among coal miners.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Chronic occupational exposure to lead is most classically associated with toxicity in which combination of organ systems?
o: Exclusively the reproductive system with no other organ involvement
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Chronic occupational lead exposure classically affects multiple organ systems, causing microcytic anemia (impaired heme synthesis), peripheral neuropathy and encephalopathy, and chronic nephropathy, among other effects.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: 'Noise-induced hearing loss,' a common occupational health hazard in industrial settings, typically first affects hearing at which characteristic audiometric frequency?
o: Around 8000 Hz exclusively with no involvement of mid-frequencies
Uniformly across all frequencies from the outset
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Noise-induced hearing loss classically produces a characteristic audiometric notch around 4000 Hz before progressing to affect a broader frequency range with continued exposure, an important early diagnostic clue in occupational hearing surveillance.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Permissible exposure limits (PELs) and threshold limit values (TLVs) for occupational chemical exposures are established primarily to achieve which purpose?
o: Guarantee complete elimination of all risk regardless of exposure duration
Define the maximum concentration of a substance to which most workers can be exposed without adverse health effects
Set the minimum wage for hazardous occupations
Determine the retirement age for exposed workers
Establish criminal penalties for employers unrelated to health outcomes
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Permissible exposure limits and threshold limit values are occupational health standards defining the maximum airborne concentration of a substance to which nearly all workers can be repeatedly exposed without adverse health effects, guiding workplace safety regulation.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: The hierarchy of controls in occupational health and safety places which intervention as the most effective (preferred) approach to hazard control?
o: Provision of personal protective equipment (PPE) as the primary and only measure
Administrative controls such as work rotation alone
Engineering controls used only as a last resort
Reliance solely on worker training without any physical changes
Elimination or substitution of the hazard at its source
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: The hierarchy of controls ranks elimination and substitution of the hazard as the most effective interventions, followed by engineering controls, then administrative controls, with personal protective equipment considered the last line of defense due to its reliance on correct and consistent use.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Pre-employment and periodic medical examinations in occupational health programs primarily serve which purpose?
o: Detecting early signs of occupation-related disease and assessing fitness for specific job tasks
Replacing the need for any workplace safety measures
Screening exclusively for unrelated genetic conditions with no occupational relevance
Eliminating the need for any hazard control measures at the workplace
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Occupational health surveillance through pre-placement and periodic medical examinations helps detect early signs of work-related disease, monitor the effectiveness of control measures, and assess a worker's fitness for specific hazardous tasks.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: The 'sick building syndrome' refers to which occupational/environmental health phenomenon?
o: A structural engineering defect causing building collapse
An infectious outbreak confined to a single building with an identified pathogen
A regulatory classification for condemned buildings
A cluster of nonspecific symptoms (headache, fatigue, irritation) experienced by occupants of a building, without an identifiable single cause, that improve away from the building
A term describing buildings contaminated exclusively with asbestos
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Sick building syndrome describes a constellation of nonspecific symptoms experienced by building occupants, often linked to poor ventilation, indoor air pollutants, or other environmental factors, that characteristically improve when the person leaves the building.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: 'Legionnaires' disease,' associated with contaminated water systems such as air conditioning cooling towers, is caused by which organism?
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Legionnaires' disease is a severe pneumonia caused by Legionella pneumophila, which proliferates in warm, stagnant water systems such as cooling towers, water heaters, and air conditioning systems, transmitted via inhalation of contaminated aerosols.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Heat-related illness in occupational settings, ranging from heat cramps to heat stroke, is best prevented primarily through which combination of measures?
o: Complete avoidance of any physical activity in all climates
Providing only cold beverages with no other intervention
Relying solely on individual worker judgment without organizational policy
Adequate hydration, scheduled rest breaks, acclimatization, and engineering/administrative controls to reduce heat exposure
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Prevention of occupational heat illness relies on a combination of adequate hydration, work-rest cycles, gradual heat acclimatization, and engineering/administrative controls (e.g., shading, ventilation, scheduling) to reduce cumulative heat stress.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Radiation protection in occupational settings follows the ALARA principle, which stands for which concept?
o: As Low As Reasonably Achievable exposure to ionizing radiation
Automatic Local Alarm for Radiation Accidents
Annual Limit on Absorbed Radioactive Amounts only
A Legislated Approach to Radioactive Assessment
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) is a foundational radiation protection principle guiding efforts to minimize occupational and public exposure to ionizing radiation to the lowest level reasonably achievable, considering economic and social factors.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Ergonomic hazards in the workplace, such as repetitive strain injuries, are best prevented through which primary approach?
o: Increasing the speed of repetitive tasks to reduce total exposure time
Eliminating all rest breaks to increase productivity
Workstation and task design modification to reduce awkward postures and repetitive movements
Providing only verbal warnings without physical changes to the workplace
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Ergonomic intervention through proper workstation and task design (adjusting posture, reducing repetitive strain, appropriate tool design) is the primary and most effective approach to preventing musculoskeletal disorders in occupational settings.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: The Minamata disease outbreak in Japan, characterized by severe neurological damage, was ultimately traced to environmental contamination with which substance?
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Minamata disease resulted from consumption of fish and shellfish contaminated with methylmercury discharged into Minamata Bay by a local chemical factory, causing severe and often irreversible neurological damage in affected populations.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: The Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984, one of the world's worst industrial disasters, resulted from the accidental release of which toxic gas?
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: The Bhopal disaster resulted from the accidental release of methyl isocyanate gas from a pesticide manufacturing plant, causing immediate mass casualties and long-term health consequences among the exposed population.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: 'Itai-itai disease,' a painful bone disease documented in Japan, was linked to chronic environmental exposure to which heavy metal?
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Itai-itai disease resulted from chronic cadmium exposure through contaminated rice grown in cadmium-polluted irrigation water, causing severe bone pain, osteomalacia, and renal tubular dysfunction.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Industrial hygiene monitoring for airborne contaminants in a workplace typically involves which type of sampling to best estimate an individual worker's exposure?
o: Only fixed-area sampling at a single stationary point in the facility
Sampling conducted exclusively outside the facility perimeter
Sampling performed only once per year regardless of process changes
Personal air sampling using a monitor worn by the worker in the breathing zone
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Personal air sampling, using monitoring devices worn within a worker's breathing zone, provides the most accurate estimate of individual exposure to airborne contaminants, compared to fixed-area sampling which reflects general workplace air quality.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Which of the following best describes 'vector control' as an environmental health strategy against diseases such as malaria and dengue?
o: Treating only human cases after they occur, without addressing the vector
Relying exclusively on vaccination with no environmental intervention
Eliminating all animal reservoir hosts of the disease
Reducing vector breeding sites and vector populations through source reduction, larvicides, and insecticide use
Focusing exclusively on improving human nutrition
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Vector control strategies target the mosquito or other arthropod vector directly through measures such as source reduction (eliminating breeding sites), larviciding, indoor residual spraying, and insecticide-treated nets, reducing disease transmission at its source.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Indoor air pollution from biomass fuel combustion (wood, dung, crop residue) for cooking is a major public health concern in low-resource settings primarily due to which health effect?
o: Increased risk of chronic respiratory disease and acute respiratory infections, particularly in women and young children
Complete absence of any health risk
Exclusive association with skin cancer only
Only affecting outdoor air quality with no indoor exposure
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Indoor air pollution from biomass fuel combustion, often in poorly ventilated kitchens, significantly increases the risk of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, acute respiratory infections, and other health effects, disproportionately affecting women and young children who spend more time near cooking areas.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Environmental sanitation programs addressing excreta disposal in rural areas most commonly promote which basic infrastructure intervention?
o: Open defecation as an acceptable interim practice
Construction and use of sanitary latrines
Direct discharge of excreta into nearby water bodies
Exclusive reliance on individual household water boiling
Elimination of all rural sanitation programs in favor of urban focus only
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Promoting the construction and consistent use of sanitary latrines is a cornerstone environmental sanitation intervention for reducing fecal-oral disease transmission in communities lacking sewage infrastructure.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: The 'safe drinking water' standard set by WHO guidelines primarily specifies acceptable limits for which categories of contaminants?
o: Only the water's color, with no other parameters considered
Microbiological, chemical, and physical parameters that could pose a health risk
Only the presence of dissolved oxygen
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: WHO drinking water quality guidelines establish acceptable limits across microbiological (pathogens), chemical (e.g., heavy metals, nitrates), and physical/aesthetic parameters to ensure water is safe for human consumption.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: 'Sanitary survey' of a water source is conducted primarily to identify which type of risk?
o: The exact chemical composition of the water using advanced spectroscopy
Potential sources of contamination and sanitary risk factors affecting water quality at or near the source
The market price of water treatment chemicals
The legal ownership status of the water source
The aesthetic appearance of the surrounding landscape only
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: A sanitary survey is an on-site inspection assessing potential sources of contamination (such as nearby latrines, animal waste, or improper well construction) that could compromise the safety of a water source, complementing laboratory water quality testing.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Occupational exposure to benzene, a solvent used in various industries, is most classically associated with which serious hematological consequence?
o: Aplastic anemia and acute myeloid leukemia
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Chronic occupational benzene exposure is a well-established cause of bone marrow toxicity, including aplastic anemia and an increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia, due to its myelotoxic and carcinogenic effects on hematopoietic stem cells.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Vibration-induced white finger (hand-arm vibration syndrome), an occupational condition seen in workers using vibrating tools, primarily affects which physiological system?
o: Peripheral vascular and neurological systems of the hands and fingers
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Hand-arm vibration syndrome results from prolonged occupational exposure to vibrating hand tools, causing vasospasm (Raynaud-like white finger episodes) and peripheral nerve damage in the hands and fingers of affected workers.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: 'Decompression sickness' (the bends), an occupational hazard for divers and workers in compressed-air environments, results from which underlying mechanism?
o: Formation of nitrogen gas bubbles in blood and tissues upon rapid decompression
Excessive oxygen toxicity to the lungs
Direct mechanical injury from water pressure alone
Carbon monoxide accumulation in diving equipment
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Decompression sickness occurs when dissolved nitrogen gas comes out of solution and forms bubbles in blood and tissues during rapid ascent/decompression, causing joint pain, neurological symptoms, and other complications, hence the need for gradual staged decompression.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Occupational exposure to vinyl chloride monomer, used in PVC plastic manufacturing, is most specifically associated with increased risk of which malignancy?
o: Bladder cancer as the primary association
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Chronic occupational exposure to vinyl chloride monomer is specifically linked to hepatic angiosarcoma, a rare malignant tumor of the liver's blood vessels, among workers in PVC manufacturing.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: The concept of 'threshold limit value - time weighted average' (TLV-TWA) for occupational exposure represents which measurement?
o: The maximum instantaneous exposure permissible at any single moment
A limit that applies only to exposures lasting less than one minute
The average airborne concentration of a substance permissible for a normal 8-hour workday over a 40-hour work week
A value applicable only to non-occupational environmental exposure
A single lifetime cumulative dose limit expressed in total grams absorbed
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: TLV-TWA represents the time-weighted average airborne concentration of a substance to which workers can be repeatedly exposed during a conventional 8-hour workday and 40-hour work week without adverse health effects.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: 'Green building' and workplace design initiatives aimed at improving indoor air quality primarily focus on which intervention?
o: Eliminating all windows to reduce outdoor pollution entry
Increasing the use of volatile organic compound-emitting materials
Sealing buildings completely with no air exchange
Adequate ventilation and reduction of indoor pollutant sources
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Green building design for improved indoor air quality emphasizes adequate ventilation, source control (reducing use of materials that off-gas pollutants), and appropriate humidity management to minimize indoor air contaminant levels and occupant health risks.

community-medicine-and-public-health/env.s: Environmental impact assessment (EIA) conducted prior to major industrial or infrastructure projects primarily serves which regulatory purpose?
o: Guaranteeing project approval regardless of environmental risk
Replacing the need for any occupational health and safety measures during construction
Assessing only the projected financial profitability of the project
Evaluating exclusively the aesthetic appearance of the proposed structure
Identifying and mitigating potential adverse environmental and health effects of a proposed project before approval
community-medicine-and-public-health/env.e: Environmental impact assessment is a regulatory and planning tool used to systematically identify, predict, and mitigate the potential environmental and public health consequences of a proposed project before it proceeds, informing decision-making and approval conditions.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The World Health Organization defines a 'health system' as encompassing which of the following?
o: Only hospitals and clinics providing curative care
All organizations, people, and actions whose primary intent is to promote, restore, or maintain health
Only the ministry of health and government bodies
Only private healthcare providers and insurance companies
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: WHO's broad definition of a health system includes all organizations, institutions, resources, and people whose primary purpose is to improve health, encompassing public and private providers, financing mechanisms, and governance structures.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The 'building blocks' framework of health systems, as described by WHO, includes which of the following as one of its six core components?
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: The WHO health systems building blocks framework identifies six core components: service delivery, health workforce, health information systems, medical products/technologies, financing, and leadership/governance.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Universal health coverage (UHC), a global health policy goal, is defined as ensuring which of the following for all people?
o: Free healthcare provided exclusively by private hospitals
Access to needed quality health services without incurring financial hardship
Access limited only to emergency care
Coverage restricted to communicable diseases only
Health insurance available only to formally employed workers
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Universal health coverage aims to ensure that all individuals and communities receive the quality health services they need without suffering financial hardship, encompassing promotive, preventive, curative, rehabilitative, and palliative care.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: 'Out-of-pocket expenditure' as a method of healthcare financing is generally considered problematic primarily because it can lead to which consequence?
o: Complete elimination of any healthcare costs for patients
Guaranteed equitable access to care for all income groups
Automatic government reimbursement in every case
Catastrophic health expenditure and financial hardship, particularly for poorer households
Elimination of the need for health insurance entirely
