community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: High reliance on out-of-pocket payments at the point of care disproportionately burdens poorer households, often resulting in catastrophic health expenditure, delayed care-seeking, or medical impoverishment, undermining equitable access to healthcare.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Community health workers, as a component of primary health care delivery, primarily serve which function?
o: Bridging the gap between formal health services and communities, providing basic health education and services at the local level
Replacing the need for any physician involvement in a health system
Managing national health insurance schemes exclusively
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Community health workers, typically trained local residents, extend the reach of the formal health system by providing basic health education, preventive services, and referral linkages, particularly valuable in underserved and remote areas.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Antenatal care visits during pregnancy primarily aim to achieve which key objective?
o: Early identification and management of pregnancy-related risk factors and complications
Determining the exact date of conception with certainty
Replacing the need for skilled birth attendance at delivery
Eliminating the need for postnatal care entirely
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Antenatal care aims to monitor maternal and fetal well-being throughout pregnancy, enabling early detection and management of complications such as hypertensive disorders, anemia, and malpresentation, thereby improving maternal and perinatal outcomes.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The WHO currently recommends a minimum of how many antenatal care contacts during a normal, uncomplicated pregnancy for a positive pregnancy experience?
o: Zero contacts if the woman feels well
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: The updated WHO antenatal care model recommends a minimum of eight contacts throughout pregnancy to reduce perinatal mortality and improve women's overall experience of care, an increase from the previously recommended four-visit model.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: 'Skilled birth attendance,' a key strategy for reducing maternal mortality, refers to delivery being conducted by which type of provider?
o: Any family member present at the time of delivery
A traditional birth attendant without formal medical training
No attendant at all, with delivery occurring unassisted
A pharmacist dispensing medication during labor
An accredited health professional trained to manage normal deliveries and identify/manage/refer complications
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Skilled birth attendance refers to delivery conducted by an accredited health professional (midwife, doctor, or nurse) with the competency to manage normal childbirth and to identify, manage, and refer complications, a key evidence-based strategy for reducing maternal and neonatal mortality.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The 'partograph,' a graphical tool used during labor monitoring, is primarily designed to help detect which complication early?
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: The partograph plots cervical dilation and other parameters against time during labor, allowing early graphical identification of abnormally slow progress (prolonged or obstructed labor) that requires timely intervention.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Postpartum hemorrhage, a leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide, is most commonly caused by which underlying mechanism?
o: Uterine atony (failure of the uterus to contract adequately after delivery)
Placenta previa diagnosed antenatally with elective cesarean
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Uterine atony, the failure of the uterine musculature to contract effectively after delivery of the placenta, is the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage, classically remembered as the first of the '4 Ts' (Tone, Trauma, Tissue, Thrombin).

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Active management of the third stage of labor, a strategy to prevent postpartum hemorrhage, typically includes administration of which class of medication?
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Active management of the third stage of labor includes prophylactic administration of a uterotonic agent (most commonly oxytocin) immediately after delivery, along with controlled cord traction, significantly reducing the risk of postpartum hemorrhage.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Family planning programs, by enabling birth spacing and limiting unintended pregnancies, contribute to reducing maternal mortality primarily through which mechanism?
o: Guaranteeing complete elimination of all pregnancy complications
Reducing the total number of pregnancies (and therefore cumulative lifetime risk) a woman is exposed to, including high-risk pregnancies
Eliminating the need for any antenatal care
Increasing the total fertility rate of the population
Replacing the need for skilled birth attendance
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: By enabling women to avoid unintended and high-risk pregnancies (including those at very young or advanced maternal age, or closely spaced), family planning reduces the cumulative number of pregnancies a woman undergoes, thereby reducing her overall lifetime risk of pregnancy-related death.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The 'three delays model' in maternal mortality frameworks identifies delay in deciding to seek care, delay in reaching a health facility, and which third delay?
o: Delay in registering the birth certificate
Delay in receiving adequate care once at the health facility
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: The three delays model identifies delays in (1) deciding to seek care, (2) reaching an appropriate health facility, and (3) receiving adequate care once at the facility, as key contributing factors to preventable maternal deaths.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Which of the following is classified as a 'direct' obstetric cause of maternal death, as opposed to an 'indirect' cause?
o: Pre-existing cardiac disease aggravated by pregnancy
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Direct obstetric deaths result from complications of pregnancy, labor, or the puerperium itself (e.g., postpartum hemorrhage, eclampsia, obstructed labor), whereas indirect deaths result from a pre-existing disease or a disease that develops during pregnancy but is aggravated by physiological changes of pregnancy (e.g., cardiac disease, malaria).

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Eclampsia, a leading direct cause of maternal mortality, is defined as which of the following?
o: Mild elevation of blood pressure without proteinuria
Occurrence of generalized seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia, not attributable to other causes
Rupture of the uterus during labor
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Eclampsia is defined as the onset of generalized tonic-clonic seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia (hypertension with proteinuria or other severe features), representing a life-threatening obstetric emergency requiring prompt management.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice for which obstetric indication?
o: Prevention and treatment of eclamptic seizures
Induction of labor as a primary agent
Treatment of postpartum hemorrhage as first-line therapy
Prevention of preterm labor exclusively with no role in eclampsia
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Magnesium sulfate is the evidence-based drug of choice for both preventing eclamptic seizures in women with severe pre-eclampsia and for treating active eclamptic seizures, significantly reducing maternal morbidity and mortality.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The concept of 'birth spacing,' recommending an interval between pregnancies, is generally advised to be at least how long to optimize maternal and child health outcomes?
o: Pregnancies should always be spaced less than 1 year apart
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: WHO guidance generally recommends an interval of at least 2 years between a live birth and the next pregnancy to reduce risks of adverse maternal, perinatal, and infant outcomes associated with short inter-pregnancy intervals.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Contraceptive methods are broadly classified into reversible and permanent (irreversible) methods; which of the following is an example of a permanent contraceptive method?
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Tubal ligation (female sterilization) and vasectomy (male sterilization) are permanent, surgical contraceptive methods intended for individuals or couples who have completed their desired family size, distinct from reversible hormonal or barrier methods.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The intrauterine device (IUD) as a contraceptive method primarily acts through which mechanism?
o: Local inflammatory/foreign body reaction in the endometrium impairing fertilization and implantation (with copper IUDs also being spermicidal)
Systemic suppression of ovulation exclusively in every type of IUD
Permanent blockage of the fallopian tubes
Hormonal suppression of the entire menstrual cycle in all types
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: IUDs primarily act locally by inducing an inflammatory/foreign body reaction within the endometrium that impairs sperm function and prevents fertilization/implantation, with copper IUDs providing additional spermicidal activity through copper ion release.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Which reproductive/maternal health indicator specifically reflects the proportion of deliveries attended by a trained health professional in a population?
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Skilled birth attendance rate measures the proportion of total live births in a population attended by personnel trained to provide safe delivery care, a key process indicator for maternal and newborn health system performance.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: 'Contraceptive prevalence rate' is defined as which of the following measures?
o: The total number of contraceptive products manufactured annually
The percentage of pregnancies that are unintended
The number of maternal deaths averted by family planning
The average number of children born per woman
The percentage of women of reproductive age (or their partners) currently using a method of contraception
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Contraceptive prevalence rate measures the proportion of women (typically of reproductive age, in a union) who are currently using, or whose partner is using, at least one method of contraception, an important indicator of family planning program reach.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The 'referral system' in a tiered health system is designed to achieve which purpose?
o: Eliminating the need for primary health care facilities entirely
Restricting all patients to tertiary care regardless of condition severity
Preventing any communication between different levels of care
Ensuring that only wealthy patients can access specialist care
Ensuring patients receive appropriate care at the correct level of the health system, from primary to higher levels of complexity as needed
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: A well-functioning referral system ensures that patients move appropriately between levels of the health system (primary, secondary, tertiary) based on the complexity of their condition, optimizing resource use and improving continuity and quality of care.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Health financing mechanisms based on 'social health insurance' typically rely primarily on which funding source?
o: Mandatory contributions from employers and employees (payroll-based premiums)
General taxation exclusively with no dedicated contributions
Out-of-pocket payment at the point of service exclusively
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Social health insurance schemes are typically financed through mandatory, often payroll-based, contributions from employers and employees, pooling risk and providing a dedicated revenue stream for covered health services.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: 'Catastrophic health expenditure' is generally defined in health financing literature as out-of-pocket health spending exceeding what threshold of a household's income/capacity to pay?
o: A defined high percentage threshold (commonly cited around 10% or more of total household income/expenditure)
Only expenditure exceeding the entire household's total assets
A fixed absolute dollar amount identical worldwide regardless of income
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Catastrophic health expenditure is commonly defined as out-of-pocket health spending exceeding a substantial proportion (often cited as approximately 10% or more) of total household income or expenditure, indicating significant financial hardship due to healthcare costs.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The concept of 'health system resilience' refers to a system's capacity to do which of the following?
o: Guarantee zero disease outbreaks will ever occur
Eliminate the need for any emergency preparedness planning
Focus exclusively on curative hospital-based services during a crisis
Absorb, adapt to, and recover from shocks such as disease outbreaks or disasters while maintaining core functions
Operate identically regardless of any external stressor
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Health system resilience describes the capacity of a health system to anticipate, absorb, adapt to, and recover from shocks (such as pandemics, natural disasters, or conflict) while continuing to provide essential health services.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer, and chronic respiratory disease are collectively responsible for which general trend in global mortality?
o: An increasing share of global mortality, now representing the majority of deaths worldwide
A negligible and declining share of global mortality
Mortality exclusively confined to high-income countries
No significant contribution to global disease burden
Mortality limited only to elderly populations above age 90
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Non-communicable diseases now account for the majority of global deaths, with an increasing burden also observed in low- and middle-income countries, reflecting the ongoing epidemiological transition and necessitating integrated NCD prevention and control strategies.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The 'four modifiable risk factors' most commonly targeted in global non-communicable disease prevention strategies include tobacco use, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, and which fourth factor?
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Global NCD prevention frameworks (e.g., WHO's Global Action Plan) commonly target four major modifiable behavioral risk factors: tobacco use, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, and harmful use of alcohol, as these drive the majority of preventable NCD burden.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: 'Health literacy' refers to which capacity of individuals within a population?
o: The ability to read any type of text regardless of subject matter
The ability to obtain, process, and understand basic health information needed to make appropriate health decisions
A measure of a population's overall literacy rate unrelated to health
The number of years of formal schooling completed
A hospital's compliance with regulatory documentation requirements
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Health literacy specifically refers to an individual's capacity to obtain, process, and understand basic health information and services needed to make appropriate health-related decisions, distinct from general literacy.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: District Health Information Systems (DHIS) in health information management primarily serve which function?
o: Routine collection, aggregation, and analysis of health service data to support decision-making at various administrative levels
Providing direct clinical diagnosis to individual patients
Replacing the need for any clinical record-keeping at the facility level
Serving exclusively as a financial billing system with no health data component
Functioning only as a hospital appointment scheduling tool
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: District Health Information Systems aggregate routine health service data from facilities to support monitoring, evaluation, and evidence-based decision-making at district, regional, and national levels of a health system.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: 'Task-shifting' in human resources for health refers to which strategy?
o: Delegating specific clinical tasks from highly trained health workers to those with less training, where appropriate and with adequate supervision
Eliminating all training requirements for healthcare workers
Transferring administrative tasks to patients themselves
Replacing all physicians with unlicensed personnel with no oversight
Randomly reassigning staff without regard to competency
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Task-shifting is a strategy to address health workforce shortages by rationally redistributing specific clinical tasks from more specialized health workers to those with appropriate but less extensive training, supported by adequate training, protocols, and supervision.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The 'continuum of care' concept in maternal, newborn, and child health emphasizes which principle?
o: Providing care only during the intrapartum period, with no antenatal or postnatal component
Focusing exclusively on hospital-based care with no community linkage
Ensuring uninterrupted, linked care from pre-pregnancy through pregnancy, childbirth, postnatal period, and childhood
Limiting care exclusively to the neonatal period
Providing care only to first-time mothers
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: The continuum of care framework emphasizes seamless, linked service provision across time (pre-pregnancy to childhood) and place (community to hospital), recognizing that gaps at any stage can compromise maternal and child health outcomes.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: 'Emergency obstetric care' services are classified into basic and comprehensive levels; comprehensive emergency obstetric care specifically adds which capability beyond basic services?
o: Provision of oral rehydration therapy only
Manual removal of the placenta only
Capacity for cesarean section and blood transfusion
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Comprehensive emergency obstetric care includes all basic emergency obstetric functions plus the additional critical capacity to perform surgery (cesarean section) and administer blood transfusion, essential for managing severe obstetric complications.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The Safe Motherhood Initiative, launched internationally to reduce maternal mortality, primarily emphasizes which strategic approach?
o: Focusing exclusively on family planning with no attention to delivery care
Relying solely on traditional birth attendants without skilled care linkage
Addressing only nutritional deficiencies in pregnant women
Strengthening access to skilled care throughout pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period, particularly emergency obstetric care
Limiting interventions strictly to high-income countries
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: The Safe Motherhood Initiative emphasizes a comprehensive strategy centered on ensuring access to skilled care at every stage of pregnancy and childbirth, with particular emphasis on timely access to emergency obstetric care for complications.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: 'Health system governance,' one of the WHO health system building blocks, primarily refers to which function?
o: Direct provision of clinical care to individual patients
Ensuring strategic policy frameworks, oversight, regulation, and accountability within the health system
Training of individual healthcare workers exclusively
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Governance/stewardship, a core health system building block, encompasses the strategic policy direction, regulatory oversight, coalition-building, and accountability mechanisms that guide the functioning of the overall health system.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Which of the following best describes the goal of 'reproductive health' as defined internationally (e.g., at the ICPD Cairo Conference)?
o: Exclusively the prevention of sexually transmitted infections
A concept limited only to fertility treatment services
A term applicable only to married individuals
A state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being in all matters relating to the reproductive system and its functions, not merely the absence of disease
A concept applicable only to women, excluding men's reproductive health
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Reproductive health, as articulated at the 1994 International Conference on Population and Development (Cairo), encompasses comprehensive physical, mental, and social well-being related to the reproductive system, including access to family planning, safe pregnancy and childbirth, and prevention/treatment of reproductive tract infections, applicable to both men and women.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: 'Unmet need for family planning' refers to which population of women?
o: All women of reproductive age regardless of desire for pregnancy
Only women who have never been pregnant
Fertile, sexually active women who wish to delay or avoid pregnancy but are not using any method of contraception
Only women currently using a highly effective contraceptive method
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: Unmet need for family planning describes fecund, sexually active women who want to postpone or limit childbearing but are not using any contraceptive method, an important indicator for targeting family planning program efforts.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Postnatal care visits within the first days to weeks after delivery are important primarily because most maternal and neonatal deaths occur during which period?
o: The first 24-48 hours and first week after delivery
Between 6 months and 1 year after delivery
Exclusively during the antenatal period before delivery
Only after the child reaches school age
Uniformly distributed with no particular high-risk period
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: The majority of maternal and neonatal deaths occur in the immediate postpartum/postnatal period, particularly within the first 24-48 hours and the first week after birth, underscoring the critical importance of early postnatal care contacts.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The concept of 'gatekeeping' in a primary-care-based referral system refers to which function of the primary care provider?
o: Physically restricting patient movement within a hospital
Denying care to all patients regardless of clinical need
Providing only administrative billing services with no clinical role
Replacing the role of specialists entirely
Acting as the first point of contact who coordinates and, where necessary, refers patients to specialist or higher-level care
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: In gatekeeping models, primary care providers serve as the first point of contact for patients, managing most health needs directly and coordinating referrals to specialist or higher-level care only when clinically necessary, helping ensure appropriate and efficient resource use.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: The 'Health Management Information System' (HMIS) in a national health system serves which core function?
o: Direct delivery of clinical care to patients
Training of community health workers exclusively with no data component
Providing legal representation for healthcare providers
Systematic collection, analysis, and use of health data to inform planning, monitoring, and evaluation
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: A Health Management Information System provides the infrastructure and processes for systematically collecting, analyzing, and using health-related data to support evidence-based planning, resource allocation, monitoring, and evaluation across a health system.

community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.s: Which of the following best describes 'essential drugs' or 'essential medicines' as conceptualized by WHO?
o: Only the most expensive, brand-name medications available
Medicines used exclusively in tertiary care hospitals
Medicines that satisfy the priority healthcare needs of a population, selected based on disease prevalence, efficacy, safety, and cost-effectiveness
Medications that require no regulatory approval
Drugs used only for rare, orphan diseases
community-medicine-and-public-health/hea.e: The WHO Essential Medicines concept identifies medicines that satisfy the priority healthcare needs of a population, selected based on disease relevance, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness, forming the basis of national essential medicines lists to guide procurement and rational use.
